patterns.title: Layers
patterns.short_description: Organize responsibilities into ordered abstractions with explicit rules for which layers may use others.
use_when: Responsibilities form a useful abstraction order
Several entry points need the same business rules
Storage or presentation details leak into unrelated components
not_ideal_when: A small operation is already clear as a few functions
Proposed layers only forward unchanged requests
The main changes cut across every proposed horizontal boundary
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with modules, imports, and function calls
example_user_queries: Our website and batch tool keep calculating different totals.
How can we keep database details out of screen code?
We renamed our folders but everything still depends on everything else.
Where should business rules live when several interfaces use them?
Does separating responsibilities mean we need separate servers?
Can a screen read a database directly without bypassing important rules?
How do we make module dependency rules explicit?
Changing how results are displayed keeps breaking storage code.
Our service classes just forward calls and make changes harder.
How can we replace storage without teaching every caller its details?

graphics.alt_text: Closed layering permits presentation to use business logic and business logic to use price access. The open example also permits a direct presentation-to-price-access dependency for a separately defined read-only operation.
graphics.caption: Arrows show allowed dependencies. Closed layers permit adjacent access; the open example deliberately allows an additional lower-layer dependency.

graphics.alt_text: One deployment contains presentation, business logic, and price access in one process. A second deployment keeps presentation and business together but places price access in a separate service, requiring a network protocol.
graphics.caption: The logical ordering does not determine deployment. A remote boundary adds protocol and failure decisions; moving a box does not supply them.

patterns.title: Ports and Adapters
patterns.short_description: Define application-owned ports for meaningful interactions and connect external technologies through replaceable adapters.
use_when: Several interfaces need the same application behavior
Frameworks and external systems obstruct application tests
Storage and provider details spread into business decisions
not_ideal_when: A small program already isolates its stable I/O with a few functions
Proposed ports merely copy a vendor SDK
Additional contracts have no useful variation or testing boundary
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with modules, function calls, and interfaces
example_user_queries: I cannot test our business rules without starting the whole web application.
How can a batch importer use the same behavior as our website?
Our service classes still create database connections themselves.
We want to build application behavior before deciding on a web framework.
How do we keep provider SDK types out of our business code?
Our test doubles pass but the real storage adapter behaves differently.
Who should define the interface when application code needs storage?
Can we replace a database adapter without changing reservation rules?
How can an application call an external service without importing its implementation?
Our controllers contain rules that other entry points keep duplicating.

graphics.alt_text: Console and test drivers enter the same reservation operation. The application calls its own stock port, which can be served by a SQLite adapter or an in-memory substitute selected at startup.
graphics.caption: Arrows show possible calls. Drivers use the same application operation; one selected stock adapter serves the outgoing port. Ports belong to the application.

graphics.alt_text: Runtime calls go from the application to a SQLite adapter through the stock port. The source import goes in the opposite direction: adapters.py imports definitions from application.py, while application.py imports no adapters.
graphics.caption: Runtime calls and source imports are different relationships. The storage implementation is supplied from outside; the application defines the contract it calls.

patterns.title: Microkernel
patterns.short_description: Keep a stable operational core and add specialized capabilities through plug-ins governed by explicit extension contracts.
use_when: A stable product workflow needs independently selected capabilities
Customer variations keep changing central conditionals
Optional features bring dependencies that minimal installations should not need
not_ideal_when: Only configuration values vary
A few fixed choices are clear as ordinary functions or strategies
The proposed core and extension contracts change together on nearly every feature
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with modules, interfaces, and application startup
example_user_queries: Every customer-specific feature requires another change to our central processing function.
We want a small base product with optional capabilities.
How can teams add features without editing the common application workflow?
Installing a simple feature brings dependencies for tools we do not use.
How should we check whether an extension works with this version of our host?
Two extensions register the same name and one silently replaces the other.
Our plug-ins keep importing each other until nothing is optional anymore.
Can we add a new document analysis without changing the report engine?
When should extensions be registered and when should the configured set stop changing?
We split features into modules but a broken extension can still stop the application.

graphics.alt_text: A document request enters the core, which normalizes text and produces the base line count. Through the analyzer contract, the core calls independent word-count and TODO-count plug-ins, then assembles their results.
graphics.caption: Through the analyzer contract, the core calls both configured extensions with the same normalized text. Neither consumes the other's result.

graphics.alt_text: During configuration, the core checks each extension's declared API version and unique identity before registration. The first string input seals the registry. Requests then execute against that fixed set; later registration is rejected.
graphics.caption: This example separates startup registration from request execution. Sealing fixes the configured set; it does not sandbox plug-ins or make their internal state thread-safe.

patterns.title: Pipes and Filters
patterns.short_description: Decompose processing into independent filters connected by one-way streams, with each stage consuming the previous stage's output.
use_when: Processing has successive transformations with explicit data boundaries
Useful stages recur across several processing tasks
Intermediate representations help separate testing and inspection
not_ideal_when: A short stable transformation is clearer as a single function
Stages require tightly shared mutable state or one indivisible transaction
Additional boundaries mainly add serialization and coordination overhead
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with functions, iteration, and data representations
example_user_queries: Our import code mixes parsing, validation, conversion, and output in one giant loop.
Two reports repeat the same parsing and unit conversion logic.
How can we add a processing step without rewriting every transformation?
We need to inspect intermediate results to see where data changed incorrectly.
Can a consumer process records as they arrive without building every intermediate list?
Our producer keeps generating data faster than the next stage can consume it.
We reordered two transformations and the results changed even though the types matched.
How do we keep measurement units explicit between processing stages?
A bad record stops our job after some output has already been written.
We want to test and reuse processing stages without tying them to their neighbors.

graphics.alt_text: CSV records become Celsius readings, are selected at a 25 °C threshold, converted to Fahrenheit pairs, and formatted as text. A reading of 25 °C becomes 77.0 F; 18 °C is omitted.
graphics.caption: Arrows carry each stage's output to the next. Parsing, selection, conversion, and formatting are all filters; only selection drops valid records here.

graphics.alt_text: Solid arrows carry data from the CSV source through the filter chain to the consumer. Dashed arrows carry requests for the next result upstream. The first result consumes the 18 °C and 25 °C records; the 30 °C record waits for another request.
graphics.caption: Solid arrows show data; dashed arrows show demand for another result. This in-process pull implementation creates no background workers or queues.

patterns.title: Blackboard
patterns.short_description: Let independent knowledge sources build partial solutions in a shared workspace while a controller selects useful contributions from its current state.
use_when: Diverse expertise contributes partial results to one developing solution
Useful execution order depends on emerging evidence
Specialists should cooperate without direct calls to one another
not_ideal_when: A fixed processing sequence or explicit workflow is already clear
Independent computations only need a shared cache
Shared representations and control costs outweigh useful collaboration
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with functions, mappings, and modular application design
example_user_queries: We cannot decide which analysis to run next until we see the partial results.
Several specialist modules need to contribute evidence to the same developing interpretation.
Our analysts keep calling one another and the dependencies are becoming tangled.
How can we keep uncertain hypotheses separate from observed facts?
We want to choose useful work instead of always running every analysis in a fixed order.
New evidence should make previously blocked reasoning steps eligible.
Our problem solver stops but we cannot tell success from lack of progress.
How should we limit reasoning work without pretending an incomplete result is an answer?
Different specialists overwrite one another's conclusions in a shared dictionary.
We need a trace of which contributions led to the current hypothesis.

graphics.alt_text: A shared blackboard holds input features, intermediate evidence, and a document hypothesis. Independent text, layout, and combination knowledge sources read snapshots and propose additions. A separate controller chooses an eligible source and commits its contribution.
graphics.caption: Solid arrows show knowledge contributions and board access. Dashed arrows show the controller's selection of work; specialists do not call one another.

graphics.alt_text: With text and layout features present, layout and text sources are eligible while combination is blocked. The controller chooses layout, then text, then the newly enabled combination source. Their additions remain on the board until the declared goal is met.
graphics.caption: The example chooses the highest-priority eligible source and rechecks after every commit. Priority is a scheduling preference, not a probability that a hypothesis is true.

patterns.title: Modular Monolith
patterns.short_description: Organize one deployable application into cohesive modules with explicit public interfaces and ownership of internal code and data.
use_when: Several capabilities benefit from explicit ownership while one release remains useful
Private record representations leak across application boundaries
A team needs local refactoring and enforceable interfaces without independent services
not_ideal_when: A tiny program needs only a few functions
Capabilities require genuinely independent deployment or fault containment
Shared runtime or whole-application scaling no longer fits the workload
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with packages, public APIs, and application deployment
example_user_queries: Our application is one deployment but every feature reaches into every other feature's internals.
We want clear ownership between business capabilities without operating many services.
Renaming a customer database field keeps breaking unrelated ticket code.
Different teams share one codebase and need explicit interfaces between their work.
We reorganized classes into folders but cross-module dependencies are still tangled.
Can modules own their tables even when they use the same physical database?
How can we check that code only imports another module's public API?
Do we need separate services before our application can have meaningful boundaries?
We need to run more application instances while keeping one release process.
How can we change a module's storage representation without rewriting its callers?

graphics.alt_text: One application release contains Customers and Tickets modules. Startup code composes their public APIs. Tickets calls the Customers API locally, while each module keeps its own records behind that interface.
graphics.caption: Dashed arrows show startup wiring; the solid arrow shows the allowed local call between public APIs. Each module owns its internal representation and records.

graphics.alt_text: A router sends each request to one of two replicas of the same application release. Each replica contains both Customers and Tickets; the modules remain part of the same deployment unit.
graphics.caption: Each replica contains the complete application. Module ownership remains a logical boundary; storage and concurrency still need explicit design across replicas.

patterns.title: Microservices
patterns.short_description: Divide an application into independently deployable services around business capabilities, with explicit communication contracts and ownership of their data.
use_when: Established capabilities need different deployment schedules or capacity
Teams can own service contracts, operations, and business data
Independent releases justify explicit distributed recovery workflows
not_ideal_when: One deployment meets the actual requirements
Business boundaries are uncertain or interactions require frequent coordinated changes
Deployment automation, observability, and incident ownership are not ready
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with service contracts, network failure, and local transactions
example_user_queries: Our checkout and warehouse teams need to release changes on different schedules.
One busy capability forces us to scale the entire application.
How can teams own business capabilities and deploy them independently?
We split an application into containers but still have to release everything together.
How should services keep control of their data without a shared writable schema?
A remote reservation may have succeeded even though our order service timed out.
What needs to change when a local transaction becomes a workflow across services?
How can an updated service keep working with callers that are still on older versions?
We want separate operational ownership but need to understand the cost of network boundaries.
When is operating multiple independently released services worth the extra complexity?

graphics.alt_text: Orders release 7 and Inventory release 12 are separate deployment units. Orders sends a reservation request to Inventory through its contract. Each service accesses only its own records.
graphics.caption: Each boundary owns a release and its records. The inter-service arrow is a network request, not direct access to another service's storage.

graphics.alt_text: Inventory accepts a reservation and reduces stock, but its reply is lost. Orders stays pending. A later retry with the same order identity retrieves the existing reservation and lets Orders confirm without reducing stock again.
graphics.caption: A missing response leaves an uncertain outcome. Reusing the same identity resolves this example without repeating the stock deduction; it does not create a cross-service transaction.

patterns.title: Dependency Injection
patterns.short_description: Supply a component's collaborators from outside so it can use their contracts without choosing or constructing their implementations.
use_when: A consumer constructs infrastructure whose configuration belongs to the caller
Several entry points reuse behavior with different collaborators
Tests need controlled collaborators and explicit ownership of external resources
not_ideal_when: A pure function with ordinary data inputs is sufficient
A proposed container only hides a very small graph
An interface adds no useful capability boundary or contract
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with constructors, collaborators, and resource lifetimes
example_user_queries: My calculation opens a database connection even when I only want to test the arithmetic.
How can the same business code work with a real price database and a small test fixture?
We keep changing globals to substitute an email sender or clock during tests.
Who should create and close a connection that several objects borrow?
Our service resolves dependencies from a global registry and its requirements are hard to see.
Do we need a framework to wire a few collaborating objects?
A long-lived service holds a request resource that has already been closed.
Where should application startup choose concrete implementations?
Our constructor has so many collaborators that we cannot understand what the object does.
How can we switch infrastructure without changing the component that uses it?

graphics.alt_text: Startup code chooses a price source and supplies it to QuoteService. Once assembled, QuoteService calls the supplied source through unit_price rather than constructing or looking up a provider.
graphics.caption: Dashed arrows show startup construction and supply; the solid arrow shows the later operational call. The consumer does not select its provider.

graphics.alt_text: The application opens a database connection, builds SqlitePrices and QuoteService, uses the service while the connection is open, and closes the connection when its owning scope ends. The consumer borrows the collaborator and cannot safely keep using it afterward.
graphics.caption: The connection's owning scope encloses every database-backed quote. Closing belongs to the application; injection does not extend the resource's lifetime.

patterns.title: Functional Core, Imperative Shell
patterns.short_description: Keep decisions and transformations in pure functions over values, while an outer shell gathers inputs and performs effects from their results.
use_when: Policy branches are entangled with file, database, clock, or network operations
Business decisions can be expressed over explicit value snapshots
The application needs reproducible decisions and visible effect ordering
not_ideal_when: The operation has almost no policy beyond simple I/O
Loading every possible input would be too expensive
The design treats purity as a substitute for consistency or safe effect execution
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with functions, values, and observable side effects
example_user_queries: I need files and a running database just to test a small business rule.
Our batch job writes output before discovering that a later row is invalid.
How can we keep decisions separate from reading and writing external state?
An injected repository makes tests easier but the rule still performs I/O.
I want to replay a decision from the values that were used originally.
Where should reading the current date happen in an expiry calculation?
Can a function return proposed actions without executing them?
Our rules are spread between file handling, SQL calls, and message sending.
A deterministic calculation used an old stock snapshot before a concurrent update.
How much shell integration testing is still needed when the business logic is pure?

graphics.alt_text: An imperative shell reads inventory from a CSV file and converts it to immutable item values. A functional core returns replenishment proposals. The shell writes those proposals to a CSV file; the core receives no file handle.
graphics.caption: Arrows carry values between steps. Reading and writing belong to the shell; the core decides which proposals exist without performing I/O.

graphics.alt_text: An observed stock value of three produces a proposal for seven units toward a target of ten. If actual stock becomes eight before execution, the saved proposal still says seven. A pure computation is repeatable but does not refresh its observations.
graphics.caption: The result describes the supplied snapshot. Acting on current stock would require a fresh decision or a consistency policy; the pure core does not lock external state.

patterns.title: Domain Model
patterns.short_description: Organize business rules and state into collaborating domain objects whose operations preserve the model's invariants.
use_when: Several operations share interacting business invariants
Rules are duplicated or bypassed by different application entry points
Business concepts and intent-revealing operations clarify valid state changes
not_ideal_when: Straightforward CRUD behavior is clearer as procedures
The object structure adds persistence complexity without organizing meaningful rules
The model is treated as automatic concurrency or transaction protection
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with objects, encapsulation, and business-rule validation
example_user_queries: Our website checks capacity but a batch importer can bypass the same rule.
Business rules are duplicated across controllers, jobs, and API handlers.
How can objects express valid business operations instead of only getters and setters?
Cancelling a booking leaves our remaining-capacity counter inconsistent.
We have lots of entity classes but all the behavior sits in large service functions.
Where should validation live when multiple workflows change the same business state?
Our database table layout is driving every concept in the business code.
How can we stop callers from appending invalid records to an owned collection?
Do object methods protect a capacity limit when two processes save concurrent changes?
When is organizing business logic around objects worth more complexity than simple procedures?

graphics.alt_text: The website and batch importer both invoke Workshop operations. Workshop owns capacity, registration state, and its reservation collection. Reservations are created and removed through those operations, while callers receive an immutable view of the records.
graphics.caption: Both entry points ask the same model to reserve or cancel. Workshop checks the rules before changing its owned reservation collection; callers do not append records directly.

graphics.alt_text: While registration is open, reserve and cancel can change reservations after their checks pass. close_registration moves the workshop to closed. Closed registration rejects reserve and cancel; closing it again leaves it closed.
graphics.caption: Open and closed describe this example's registration policy. Rejected operations leave the existing bookings unchanged; no timer, database lock, or State-pattern class hierarchy is implied.

Positive whole-seat reservations, fixed capacity, unique references, cancellation while registration is open, and explicit closure are teaching rules. Single-threaded in-memory state provides no persistence transaction, concurrent capacity guarantee, automatic authorization, or external-effect rollback.

patterns.title: Entity
patterns.short_description: Track a domain object by a stable identity across changes and representations, rather than defining it by its current attributes.
use_when: A continuing domain concept must retain history and references as attributes change
Several runtime or stored representations must identify the same domain thing
Matching current descriptive fields would merge distinct things or split one lifecycle
not_ideal_when: Only attribute values matter and equivalent values are interchangeable
The design adds identifiers without a meaningful identity or lifecycle policy
Identity equality is mistaken for freshness, uniqueness enforcement, or authorization
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with object equality, identifiers, and domain modeling
example_user_queries: Renaming an asset makes our import treat it as a new thing.
Two cameras have the same label but must keep separate maintenance histories.
How can a reloaded object represent the same business thing without being the same memory object?
Our equality method compares every field and breaks when a descriptive attribute changes.
A customer number is unique inside one tenant but collides with numbers in another tenant.
What should an object identifier mean across saves, reloads, and different representations?
Two objects have the same business key but different state; which questions does equality answer?
How can dictionary lookups stay stable when the object display name changes?
We assigned different IDs in two systems and still need to decide whether they refer to one physical asset.
When should a domain concept have a lifecycle identity rather than just value equality?

graphics.alt_text: Equipment studio / 42 is registered with label Camera, renamed Camera B, and reconstructed as another object from a serialized record. The identity stays studio / 42 across all three representations.
graphics.caption: Arrows show a business update followed by reconstruction from serialized data. The identity persists; mutable labels and runtime object instances do not define it.

graphics.alt_text: Three comparisons distinguish identity from state: studio / 42 with Camera B and studio / 42 with Camera C identify the same entity; studio / 42 and studio / 43 with identical labels identify different entities; rental / 42 is different from studio / 42 because the catalog scope differs.
graphics.caption: The example compares Equipment type and the complete catalog-and-number key. Matching labels do not establish identity; matching identity does not establish matching state.

sources.title: Domain-Driven Design Reference — Entities
sources.author: Eric Evans
sources.supports: Entities on printed page 11: continuity and identity through lifecycle and representations, distinguishing the same thing despite changed attributes and different things despite equal attributes. The accessible original reference was consulted.

sources.title: Evans Classification
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Entity/reference-object terminology and distinction from Value Objects; warns that entity is overloaded with database meanings. Equality is an implementation policy, not an automatic requirement to override operators.

sources.title: Designing a microservice domain model
sources.supports: Domain identity, behavior, continuity, and context-specific representations even when identifiers are shared.

sources.title: Identity Map
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Keeping one loaded object per identity within a business transaction and the risks from duplicate mutable loaded objects; no global synchronization guarantee is inferred.

sources.title: Python data model — identity, equality and hashing
sources.supports: Runtime identity versus equality, NotImplemented for unsupported comparisons, and the hash stability obligations of keys. The example makes mutable Equipment unhashable and uses an immutable typed identity as its dictionary key.

sources.title: Python dataclasses
sources.supports: Generated field-based equality, frozen fields, and generated hash behavior. Frozen identity fields contain only validated strings.

sources.title: Python private variables
sources.supports: Leading underscores express non-public intent rather than enforcing access control or preventing deliberate key reassignment.

patterns.example_provenance: Original equipment catalog scenario, scoped EquipmentId value, explicit concrete-type-and-key equality policy, two-file Python example, and SVG compositions. JSON reconstruction is not a database or durable commit. Catalog allocation uniqueness is assumed rather than implemented, and reconstructed objects remain independent and unsynchronized.

patterns.title: Value Object
patterns.short_description: Represent a meaningful domain value as an immutable whole, with equality determined by its attributes and operations that return new values.
use_when: Several fields form one meaning with shared validity and equality rules
Equivalent descriptions should be interchangeable rather than tracked by identity
Mutation of shared descriptive data causes aliasing bugs
not_ideal_when: A domain concept requires continuing entity identity or history
A primitive already expresses the meaning without scattered rules or unit ambiguity
A frozen wrapper hides mutable contents or invalid combinations
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with object equality, immutable values, and domain validation
example_user_queries: Editing a proposed date range accidentally changes the dates stored on another object.
Two separately constructed descriptions contain identical fields but compare as different objects.
We keep repeating start-before-end checks throughout our application.
How can a group of fields express one valid domain concept instead of unrelated primitives?
A read-only object still exposes a mutable list that callers can change.
How should equality and dictionary hashing work for immutable domain values?
Do dates that touch at checkout overlap or merely sit next to one another?
I want to shift a proposed stay without changing any shared booked value.
When does a domain concept need identity rather than comparison by its attributes?
Our transport records and domain values look similar but have different responsibilities.

graphics.alt_text: Two separately constructed StayDates instances both contain check-in 2026-10-29 and checkout 2026-11-01. They represent equal three-night values even though they are different runtime objects.
graphics.caption: Equality uses the complete stay-dates value. Runtime object identity and a separate business identifier are not part of this comparison.

graphics.alt_text: Before a change, booked and proposed refer to the same stay value, 2026-10-29 to 2026-11-01. After proposed is assigned the result of shifted(2), booked still refers to the original dates while proposed refers to 2026-10-31 to 2026-11-03.
graphics.caption: Arrows show references held by variables. shifted(2) returns a new value; assigning it to proposed leaves the original value and booked reference unchanged.

sources.title: Domain-Driven Design Reference — Value Objects
sources.author: Eric Evans
sources.supports: Original accessible reference, Value Objects on printed page 12: conceptual lack of identity, meaningful attributes and functionality, immutable values, and side-effect-free operations.

sources.title: Value Object
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Property-based equality, aliasing bugs, immutable replacement, validation and meaningful operations, and classification depending on domain context.

sources.title: Data Transfer Object
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Transport responsibility and the historical Sun/Java overload of the term value object for DTOs; the article keeps these meanings separate.

sources.title: Implementing value objects
sources.supports: No domain identity, component-based equality and immutability, and persistence identifiers as implementation details rather than business identity. Framework-specific persistence choices are not made requirements of the pattern.

sources.title: Python dataclasses
sources.supports: Concrete-type and field-based equality, frozen-field behavior, generated compatible hashes, and the absence of general deep freezing.

sources.title: Python datetime date objects
sources.supports: Immutable calendar dates, whole-day date arithmetic, supported date bounds, and the distinction between dates and datetime timestamps.

sources.title: Python data model — equality and hashing
sources.supports: Equal hashable objects require equal hashes; stable keys must not change equality-relevant state. No persistent or cross-process hash value is promised.

patterns.example_provenance: Original StayDates model, half-open nonempty stay policy, two-file Python demo, and native SVG figures. Exact calendar-date fields count nights rather than elapsed hours; immutable replacement does not reserve rooms, coordinate concurrent booking, or persist owner updates.

patterns.title: Aggregate
patterns.short_description: Group domain objects that must stay consistent behind one root, and make that boundary the unit of controlled change and atomic persistence.
use_when: Several owned objects must satisfy one invariant after accepted changes
Independent child writes keep bypassing rules of the complete unit
A domain model needs deliberate transaction and concurrency boundaries
not_ideal_when: Objects merely appear together on a read-only screen
A simple validated record or transaction script already expresses the rules
The proposed root includes unbounded independent histories or unrelated lifecycles
prerequisites: Basic understanding of domain entities, immutable values, and atomic transactions
example_user_queries: Each child record is valid, but updating them independently breaks a rule about their combined state.
How do I decide which objects must be saved together in one transaction?
Callers can edit a child collection without going through the business rules on its owner.
Two users load the same plan and both pass validation before competing to save it.
Our root object loads years of unrelated history just to change one small allocation.
We need to keep the combined allocated weight within one plan’s capacity.
Should a screen that displays several related objects make them one consistency boundary?
How can I expose child data without letting clients mutate the live objects?
A child-row update bypasses the version check on its parent and overwrites another user’s changes.
One operation spans independently managed objects, and we need to decide which rules can tolerate delay.

graphics.alt_text: An application sends allocate(package_id, kg) to the LoadPlan root. Inside its boundary are a capacity of 100 kilograms and allocation values A at 60 kilograms and B at 40 kilograms. The root protects their combined weight. Package records remain outside and are referenced by ID.
graphics.caption: The boundary contains the capacity rule and the allocations it governs. The application changes allocations through LoadPlan; referenced packages keep their independent lifecycle.

graphics.alt_text: Two writers load version 7 of a plan holding 60 kilograms. One proposes adding 40 kilograms and the other 30 kilograms; both pass their local capacity check. The first atomic save advances to version 8 at 100 kilograms. The second save expects version 7 and is rejected. Re-evaluating its command against version 8 exceeds capacity.
graphics.caption: This is a required storage protocol for competing copies, not a feature of the in-memory example. The version check and the complete aggregate write must be atomic.

sources.title: Domain-Driven Design Reference — Aggregates
sources.author: Eric Evans
sources.supports: Original accessible reference, Aggregates on printed page 16: root-controlled references, whole-unit invariants, transaction boundaries, and consistency within versus across aggregates.

sources.title: DDD Aggregate
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Domain clusters and roots, unit-of-storage behavior, and distinction from collections and overloaded UML terminology.

sources.title: Effective Aggregate Design, Part I: Modeling a Single Aggregate
sources.author: Vaughn Vernon
sources.supports: Real invariants determine consistency boundaries; oversized graphs cause loading costs and contention. One-aggregate transactions are a design goal, with domain analysis needed for cross-boundary rules.

sources.title: Designing a microservice domain model
sources.supports: Root is the update entry point; aggregates may contain just the root and values. References to other roots by identifier keep independent lifecycles separate. Microservice-specific examples are not requirements of the pattern.

sources.title: Handling Concurrency Conflicts — EF Core
sources.supports: Conditional version-based writes, zero affected rows on stale updates, and handling a conflict through re-evaluation. The article does not require EF Core or imply that a child write automatically updates a root token.

sources.title: Python dataclasses — frozen instances
sources.supports: Frozen fields emulate immutability; the example returns tuple snapshots containing immutable string/integer allocation values and acknowledges runtime bypass limits.

patterns.example_provenance: Original LoadPlan example, weight-only positive-integer-kilogram policy, two-file Python code, boundary drawing, and competing-copy version trace. The root owns allocation values and references packages by opaque IDs. Local code is sequential and in memory; the version protocol is illustrated as a required storage mechanism rather than claimed to be implemented.

patterns.title: Domain Service
patterns.short_description: Express a meaningful domain operation that has no natural entity or value-object owner as a focused, stateless service with a domain-language contract.
use_when: A named business operation has no natural entity or value-object owner
Several entry points duplicate a cross-object comparison or domain policy
Assigning an operation to one participant would distort its responsibility
not_ideal_when: An existing entity or value already naturally owns the rule
The code only coordinates loading, saving, or presentation
A generic service class is accumulating unrelated business responsibilities
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with domain entities, immutable values, and application coordination
example_user_queries: Our booking screen and import job choose different rooms for the same workshop request.
A business operation compares several domain objects but does not seem to belong on any one of them.
How do I separate the business decision from loading data and committing a use case?
Putting a selection policy on one entity makes it depend on every competing candidate.
We moved all our validation into service classes and the domain objects have become empty records.
I need the same choice regardless of the order in which candidate snapshots arrive.
What is the difference between a domain service, an application service, and a network service?
Our stateless-looking service retains the previous request and behaves differently on the next call.
A room was selected successfully but another booking claimed it before we could save.
An availability-query failure is being treated as proof that no suitable room exists.

graphics.alt_text: A booking use case supplies a workshop request and room-offer snapshots to the select_room domain service. RoomOffer.can_host checks each offer's own compatibility; select_room compares qualifying offers by seat count and room ID, then returns a selected offer or no match.
graphics.caption: Local compatibility stays with RoomOffer. The domain service owns comparison across candidates; the application owns loading inputs and acting on the result.

graphics.alt_text: The application obtains candidate snapshots, asks the domain service to select a room, and submits a booking command to the room owner. If the selected room has been taken meanwhile, the booking is rejected and the application reloads candidates and re-evaluates selection.
graphics.caption: Selection is a decision over supplied snapshots. The room owner and its persistence mechanism must protect booking against concurrent changes; the domain service does not reserve the result.

sources.title: Domain-Driven Design Reference — Services
sources.author: Eric Evans
sources.supports: Original accessible reference, Services on printed page 14: a significant domain operation with no natural entity or value-object owner, a standalone service contract, and naming/assertions in domain language.

sources.title: Implementing Domain-Driven Design — Services chapter overview
sources.author: Vaughn Vernon
sources.supports: The publisher sample’s chapter overview on printed page xxv describes focused stateless domain services and their business and integration uses. This is cited as an overview, not as access to the full Services chapter.

sources.title: Use tactical DDD to design microservices
sources.supports: Domain services encapsulate ownerless domain logic; application services coordinate use cases, repositories, transactions, and technical concerns. The software pattern is not automatically a deployed microservice.

sources.title: Service Layer
sources.author: Randy Stafford, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture catalog
sources.supports: Application boundary, available use cases, transaction management, and coordination; distinguished from the focused domain operation.

sources.title: Anemic Domain Model
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Moving all business behavior to services empties domain objects; a coordinating service layer can coexist with behavior-rich domain objects.

sources.title: Python dataclasses — frozen instances
sources.supports: Frozen fields emulate immutability. The example uses only immutable component values and acknowledges deliberate runtime-bypass limits.

sources.title: Python built-in min
sources.supports: A key selects the minimum qualifying candidate, and a default supplies None for an empty candidate set. Unique room IDs complete a deterministic tuple-key order independent of input ordering.

patterns.example_provenance: Original room-selection policy and Python implementation: smallest sufficient seat count, exact required-feature matching, case-sensitive room-ID tie-break, immutable supplied offers, rejection of duplicate IDs, and explicit distinction between no match and malformed or unavailable data. Both native diagrams are original; the booking conflict is a conceptual application protocol rather than an implemented reservation store.

patterns.title: Domain Event
patterns.short_description: Represent a meaningful occurrence in the domain as an immutable fact, so its owner can record what happened without knowing every reaction.
use_when: Several independent reactions need the original context of a meaningful occurrence
Adding a reaction repeatedly changes the entity that owns a transition
The model needs to distinguish a requested action from its accepted outcome
not_ideal_when: A direct method call expresses one mandatory collaboration more clearly
The information is only a technical diagnostic with no domain meaning
The design relies on an in-memory event list as proof of durable commitment or delivery
prerequisites: Basic understanding of aggregates, immutable values, and transaction boundaries
example_user_queries: Every time a shipment changes state we add another notification call inside its domain method.
A generic changed notification loses the business reason for an update.
Delayed handlers read the latest entity and miss the values that belonged to the original occurrence.
How do I distinguish a command that might be rejected from a fact that was accepted?
Our tests unexpectedly trigger global callbacks while exercising a domain object.
An event exists in memory but the database transaction has not committed yet.
We need to decide whether reactions run before or after committing the business change.
The database commits but a crash prevents the notification from being published.
The same event can arrive twice and our consumer must avoid applying its effect twice.
Do domain events require event sourcing, a message broker, or a complete persistent event history?

graphics.alt_text: A dispatch request reaches Shipment, which checks its ready state and records a ShipmentDispatched fact with event ID, shipment ID, tracking code, and occurrence time. Separate reactions consume the fact; Shipment does not call the archive or customer-communication code directly.
graphics.caption: The command requests a transition; the event records its accepted local outcome. Arrows distinguish requesting, recording, and reacting. Persistence and delivery require an explicit policy.

graphics.alt_text: A domain operation first holds a pending event in memory. In a durable publishing design, one atomic transaction commits business state and an outgoing record. A relay later sends the committed message to consumers; a repeated delivery retains the same event identity. A rollback leaves no committed outgoing record.
graphics.caption: Pending, committed, and delivered are different stages. This outbox design illustrates durable publication; the Python example implements only local state and pending facts.

sources.title: Domain-Driven Design Reference — Domain Events
sources.author: Eric Evans
sources.supports: Original accessible reference, Domain Events on printed page 13: meaningful domain occurrences distinct from technical events, ordinarily immutable facts, context and occurrence timestamps, and explicit propagation concerns.

sources.title: Domain Event
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Immutable occurrence/source data, separate processing data, and actual occurrence versus observation time. The source is identified as a draft; its broader input-event treatment is not reduced to only outgoing aggregate notifications.

sources.title: A better domain events pattern
sources.author: Jimmy Bogard
sources.supports: Record events on the entity, then choose a later dispatch point rather than invoking opaque global handlers during the operation. The example borrows this separation, not a particular ORM or transaction implementation.

sources.title: Domain events: Design and implementation
sources.supports: Before/after-commit choices, handler/application concerns, and internal domain events versus committed integration-event contracts. No broker, async mechanism, or cross-aggregate atomicity is made intrinsic to a domain event.

sources.title: Transactional Outbox
sources.author: Chris Richardson
sources.supports: Commit business state and outgoing publication intent atomically; relay may send again after a crash, requiring duplicate-safe consumers. This is a distinct durability mechanism, not a guarantee supplied by the event type.

sources.title: Event Sourcing
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Authoritative event history supports state reconstruction and replay. Domain Event alone does not require full-history persistence or event-sourced state. This source is identified as a draft.

sources.title: Python dataclasses — frozen instances
sources.supports: Frozen fields emulate immutability; normal API protection and immutable components do not establish a security boundary against deliberate runtime bypass.

sources.title: Python datetime — aware and naive objects
sources.supports: Aware timestamps identify instants; datetime and timezone values are immutable. Requiring timezone.utc is an explicit teaching contract, not a universal event requirement.

patterns.example_provenance: Original Shipment ready-to-dispatched policy and immutable ShipmentDispatched fact, caller-supplied opaque IDs and strict UTC datetime, pending tuple snapshots, pure archive/notice descriptions, and two native figures. The code is sequential and in memory; no persistence, ID allocator, reliable dispatch, deduplication, transaction, or physical shipment verification is implemented.

patterns.title: Specification
patterns.short_description: Give a domain matching rule its own object, so callers can reuse and combine the criterion independently of candidates and selection code.
use_when: Selection and validation repeatedly copy the same recognizable domain criterion
Matching rules vary independently of the candidate objects
A policy needs explicit combinations of smaller AND, OR, and NOT conditions
not_ideal_when: A stable local predicate or natural-owner method is already sufficient
The design assumes an opaque callable automatically translates to a database query
A Boolean result is being used as proof of authorization, reservation, or atomic enforcement
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with Boolean logic, immutable values, and domain responsibilities
example_user_queries: Our queue filter and manual validation screen contain different copies of the same eligibility rule.
Changing a matching policy forces us to add more caller-specific methods to the candidate class.
I need to combine approval or an exception with mandatory limits that must always apply.
How can selection and validation reuse one domain criterion?
A rule is mostly stable but its maximum count changes between operations.
Our predicates return truthy values instead of actual Boolean results and hide missing data.
A later condition does not run because an earlier condition short-circuits evaluation.
An in-memory rule behaves differently after translating nullable fields into a SQL query.
We selected an eligible record but it changed before we tried to commit the operation.
We need to decide whether a named predicate is enough or a composable rule object is justified.

graphics.alt_text: The print-queue selector and manual-release validator both call is_satisfied_by on the same eligible-for-print specification. The candidate is a PrintJob snapshot, and the result is a Boolean. The specification defines acceptance while callers decide what to do with the result.
graphics.caption: Selection keeps matching jobs; validation checks one proposed job. Both use the same acceptance criterion without moving selection or release effects into the rule.

graphics.alt_text: A composed printing policy requires approved OR proof copy, at most 40 pages, and NOT cancelled. Job A has approval and exactly 40 pages and passes. B has 41 pages and fails. C is an unapproved proof copy within the limit and passes. D has neither approval nor the exception and fails. E is cancelled and fails despite approval.
graphics.caption: All three groups must hold. The OR exception satisfies the approval group only; it does not bypass the page limit or the cancellation rule.

sources.title: Specifications
sources.author: Eric Evans and Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Original 19-page paper: separate the matching statement from candidates and selection, use for selection/validation/building to order, and distinguish hard-coded, parameterized, and composite variants. Composite AND/OR/NOT is one implementation option, not a requirement of every specification.

sources.title: How to use Specifications for Validation
sources.author: Ardalis.Specification documentation
sources.supports: Modern library example of the IsSatisfiedBy candidate-to-Boolean contract. The library’s query/validation evaluator capabilities are contextual examples, not universal guarantees or required dependencies.

sources.title: Work with data in ASP.NET Core Apps
sources.supports: Query-oriented specifications may additionally encapsulate returned data shape and eager-loading instructions. Such evaluator capabilities are distinct from an opaque in-memory predicate wrapper.

sources.title: Python expressions — Boolean operations
sources.supports: Left-to-right short-circuit evaluation and the fact that and/or return operands rather than necessarily Boolean values. The example validates strict Boolean results at each specification boundary.

sources.title: PostgreSQL logical operators
sources.supports: SQL uses true/false/unknown, NOT NULL stays unknown, and operand evaluation order is not a general left-to-right guarantee. Translation needs explicit semantic agreement rather than assuming Python predicate behavior.

sources.title: Python dataclasses — frozen instances
sources.supports: Frozen fields emulate immutability through the normal API; callable closure dependencies are not recursively frozen by a frozen wrapper.

patterns.example_provenance: Original print-job policy: (approved OR proof_copy) AND pages <= 40 AND NOT cancelled, positive whole page counts, strict Boolean flags/results, opaque IDs, and named composition methods. The same composed callable-backed object supports in-memory selection and validation. No inspectable expression tree, SQL translator, ranking, diagnostics, authorization, release, or persistence is implemented.

patterns.title: Bounded Context
patterns.short_description: Give each business model an explicit boundary for its terms and rules, then connect models through deliberate mappings rather than assuming shared meanings.
use_when: Teams use the same term for different identities, rules, or lifecycles
One shared model repeatedly creates contradictory states and exceptions
Related systems need explicit translation without importing each other’s assumptions
not_ideal_when: One small team already has a coherent model and vocabulary
The proposed split only mirrors every entity, database, or organizational department
The design assumes naming a boundary supplies authorization, transactions, or delivery guarantees
prerequisites: Basic understanding of domain models, identity, and integration contracts
example_user_queries: Sales, Billing, and Service Access mean different things when they call a customer active.
A shared customer status keeps importing one team’s rules into another team’s decisions.
How do we decide where a domain model and its vocabulary should apply?
One commercial account maps to several payers, so joining by company name produces incorrect actions.
We need to translate an external model without sharing its internal entities or business assumptions.
A payer’s overdue state should trigger local review rather than automatically overwriting workspace access.
We have a missing identifier mapping and need an explicit unresolved outcome instead of guessing.
Does a bounded context have to be one microservice, database, department, or transaction?
Warehouse stock on hand and order-capture availability use similar words for different measurements.
Our services are in separate deployments but still depend on unrestricted changes to the same model.

graphics.alt_text: Sales models commercial account AC-72 as an established relationship. Billing models payer BILL-19 as current and BILL-20 as overdue. Service Access models workspace WS-301 as enabled and funded by BILL-19. Identity mappings connect the models, while the funding relationship identifies which payer matters to the workspace.
graphics.caption: Northstar participates in three models. Mapped identities do not merge their states, and BILL-20's overdue condition does not define WS-301's access policy.

graphics.alt_text: A published BillingCondition for BILL-19 and a workspace funded by BILL-19 enter Access-owned interpretation. A current condition means keep current access; an overdue condition means review access. The function rejects mismatched or unresolved payer mappings and never directly changes the workspace's enabled state.
graphics.caption: The receiving context owns the interpretation. Billing's overdue state becomes a request for access review, not a copied access status.

sources.title: Domain-Driven Design Reference — Bounded Context and Context Map
sources.author: Eric Evans
sources.supports: Original accessible reference, Bounded Context on printed page 2 and Context Map on printed page 29: explicit model applicability, coherent terms within the boundary, and relationships between contexts. Organizational and physical manifestations support rather than define the model boundary automatically.

sources.title: Bounded Context
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Different meanings for common words, internally unified models, and deliberate mappings and context relationships across a larger domain.

sources.title: Use domain analysis to model microservices
sources.supports: Domain analysis and ubiquitous language establish contexts before tactical models and service design; boundaries should not mechanically copy technology or organizational divisions.

sources.title: Identify microservice boundaries
sources.supports: Deployment design considers aggregates, domain services, and operational constraints after context modeling. A bounded context is not automatically exactly one deployed service.

sources.title: Anti-Corruption Layer pattern
sources.supports: Translation protects a receiving model’s semantics; it may be an in-process component or independent service and still requires validation, observability, and consistency design.

sources.title: API Federation: growing scalable API landscapes
sources.author: Antonio Garrote, Salesforce Engineering
sources.supports: Retained documented example of consistent semantics, entity identity, and compatible schemas within a bounded context while allowing different internal service shapes. Federation is not a universal enterprise canonical model.

sources.title: Python dataclasses — frozen instances
sources.supports: Frozen fields emulate immutability for these simple value snapshots. They do not validate producer authority, freshness, or external state and do not create a runtime security boundary.

patterns.example_provenance: Retains original Patternverse Northstar AC-72/BILL-19/BILL-20/WS-301 and inventory 12-on-hand/5-reserved/7-available scenarios. New three-file teaching code separates a published BillingCondition from the Access-owned Workspace and assessment policy. Current maps to keep_current_access; overdue maps to review_access, without changing enabled. Mismatched or unresolved funding relationships are explicit errors. Native illustrations are original replacements; the legacy SVG remains retained unchanged.

patterns.title: Service Layer
patterns.short_description: Define application operations at a shared boundary that coordinates domain behavior, persistence, and transaction outcomes for different callers.
use_when: Several entry points repeat the same application operation
Transaction scope and failure handling drift between callers
Application coordination is hard to test without running the interface
not_ideal_when: A small read-only operation is already a clear function
Added service classes only forward unchanged calls
The proposed layer gathers all domain behavior into a generic procedural manager
prerequisites: Basic understanding of application boundaries, domain rules, and local database transactions
example_user_queries: Our web endpoint and command-line tool repeat the same loading, validation, and save sequence.
One caller commits an update but forgets the related record, leaving inconsistent application data.
We need a shared place to define what a successful booking operation actually means.
How can we test use-case coordination without starting a web server?
Business rules and HTTP response handling are tangled together in our controllers.
We cannot tell whether an application function or its caller owns the transaction.
A database insert fails after another update and we need both changes rolled back.
We want to add an import tool without reproducing the application workflow.
A retry after losing the response might repeat an operation that already committed.
Our service objects contain every rule and the domain entities have become passive records.

graphics.alt_text: A web adapter and a command-line adapter both call book on the service layer. The service coordinates loading, invoking Workshop.after_booking, writing availability and the booking record, then committing. Workshop owns the capacity rule; SQLite owns persistence and locking.
graphics.caption: Callers handle their interface. The service owns the use-case sequence, the model owns the rule, and the database supplies the transaction mechanism.

graphics.alt_text: The booking operation begins a write transaction, reads availability, applies the domain rule, updates remaining seats, and inserts the booking row. Commit makes both writes visible together. If the insert fails because a booking ID already exists, rollback restores the earlier capacity update and the caller receives an error.
graphics.caption: A failure after the first write must undo that write too. The application coordinates the boundary; the database makes these local changes atomic.

sources.title: Service Layer
sources.author: Randy Stafford, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture
sources.supports: Application operation boundary, reuse across client interfaces, coordination of responses and transaction control. Service Layer is not inherently a network service.

sources.title: Architecture Patterns with Python — chapter 4, Our First Use Case: Flask API and Service Layer
sources.author: Harry Percival and Bob Gregory
sources.supports: Application orchestration independent of adapters; explicit dependencies, use-case tests, and distinction from domain services. The original teaching code here uses direct SQLite instead of importing the book’s repositories or examples.

sources.title: Transaction Script
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Procedural organization of business logic by request is a separate choice from defining a shared application boundary; Service Layer does not require a rich object model.

sources.title: Anemic Domain Model
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Moving all behavior out of a domain model into procedural services can undermine the model. The example leaves capacity validation in Workshop.

sources.title: SQLite — Transaction
sources.supports: BEGIN IMMEDIATE obtains a write transaction before reads and may fail with SQLITE_BUSY; explicit COMMIT and ROLLBACK delimit the local transaction. This mechanism, not the Service Layer name, supplies the demonstrated atomicity.

sources.title: Python sqlite3 — transaction control via isolation_level
sources.supports: With legacy transaction control and isolation_level=None, explicit SQL manages transactions; in_transaction exposes low-level state. The example uses explicit SQL BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK and caller-owned connection closing.

patterns.example_provenance: Original workshop booking sequence. The model validates positive whole seat requests and capacity. The service loads a workshop under BEGIN IMMEDIATE, writes remaining seats and a booking record, commits both, or rolls back. A duplicate booking primary key intentionally fails after the first update. The demo represents two callers without a web server or CLI parser. No authentication, notifications, durable idempotency protocol, or cross-resource atomicity is implemented.

patterns.title: Transaction Script
patterns.short_description: Organize business logic around procedures that handle complete application requests, using direct data access or shared helpers as needed.
use_when: Business requests have straightforward sequential rules
A focused procedure is clearer than a rich object model
Interfaces need a reusable home for request-specific business logic
not_ideal_when: Many procedures repeat the same interacting invariants
Changes to one business rule require coordinated edits across scripts
The design assumes a procedural sequence supplies atomicity or retry safety
prerequisites: Basic procedural programming and local database transaction concepts
example_user_queries: Our admin tool has a few simple business operations and a large object model feels unnecessary.
We need a clear procedure to validate a stock request, subtract units, and record the movement.
Business rules are buried inside screen handlers and are hard to reuse from an import tool.
Should this request be one business procedure or a collaboration of domain objects?
Two consecutive writes can leave a stock change without its movement record.
A duplicate movement insert fails after stock has already been reduced.
We want to take the exact remaining quantity but reject anything beyond it.
The same invariant is being copied across many procedures and changes keep drifting.
Does calling something a transaction mean it is automatically atomic in the database?
We need to distinguish the application API boundary from how its business rules are organized.

graphics.alt_text: An issue-stock request enters the issue_stock procedure. The procedure validates the quantity, reads stock, checks units against availability, calculates the remainder, and writes stock plus a movement record. The capacity decision lives inside the procedure; database rows hold data rather than supplying business-object methods.
graphics.caption: The business rule is expressed directly in the request procedure. Data access can be direct or delegated to a thin helper.

graphics.alt_text: A successful issue starts with five units, subtracts three, inserts movement I-1, and commits two remaining units. A later attempt using duplicate movement I-1 starts with two units, temporarily subtracts one, fails to insert, and rolls back to two. The original I-1 movement remains three units.
graphics.caption: Both rows execute the same procedure. A local transaction preserves the stock-and-movement relationship when the second write fails.

sources.title: Transaction Script
sources.author: Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture
sources.supports: Original catalog meaning: organize logic around procedures for individual requests; direct database access or a thin wrapper; shared subtasks may be extracted. The pattern concerns logic organization, not a mandatory language, file format, or database transaction mechanism.

sources.title: Domain Model
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Object model combining behavior and data, providing the comparison with request-oriented procedural logic.

sources.title: Table Module
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Table- or view-oriented organization is a separate choice from a procedure per request. No new Table Module article or stub is created.

sources.title: Service Layer
sources.author: Randy Stafford
sources.supports: The application boundary and available operations are distinct from how business rules are organized. A service operation may use a transaction script or a domain model.

sources.title: SQLite — Transaction
sources.supports: Explicit BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK, single-writer concurrency, BEGIN IMMEDIATE contention, and local atomicity mechanisms. The original script owns its transaction and rejects nesting; SQL transaction guarantees are not attributed to the pattern name.

sources.title: Python sqlite3 — transaction control via isolation_level
sources.supports: Explicit SQL transaction control with isolation_level=None under legacy behavior, low-level in_transaction state, parameter binding, and caller-owned connection lifecycle. This teaching example uses explicit SQL statements rather than relying on connection context-manager semantics.

patterns.example_provenance: Original stock-issue procedure over one SKU at a time. Whole-unit validation, stock availability comparison, remainder calculation, stock update, and movement insert live in the procedure, with no domain classes. Initial P-7 stock is five units; I-1 issues three, a duplicate I-1 attempt rolls back its earlier subtraction, I-2 consumes the exact two remaining units, and I-3 is rejected on empty stock. No physical dispatch, authentication, reservation, durable idempotency, or cross-database coordination is implemented.

patterns.title: Repository
patterns.short_description: Expose a domain-oriented collection of objects while keeping storage queries and mapping details behind a deliberate access contract.
use_when: Storage queries and object mapping leak into domain-oriented callers
Several callers duplicate domain selection logic
A focused access contract would simplify business tests and storage integration
not_ideal_when: A simple ORM already provides a sufficient domain-facing interface
A wrapper only forwards generic CRUD for every table
The design assumes an in-memory fake establishes transaction or concurrency guarantees
prerequisites: Basic understanding of domain objects, identity, and persistence
example_user_queries: Our booking code knows SQL columns and reconstructs domain objects in several places.
The same storage query is copied between a screen and an import tool.
We need to find domain objects by identity without exposing database cursors to callers.
How should missing IDs, duplicate adds, and query ordering behave across storage adapters?
Our in-memory test implementation returns different results from the real database.
We want to query workshops with enough seats using a domain-level operation.
A fetched object changed locally but nothing was saved, and the persistence semantics are unclear.
A repository method commits too early and prevents several changes from sharing a transaction.
We are creating a repository for every table and exposing internal aggregate children.
A query returned enough availability, but another booking changed it before we acted.

graphics.alt_text: Application code asks the Workshops repository for workshops with room for two attendees. Either the memory implementation filters stored Workshop objects or the SQLite implementation queries rows and constructs Workshop objects. The caller receives the same ordered domain-level result without seeing SQL or cursors.
graphics.caption: One domain-facing contract, two storage implementations. Storage queries and object reconstruction remain behind the boundary.

graphics.alt_text: A repository returns workshop A with two seats left. Another booking then commits one remaining seat. The caller still holds its immutable two-seat snapshot; a new repository read can obtain the updated state. Neither the selection nor the old snapshot reserves seats; booking needs its own concurrency protection.
graphics.caption: A repository controls access, not the passage of time. Read consistency depends on the backing store and surrounding transaction; an old result is not a booking guarantee.

sources.title: Repository
sources.author: Edward Hieatt and Rob Mee, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture
sources.supports: Collection-like domain-object access mediating between domain and mapping layers, concentrating queries and hiding storage operations. This is distinct from a source-code repository or package registry.

sources.title: DDD Reference — Repositories, printed page 17
sources.author: Eric Evans
sources.supports: Domain-meaningful query criteria, storage encapsulation, and repositories for aggregate roots that need direct access. Does not require a repository for every relational table.

sources.title: Architecture Patterns with Python — chapter 2, Repository Pattern
sources.author: Harry Percival and Bob Gregory
sources.supports: Small domain-oriented access contract, persistence ignorance, memory implementations for tests, and optional duck typing instead of mandatory inheritance. The workshop implementations here are original and do not import the book’s code.

sources.title: Data Mapper
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Object/storage representation transfer is a distinct role from the repository’s collection abstraction. The SQLite example reconstructs domain snapshots explicitly.

sources.title: SQLite — UPSERT
sources.supports: ON CONFLICT(id) DO NOTHING targets the identity uniqueness constraint without suppressing unrelated CHECK or NOT NULL failures. SQLite 3.24+ supports the demonstrated syntax.

sources.title: Python sqlite3 — connection context manager
sources.supports: The caller’s connection context manager commits or rolls back transactions and does not close the connection. The example uses closing for lifetime ownership, parameter binding, and rowcount to detect the targeted no-op.

patterns.example_provenance: Original immutable Workshop snapshots with nonblank exact ASCII IDs and whole nonnegative availability. Both adapters provide add, get, and ordered with_room_for, matching missing-ID and duplicate behavior. The memory adapter filters objects; SQLite filters rows and reconstructs objects. The caller owns SQL transaction and connection lifetime. Only new additions and retrieval are implemented; no update/removal API, identity map, dirty tracking, reservation, authorization, pagination, or concurrency protocol is supplied.

patterns.title: Data Mapper
patterns.short_description: Move data between domain objects and database representations through a separate mapping layer, keeping persistence details out of the model.
use_when: Domain object structure differs from stored representation
Persistence changes repeatedly disturb business behavior
Row reconstruction and inverse write conversions are duplicated across callers
not_ideal_when: Straightforward record entry is adequately served by Active Record or a table-oriented interface
An ORM already supplies the needed mapping and another handwritten layer adds little value
The design assumes mapping alone supplies transactions, identity management, or lost-update protection
prerequisites: Basic understanding of domain objects, value objects, and relational persistence
example_user_queries: Our appointment model uses start and end times but the database stores a start and duration.
Business objects contain SQL and keep changing whenever table columns change.
Several screens reconstruct the same domain values from database rows differently.
We need to load an object with its domain behavior intact without teaching it persistence APIs.
How do we keep the read conversion and write conversion consistent in both directions?
Changing an in-memory object does not save it and the persistence lifecycle is unclear.
Loading old data accidentally triggers behavior intended only for a new business event.
Two separate loads of the same row create different objects and we need explicit identity semantics.
A persistence helper commits early and prevents the caller from rolling back a complete operation.
An update overwrites a later change because our mapper only matches the record ID.

graphics.alt_text: An Appointment contains a TimeSlot with start minute 540 and end minute 570. AppointmentMapper translates that object into an appointments row with appointment_key A-7, begin_minute 540, and duration_minutes 30. On loading, the mapper reconstructs the end as start plus duration. The model has no dependency on the mapper or SQL.
graphics.caption: Write: duration = end − start. Read: end = start + duration. The mapper owns the representation change in both directions.

graphics.alt_text: The caller constructs a replacement Appointment and explicitly asks the mapper to update it. The mapper writes a provisional row change inside a caller-owned transaction. Caller commit makes it durable, while rollback discards it. Neither mapping nor object replacement automatically saves the appointment.
graphics.caption: The mapper translates and writes. The caller decides the transaction outcome; the old domain object remains unchanged.

sources.title: Data Mapper
sources.author: Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture
sources.supports: Separate object/database representation transfer, with mapper knowledge of both sides and domain objects independent of database access and the mapper. Broader DTO or ETL data conversion alone is not this persistence pattern.

sources.title: Active Record
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Contrasting pattern that puts database-access behavior with the domain-oriented record. No Active Record stub or duplicate article is created.

sources.title: Identity Map
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Identity management for repeated loads within a business transaction is an additional pattern, not an automatic property of every Data Mapper. The example returns independent immutable snapshots.

sources.title: SQLAlchemy ORM mapping styles
sources.supports: Imperative and declarative configuration feed mapper machinery; configuration syntax alone does not imply Active Record. Imperative mapping can associate separately defined classes and tables. No SQLAlchemy dependency is added to the example.

sources.title: SQLAlchemy — Configuring a Version Counter
sources.supports: Expected-version comparisons can detect stale updates under their documented scope. The handwritten example performs unconditional ID-matched updates and deliberately supplies no such concurrency protection.

sources.title: Python sqlite3 — connection context manager
sources.supports: The caller’s connection context manager commits or rolls back transactions and does not close the connection. Explicit mapping uses parameter binding and rowcount; closing manages connection lifetime.

patterns.example_provenance: Original Appointment contains an immutable TimeSlot with whole start/end minutes in one abstract local day. The separate mapper reconstructs end = start + duration and writes duration = end - start, using differently named columns. Domain behavior uses half-open overlap rules. The demo loads [540,570), writes a replacement [600,645), observes stored (600,45), reloads 645, retains the old 570 snapshot, and returns None for a missing ID. No date/time-zone engine, scheduling-conflict enforcement, identity map, dirty tracking, deletion, version check, or authorization is implemented.

patterns.title: Active Record
patterns.short_description: Put a row's data, domain behavior, and database access operations on the same object, giving callers a direct record-oriented API.
use_when: Business concepts align reasonably closely with database records
Local record rules and persistence benefit from one direct API
A small application does not yet benefit from separate mapping machinery
not_ideal_when: Complex domain structure needs independence from storage shape
Record callbacks and associations hide substantial coordination or I/O
The design assumes save, generated IDs, or rollback imply automatic object-state or concurrency guarantees
prerequisites: Basic understanding of objects, relational records, and transactions
example_user_queries: Our small task application repeats row loading, title validation, and saving in every screen.
We want a record object that knows its local rules and how to read or write its row.
Is an object with find and save methods different from using a separate data mapper?
We changed a record in memory but never saved it and the database stayed unchanged.
A transaction rolled back but our object still contains the values we tried to save.
An inserted object has an ID even though the surrounding transaction failed.
Two loaded copies of a record overwrite each other when saved without version checks.
Our model uniqueness check passes concurrently and we still get duplicate database values.
Callbacks and association access hide database queries and external side effects.
We need to coordinate several record saves without making one record a giant application service.

graphics.alt_text: A caller loads and works with a Task object. The Task contains its title and completion flag, rename and complete business operations, and find and save persistence methods. The same class issues SQL for the corresponding tasks row; no separate mapper is used.
graphics.caption: The record object owns both business behavior and persistence knowledge. Ordinary changes and SQL writes remain separate operations in this example.

graphics.alt_text: A Task is loaded with done false. Calling complete changes the object to done true; save writes a provisional done true row.
