A later caller rollback restores the database row to done false while the object remains done true. Reloading creates an object reflecting the stored false value.
graphics.caption: Rollback restores database state, not ordinary object attributes. Reload or discard the affected record after the failed use case.

sources.title: Active Record
sources.author: Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture
sources.supports: The record object combines row data, database access behavior, and local domain logic. This is a responsibility choice distinct from separating persistence into a mapper.

sources.title: Active Record Basics
sources.author: Ruby on Rails Guides
sources.supports: Concrete framework implementation, record-oriented operations, and distinction between constructing an unsaved object and persistence operations. Framework APIs are examples, not universal requirements of the pattern or the hand-written Python implementation.

sources.title: Active Record Validations — uniqueness
sources.author: Ruby on Rails Guides
sources.supports: Model-level uniqueness checks do not establish concurrency-safe uniqueness without a database unique constraint. The example uses SQLite-generated primary keys and basic model validation rather than a uniqueness validator.

sources.title: ActiveRecord transactions
sources.author: Ruby on Rails API
sources.supports: Transaction scope is per connection; database rollback does not automatically restore object instance data. Rails save/destroy transaction wrapping and callbacks are framework behavior, distinct from this caller-owned SQLite transaction.

sources.title: ActiveRecord optimistic locking
sources.author: Ruby on Rails API
sources.supports: Version-based stale-write detection is an additional configured mechanism. The example has no version field and can overwrite later changes.

sources.title: Python sqlite3 — connection context manager
sources.supports: The caller’s with-connection context commits or rolls back transactions without closing the connection. The code uses closing for lifetime ownership, parameter binding, lastrowid, and rowcount for explicit record persistence.

patterns.example_provenance: Original Task active record combines generated row identity, printable 1–80 character title validation, a Boolean completion state, a no-rename-after-completion local policy, find, and insert/update save behavior. Public properties are read-only; supported state changes use methods. Save issues SQL without committing. A deliberate failed use case leaves the object complete while the database row rolls back; reloading and saving a fresh object then succeeds. This is not a Rails implementation and supplies no callbacks, deletion, identity caching, authorization, stale-write protection, or cross-database transaction.

patterns.title: Unit of Work
patterns.short_description: Track the objects affected by a business operation and coordinate their persistence changes within one explicit completion boundary.
use_when: A business operation changes several objects that must be persisted coherently
Writers otherwise commit independently or forget pending object changes
One explicit persistence-completion boundary would clarify lifecycle and failures
not_ideal_when: A single straightforward update is adequately handled by a transaction block
An ORM already supplies tracking and transaction coordination
The design assumes local transaction scope provides distributed atomicity or automatic stale-write protection
prerequisites: Basic understanding of persistence, change tracking, and database transactions
example_user_queries: One operation updates several objects but each helper commits independently.
We sometimes forget to save a changed object before completing a business operation.
We need to track new, modified, and removed objects in one persistence scope.
A later insert fails after an earlier update and we need the whole change set rolled back.
What is the difference between flushing pending writes and committing a transaction?
Leaving a scope without an explicit success decision should discard its pending changes.
Our code reuses a persistence session after a failed commit and its lifecycle is unclear.
We need repositories to participate in one operation instead of choosing their own commit points.
We are sharing one change tracker across concurrent requests and their changes become mixed.
A batch of writes is atomic locally but we still need to handle stale snapshots or external messages.

graphics.alt_text: One maintenance operation registers label A as modified, B as new, and C as removed. The Unit of Work tracks those object snapshots, then translates them into UPDATE, INSERT, and DELETE operations under one database transaction. No registration writes SQL by itself.
graphics.caption: Tracking and persistence are separate phases. The coordinator knows which objects need writing; the database supplies the local transaction mechanism.

graphics.alt_text: The Unit of Work updates A, then attempts to insert duplicate B. The insert fails, so the transaction rolls back the earlier update. A retains its committed value, and the failed Unit of Work is discarded. A successful batch can commit all three kinds of change together.
graphics.caption: A later write failure must undo earlier writes in the same operation. Retry decisions require a fresh scope and fresh inputs.

sources.title: Unit of Work
sources.author: Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture
sources.supports: Tracks objects affected during a business operation and coordinates new, modified, and removed persistence changes and concurrency policy. The pattern is more than a generic transaction wrapper or batch job.

sources.title: Architecture Patterns with Python — chapter 6, Unit of Work Pattern
sources.author: Harry Percival and Bob Gregory
sources.supports: A scoped persistence abstraction, explicit completion, and safe cleanup/default rollback policy. This example discards unwritten proposals on exit and owns a database transaction only during commit; it does not reproduce the book’s ORM implementation.

sources.title: SQLAlchemy Session Basics
sources.supports: Instrumented tracking, pending changes, flushing versus commit, and session scope. ORM autoflush can issue SQL before commit. No SQLAlchemy dependency or automatic tracking is added here.

sources.title: SQLAlchemy — Configuring a Version Counter
sources.supports: Expected-version comparison is one additional stale-write mechanism. The manual snapshots in this example have no version column and can overwrite a newer value collected after the proposal was formed.

sources.title: SQLite — Transaction
sources.supports: BEGIN IMMEDIATE obtains the write transaction and can fail with contention. COMMIT and ROLLBACK supply the demonstrated local atomicity; a Unit of Work name does not create it or nest ordinary BEGIN transactions.

sources.title: Python sqlite3 — transaction control via isolation_level
sources.supports: An idle connection with isolation_level=None supports explicit SQL transaction control; in_transaction identifies the low-level state. The caller owns closing the connection.

patterns.example_provenance: Original independent label rows and immutable Label snapshots. One final registered intent per ID classifies new, dirty, or deleted objects. Explicit commit applies updates, inserts, then deletes, with sorted IDs in each group, and commits one local SQLite transaction. A duplicate insert rolls back an earlier update. No commit discards only unwritten proposals. Scopes are single-use after an in-scope commit attempt or exit. The implementation provides no identity map, automatic dirty tracking, registration coalescing, read API, version checks, foreign-key dependency planner, automatic retries, authorization, or cross-resource coordination.

patterns.title: Identity Map
patterns.short_description: Keep one live object for each persistent identity within a defined scope, and reuse that object whenever the identity is loaded again.
use_when: Multiple lookup paths should share one mutable entity object during an operation
Repeated primary-key loads otherwise construct competing instances
A scoped persistence loader needs explicit identity and lifecycle ownership
not_ideal_when: Independent immutable read projections are sufficient
An ORM already provides the required identity management
The requirement is a global query cache or fresh data across processes
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with database primary keys, object references, and persistence scopes
example_user_queries: Billing and shipping load the same customer but end up with different in-memory copies.
Changing an entity through one reference does not appear through another reference to the same row.
We keep selecting the same primary key several times during one request.
Two repositories reconstruct separate objects for the same persistent identity.
How can a persistence session return the same object whenever a record is loaded again?
Our object cache returns an old value after another writer changes the database.
The same numeric ID exists in multiple tenants and our loaded-object registry mixes them up.
We need to decide when loaded objects stop being shared and can be released.
A filtered ORM query still executes SQL even though matching objects have already been loaded.
One long-lived object registry is retaining too much memory and leaking state between requests.

graphics.alt_text: The first lookup of contact 1 misses the scoped map, selects its row, constructs a Contact, and registers its reference. A later lookup finds that entry and returns the same Contact object without selecting or constructing again.
graphics.caption: The map preserves object identity within the scope. Both lookup paths receive the same live object, rather than independent copies with matching IDs.

graphics.alt_text: The current scope holds a Contact named Ada Lovelace while the database row has been changed to Augusta. A map hit retains the local object. Closing the scope clears the registry; a new scope selects the row and constructs a different Contact named Augusta in this example.
graphics.caption: Identity reuse is a local guarantee. A new scope loads again, but database isolation and refresh policy still determine which stored state it can observe.

sources.title: Identity Map
sources.author: Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture
sources.supports: Persistent-identity lookup and one loaded object per identity within a business transaction; prevents duplicate competing instances and repeated loads.

sources.title: SQLAlchemy Session Basics
sources.supports: Identity maps differ from arbitrary query-result caches. A filtered query may still execute SQL. Session lifecycle and sequential per-thread/task use are explicit responsibilities.

sources.title: SQLAlchemy — Identity Token
sources.supports: Identity namespaces can distinguish objects with the same mapped class and primary key across different schemas. The single-type, single-connection example makes these namespaces implicit rather than implementing sharding.

sources.title: SQLAlchemy — Session Referencing Behavior
sources.supports: Ordinary persistent objects may be weakly referenced; the teaching implementation deliberately chooses strong references cleared at single-use context exit.

sources.title: SQLAlchemy — Session.get
sources.supports: Identity-map hits and expired-state reloads have different behavior. Refresh/expiration and handling of deleted rows require explicit policy; none is implemented by this example.

sources.title: Python sqlite3 — transaction control via isolation_level
sources.supports: isolation_level=None allows the demo to execute statements without an implicit multi-statement transaction. The caller owns connection lifetime; ContactScope issues no save, commit, rollback, or close.

patterns.example_provenance: Original contact lookup paths share one mutable Contact object per positive integer ID in a single-use, single-connection, single-mapped-type scope. The map holds strong references and validates objects before registration. Missing rows are not cached; storage/validation failures propagate. Rename changes memory only. Direct SQL changes the stored name while a map hit retains local edits; a new scope constructs a distinct object and reads the completed update under the demo connection configuration. No query API, writes, dirty tracking, refresh/expiration, graph-cycle loading, thread/task synchronization, authorization, expected-version checks, or distributed cache is supplied.

patterns.title: Lazy Load
patterns.short_description: Load the lightweight part of an object first, keeping a way to fetch its deferred data when that data is actually needed.
use_when: Large fields or relationships are costly and often unused
Initial retrieval can return a useful lightweight object while preserving a deferred lookup
Later access can tolerate explicit I/O latency and failure within an owned loading context
not_ideal_when: Almost every caller needs the omitted data and a batch or eager read is clearer
A read-only projection never needs the deferred fields
The design assumes deferred access is free, always fresh, or usable after its loading context ends
prerequisites: Basic knowledge of object fields, database reads, and resource lifetime
example_user_queries: Our document list downloads every large body even though users open only a few.
Loading one object pulls in an enormous graph of related records.
We want to return titles quickly and fetch full details only when someone opens a record.
How do we distinguish a field that has not been loaded from a loaded empty or null value?
A property access unexpectedly queries the database while serializing our response.
Opening every row in a list causes one extra query per item.
An object tries to fetch a field after its database session has already closed.
The first attempt to read deferred data fails and we need a clear policy for later access.
We read a header now and its body later but they can reflect different database states.
Two callers can trigger the same deferred lookup and we need to define who owns loading.

graphics.alt_text: A document is first loaded with its title and an unloaded body marker. Reading the title performs no body query. The first body access selects and stores the body; later accesses return the stored value without another query. A document whose body is never accessed performs no body query.
graphics.caption: The deferred read happens at the body-access boundary. This example retains the first successful result per Document instance, including an empty string or NULL.

graphics.alt_text: An unloaded document attempts a body read. Success stores the value and releases the callback; failure propagates while the body remains unloaded. After the reader closes, unloaded access is rejected before SQL, while an already-loaded body remains readable from memory.
graphics.caption: Unloaded, loaded, and failed access have different consequences. Reader exit prevents new I/O; it does not erase a body that was already loaded.

sources.title: Lazy Load
sources.author: Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture
sources.supports: Partial objects retain a route to omitted data and fetch it on demand. Establishes lazy initialization, virtual proxy, value holder, and ghost as distinct implementation variants.

sources.title: SQLAlchemy — Column Loading Options
sources.supports: Initial queries can omit expensive columns; deferred attribute access later loads them through the owning Session. Detached objects cannot perform that lazy lookup. The example uses manual lazy initialization without SQLAlchemy.

sources.title: SQLAlchemy — Relationship Loading Techniques
sources.supports: Lazy attribute reads can produce N+1 queries; eager strategies and raiseload can control unplanned access. The article qualifies the count as one parent query plus N deferred queries rather than a universal query count.

sources.title: SQLAlchemy — Session thread and task ownership
sources.supports: A Session is stateful and not intended for unsynchronized concurrent use. The hand-written reader and document assume sequential, non-reentrant access and supply no single-flight coordination.

sources.title: SQLAlchemy — Detached instance lazy-loading error
sources.supports: Deferred access requires a usable loading context. Loading required attributes before detachment is one option; this example permits cached values after exit but forbids new reads.

sources.title: Python sqlite3 — transaction control via isolation_level
sources.supports: isolation_level=None supports this demo’s explicit connection configuration. Header and body statements are not enclosed in one multi-statement snapshot. Caller owns connection and transaction control.

patterns.example_provenance: Original DocumentReader selects only ID and title, then installs a callback capturing the original positive integer document ID. A unique sentinel distinguishes unloaded from loaded text, empty text, and NULL. First success publishes the value and releases the callback; missing-row, validation, or database failure propagates without marking it loaded, so a later access may try again. Reader exit rejects unloaded access before SQL while a cached body remains readable. The caller owns connection and transactions. Separate wrappers have independent caches; no writes, identity map, refresh, authorization, automatic retry loop, graph loading, concurrency synchronization, or performance benchmark is supplied.

patterns.title: Optimistic Offline Lock
patterns.short_description: Retain the version read at the start of an edit, and accept its final write only if that version still matches in an atomic save transaction.
use_when: A business edit spans multiple database transactions
Conflicts are uncommon and stale proposals can be reviewed explicitly
An expected version can be carried from read to conditional save
not_ideal_when: A short transaction already covers the whole operation
Costly edits conflict frequently and early reservation is preferable
Independent row versions are assumed to guard cross-row invariants automatically
prerequisites: Basic understanding of database transactions, object snapshots, and concurrent writers
example_user_queries: Two people open the same form and the later save overwrites the first person’s work.
We cannot hold a database transaction open while a user spends minutes editing.
How can a save tell whether the record changed since the editor opened it?
We check a version and then update separately, but there is still a race.
A stale write should fail without changing the newer stored data.
Our import script updates records without advancing their concurrency tokens.
An edit-log insertion fails after updating the row and we need both writes rolled back.
Should a conflict automatically retry the same replacement with the newest version?
We want a conditional edit API using the ETag from the original read.
Our row-version checks pass but an invariant involving several records can still break.

graphics.alt_text: Alice and Bob both read note version 1 and edit outside database transactions. Alice's conditional save matches version 1, writes her title, and commits version 2. Bob's later save still expects version 1, matches no row, and is rejected without overwriting Alice.
graphics.caption: The comparison and version advance belong to the same write. Two independent reads are allowed; the later stale save is rejected.

graphics.alt_text: A short save transaction conditionally changes the note and advances its version, then inserts the edit-log row. Both commit together. A stale version or later log failure rolls the transaction back. After conflict, the application reloads and reviews before making a new proposal; it does not blindly retry the old replacement.
graphics.caption: A matching version permits a provisional write, not an early success response. Report success only after the whole save transaction commits.

sources.title: Optimistic Offline Lock
sources.supports: David Rice’s entry in Fowler’s Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture establishes validation at completion for business operations spanning system transactions. Comparison and updates share one system transaction.

sources.title: SQLAlchemy — Configuring a Version Counter
sources.supports: Conditional UPDATE/DELETE checks the original version and exactly one affected row. Version-based protection is additional behavior, not a consequence of ordinary object identity.

sources.title: Microsoft — Handling Concurrency Conflicts
sources.supports: Expected tokens, zero-row conflict detection, application-managed tokens, and explicit resolution using original, proposed, and current database values.

sources.title: SQLite — Transaction
sources.supports: Single-writer behavior and BEGIN IMMEDIATE; short write transactions still acquire database locks. Physical contention is distinct from stale-version conflict.

sources.title: Python sqlite3 — affected rows and transaction configuration
sources.supports: The UPDATE affected-row count drives conflict detection. The caller owns connection closing; explicit transaction SQL uses an idle isolation_level=None connection.

sources.title: RFC 9110 — If-Match
sources.supports: Strong ETag comparison and failed preconditions prevent lost updates over HTTP. The server still must make storage validation and change atomic; no HTTP server is implemented.

patterns.example_provenance: Original immutable Note snapshots and parameterized conditional UPDATE by ID and original version. A successful short SQLite transaction changes title, advances the bounded positive integer version, inserts a local edit-log row, and commits before returning a new snapshot. A stale or deleted row produces Conflict; later log failures roll back all save writes. Two real connections deterministically demonstrate version 1 proposals, version 2 success, stale rejection, and an explicitly reviewed version 3 proposal. No automatic merge/retry, authorization, cross-row read-set validation, token-reset protection, external-effect coordination, or uncertain-commit recovery is implemented.

patterns.title: Pessimistic Offline Lock
patterns.short_description: Reserve write ownership before a long edit, retain that logical lock across requests, and validate ownership when saving or releasing it.
use_when: Lengthy competing edits frequently lose work at completion
Early write reservation is acceptable and can be made visible
A shared ownership manager and abandoned-lock policy can cover every participating writer
not_ideal_when: Rare conflicts are handled adequately by optimistic validation
A short operation fits ordinary database transaction locking
The design assumes a local logical lock automatically fences external resources or blocks uncooperative writers
prerequisites: Basic understanding of database transactions, object snapshots, and concurrent writers
example_user_queries: Our editors spend twenty minutes working before discovering that somebody else saved first.
We want to reserve a record before starting a long edit.
How can checkout ownership survive across requests without an open database transaction?
Two users both check whether a record is unlocked and then both acquire it.
An old edit handle must not save after a new owner has checked out the record.
A late unlock request is deleting somebody else’s newer reservation.
What happens to a committed application lock when the client crashes or disconnects?
We need to save changes and release ownership atomically so failure does not lose the lock.
Should a write reservation block ordinary read-only access too?
We need to distinguish a logical checkout refusal from the database being physically busy.

graphics.alt_text: A short acquisition transaction stores Alice's unique owner token and commits. Alice edits with no database transaction held open. Bob's competing acquisition is refused while that lock row exists. Alice later saves under an ownership check and removes the lock in one short transaction.
graphics.caption: The committed lock row outlives each database transaction. The reservation controls participating writers, not ordinary read-only access.

graphics.alt_text: After Alice's ownership ends, Bob acquires the note using a fresh token. A late save using Alice's old token matches no ownership row and is rejected. A late cancellation using that token cannot remove Bob's lock. Bob can still save or cancel his own reservation.
graphics.caption: Use a token per acquisition, not just a username or resource ID. Validate the current owner at the protected write and at release.

sources.title: Pessimistic Offline Lock
sources.supports: David Rice’s entry in Fowler’s Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture establishes early ownership for a business operation spanning requests, avoiding costly end-of-edit conflicts.

sources.title: PostgreSQL — Explicit Locking
sources.supports: Database row locks end with transactions; advisory locks have session or transaction lifetimes. Long user-input transactions and inconsistent acquisition order have resource/deadlock costs. This example instead uses committed ownership rows.

sources.title: SQLite — UPSERT
sources.supports: A targeted ON CONFLICT(note_id) DO NOTHING handles only the unique resource-key collision, not unrelated integrity failures.

sources.title: SQLite — Transaction
sources.supports: Short BEGIN IMMEDIATE transactions serialize lock-table and data changes; a durable logical row, rather than the physical write transaction, spans editing calls.

sources.title: Python sqlite3 — affected rows and transaction configuration
sources.supports: Affected-row checks distinguish acquisition, ownership, and release results. Connections are caller-owned, explicitly configured, and not held in database transactions during editing.

sources.title: Python uuid.uuid4
sources.supports: A random UUID supplies a fresh opaque acquisition identifier. It is not an authentication credential, clock, expiry policy, or monotonic distributed fencing token.

patterns.example_provenance: Original note checkout uses a unique persistent lock row and a fresh UUID token per acquisition. Short acquire/save/cancel transactions are committed between editing requests. Acquisition atomically reserves and reads a title; competing acquisition raises Busy. Save checks the note/token predicate, writes, and removes ownership in one local transaction; cancellation removes only matching ownership. Stale handles cannot save through or release a later token. Read-only queries remain allowed. A reservation survives connection closing and requires explicit trusted recovery after abandonment. No lease/expiry/renewal, fairness queue, multi-resource protocol, authentication, external-resource fencing, or bypass-writer protection is implemented. Unknown-commit reconciliation is not implemented.

patterns.title: Model-View-Controller
patterns.short_description: Separate application state and rules, presentation of that state, and interpretation of user input so each responsibility can change without absorbing the others.
use_when: Multiple displays share meaningful application state
Input interpretation and rendering need independent change
Business rules should be testable without UI machinery
not_ideal_when: A static display or small form is already clear as a few separated functions
Three folders are being used to hide unchanged coupling
The design assumes MVC provides persistence, synchronization, or concurrency guarantees automatically
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with state, functions, and user-input handling
example_user_queries: One button updates a count but another display still shows the old value.
Every screen copies the same business validation rules into its event handlers.
We want to add a second representation without rewriting how the application state changes.
Changing from keyboard input to buttons keeps breaking business behavior.
Our controller has become a huge class containing calculations and HTML formatting.
We need to test reservation rules without launching a browser or GUI toolkit.
Does the model in MVC mean only a database row or ORM class?
Our old snapshots look current even though the underlying model has changed.
We keep retrying a business action when only the screen rendering failed.
Why do desktop MVC diagrams and web MVC request flows show different interactions?

graphics.alt_text: User input reaches a controller, which translates reserve or cancel into a model operation. The model owns reservation state and capacity rules. After the operation, the composition code takes one snapshot and passes it to two views: a reserved-seat summary and a free-seat display. The controller does not format either view.
graphics.caption: The three roles separate responsibilities. These arrows describe this example's calls and data flow, rather than a mandatory message diagram for every MVC framework.

graphics.alt_text: Two displays first render the same snapshot with two reserved seats out of three and one free seat. A request to reserve two more is rejected by the model before state changes. A fresh snapshot still contains two reserved seats, and both displays remain consistent.
graphics.caption: The model rejects an invalid change before mutation. Re-rendering reads the resulting state; views do not invent or repair a different reservation count.

sources.title: The Model-View-Controller: Its Past and Present
sources.author: Trygve Reenskaug, 2003 author retrospective; teaching copy
sources.supports: Original author explains users inspecting and editing information through multiple perspectives. Used in place of unavailable original 1979 note URLs; the retrospective is explicitly identified.

sources.title: A Cookbook for Using the Model-View-Controller User Interface Paradigm in Smalltalk-80
sources.author: Glenn E. Krasner and Stephen T. Pope, JOOP, 1988; university-hosted copy
sources.supports: Historical primary publication describes separate domain, display, and interaction responsibilities and dependent-view collaboration. The teaching example does not reproduce Smalltalk widget scheduling.

sources.title: GUI Architectures
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Explains separated presentation, observer versus flow synchronization, and differences among classic MVC, application models, MVP, and passive views. The article explicitly labels its caller-controlled refresh policy rather than claiming all MVC uses the same message triangle.

sources.title: Rails — Action Controller Overview
sources.supports: A router selects a request controller action that processes input and makes model data available for output; request-oriented MVC differs from long-lived desktop collaborations.

sources.title: Rails — Action View Overview
sources.supports: Templates, layouts, and partials compose request/response presentation. The Python example has no HTML renderer or web server.

sources.title: Python dataclasses — Frozen instances
sources.supports: Frozen dataclasses prevent ordinary field assignment. The teaching snapshot contains only integers, remains a past value rather than a live binding, and does not provide synchronization or a security boundary.

patterns.example_provenance: Original sequential in-memory seat counter. Model methods enforce positive whole seat counts, capacity, and cancellation bounds independently of UI parsing. A controller accepts one to six ASCII digits and maps reserve/cancel actions to model operations, returning local status messages. The model snapshot supplies the remaining-seat query. Two pure text views format the same frozen model snapshot; outer composition explicitly refreshes them. Failed rules reject before mutation. No observer subscription, widget event loop, database, shared booking service, authorization, HTML output, transaction rollback, or cross-process concurrency guarantee is supplied.

patterns.title: Model-View-Presenter
patterns.short_description: Put a presenter between user gestures, application behavior, and screen updates so presentation decisions can be tested independently of GUI widgets.
use_when: Form event handlers contain substantial interaction and display decisions
Presentation behavior needs fast tests without GUI startup
Real and recording views should share one narrow screen-update contract
not_ideal_when: A static screen or trivial form is already clear
A declarative presentation-state framework already offers the needed testability
The design would copy business rules into a presenter or create two competing synchronization paths
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with objects, event handlers, and model/view separation
example_user_queries: Our form click handlers contain so much logic that every test needs a desktop window.
I want to test button enablement and error messages without loading the GUI toolkit.
The screen mixes parsing input, booking rules, and changing widget properties.
Can a recording object replace our real window while we test interaction behavior?
Our presenters know about concrete text fields and are still impossible to test in isolation.
Two screens perform the same workflow but produce inconsistent feedback.
We disabled the button but a queued click still attempted an invalid operation.
Bindings and manual updates keep overwriting the same field on our form.
What is the difference between a passive view and a supervising presenter?
A closed window still receives updates from its presenter after a background task finishes.

graphics.alt_text: A reservation view forwards quantity text to a presenter. The presenter commands the booking model and reads its remaining seats, then sends display text, button availability, and a message back to the view. In the Passive View example there is no direct model-to-view connection. A recording view implements the same render contract during tests.
graphics.caption: The presenter owns presentation coordination. The booking model owns capacity rules; a real or recording view receives the same screen values.

graphics.alt_text: A three-seat model accepts a reservation of two seats, and the presenter renders one remaining seat with Reserve enabled. A second request for two is rejected without mutation. The presenter reads the unchanged remaining count and renders the same availability with an error message. The recording view captures that screen result without a GUI.
graphics.caption: A rejected request changes the feedback, not the booking count. Tests observe the presenter's complete screen result through the view contract.

sources.title: MVP: Model-View-Presenter — The Taligent Programming Model for C++ and Java
sources.author: Mike Potel, Taligent, 1996
sources.supports: Historical primary source for MVP as a generalized MVC programming model with selections, commands, interactors, and application-level coordination. The article explicitly distinguishes its later Passive View example from the full Taligent framework.

sources.title: GUI Architectures
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Traces differences between Taligent, Dolphin, and test-oriented MVP; view synchronization ranges from observer updates to presenter-directed display. MVP is a family, not one universal triangle.

sources.title: Retirement note for Model View Presenter Pattern
sources.author: Martin Fowler, 2006
sources.supports: Fowler split his own MVP entry into Supervising Controller and Passive View. This does not establish that all MVP implementations became obsolete.

sources.title: Passive View
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Presenter/controller handles input and display values through a replaceable view contract; direct model/view synchronization is absent. Test doubles support testing most presentation behavior without widgets; real adapter wiring still needs verification.

sources.title: Supervising Controller
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Simple view/model mapping may remain in the view; presenter handles input and complex display decisions. Variant contrasts and original assessment-screen second context follow this distinction.

sources.title: typing — Protocol
sources.author: Python documentation
sources.supports: Structural protocol describes render for type checkers; annotations do not enforce runtime implementation. The demo uses standard-library typing and dataclasses, no GUI toolkit.

patterns.example_provenance: Original sequential in-memory reservation form demonstrating the Passive View variant of MVP. The booking model owns positive whole-seat and capacity rules. The presenter accepts one to three ASCII digits, translates expected BookingError failures into feedback, reads remaining seats, and sends one immutable Screen value to a View render contract. RecordingView stores those values without a model dependency or GUI. It deliberately receives a stale click after Reserve is disabled. The second assessment-screen context illustrates the Supervising Controller tradeoff described by Fowler; it is not a full binding implementation. No GUI event wiring, observers, async work, disposal implementation, persistence, cross-process concurrency, authorization, or rollback is supplied. Unexpected failures propagate; rendering failure does not undo a booking.

patterns.title: Presentation Model
patterns.short_description: Represent a screen's editable state, derived display properties, and actions in an object independent of widgets, then synchronize the view with that object.
use_when: Drafts, selection, validation, and command availability contain substantial presentation behavior
Presentation behavior needs tests without controls or mock windows
A declarative or explicitly synchronized view should use a widget-independent editing model
not_ideal_when: A static display or trivial form is clearer as a few separated functions
The proposed view model merely copies the entire domain object graph
The implementation assumes bindings, notification dependencies, or concurrency protection are automatic
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with editable state, model/view separation, and object properties
example_user_queries: Our Cancel button cannot undo typing because the text box edits the saved object directly.
I want to test draft validation and Apply button availability without constructing a window.
The screen stores its selection and dirty state only inside concrete widgets.
Typing changes a field but the derived error label and command availability stay stale.
Apply reads the old value because the binding has not copied the latest text yet.
We are redesigning the controls but want to retain the same editing behavior.
Our view model keeps calling concrete button and text box methods.
How can invalid temporary text coexist with a domain object that must always be valid?
Two-way binding keeps triggering a loop when we copy formatted values back to the screen.
An older search response overwrites the results of a newer query in our UI.

graphics.alt_text: A view maps its name field, feedback label, and enabled buttons to a presentation model containing draft text, validation, and Apply/Cancel behavior. Apply invokes the domain profile's rename operation; Cancel reloads the current name. The presentation model has no widget reference. The view owns mapping or binding.
graphics.caption: The draft models an editing session. The domain profile owns the accepted name; the view owns layout and synchronization with the presentation model.

graphics.alt_text: The accepted profile name is Ada. A blank draft produces an error, disables Apply, and leaves Ada unchanged. Replacing the draft with Grace enables Apply. Applying invokes domain validation and changes the accepted name to Grace, after which Apply and Cancel are disabled.
graphics.caption: Invalid text can remain visible without entering the domain model. Apply validates again before accepting a meaningful change.

sources.title: Presentation Model
sources.author: Martin Fowler, 2004 catalog entry and later naming note
sources.supports: State and behavior of the presentation are represented independently of GUI controls. The catalog lists MVVM as another name and acknowledges synchronization choices. This article uses one canonical Presentation Model record with MVVM aliases rather than creating duplicate entries.

sources.title: Introduction to Model/View/ViewModel pattern for building WPF apps
sources.author: John Gossman, original Microsoft blog; archived by Microsoft Learn
sources.supports: Primary author describes a binding-oriented MVC refinement with presentation-specific conversions, interaction modes, selection, and commands; provides MVVM lineage without treating every Presentation Model implementation as a WPF binding system.

sources.title: Model-View-ViewModel (MVVM)
sources.author: Microsoft .NET architecture documentation
sources.supports: View-model properties and commands, view independence, domain model separation, and coherent notifications including calculated properties. The Python example deliberately models explicit synchronization and does not implement framework notification APIs.

sources.title: Control When the TextBox Text Updates the Source
sources.author: Microsoft WPF documentation
sources.supports: Binding source updates can occur on focus loss, while typing, or explicitly. Binding timing must be selected so actions read current input.

sources.title: RelayCommand and RelayCommand<T>
sources.author: Microsoft CommunityToolkit.Mvvm documentation
sources.supports: Bindable commands and explicit NotifyCanExecuteChanged support; a command library does not universally infer all property-to-command dependency notifications.

patterns.example_provenance: Original sequential in-memory profile editing session. Profile owns a trimmed 1–40 Unicode-code-point name and independently validates rename before assignment. ProfileEditor owns raw drafts, feedback, derived Apply/Cancel availability, and actions without any view reference. Invalid Apply leaves accepted state unchanged; successful Apply normalizes and accepts the draft; Cancel reloads the current domain value, not an initial snapshot or save rollback. The console view explicitly pulls properties after each interaction and prints the domain name only as diagnostic evidence. No GUI, binding engine, change notification, async service, persistence, authorization, or concurrent-edit protection is implemented. A search-screen second context illustrates stale completion policy but is not runnable search code.

patterns.title: Front Controller
patterns.short_description: Channel a web application's requests through a common processing entry point, then delegate request-specific work to selected handlers.
use_when: Many mapped web requests share context, routing, completion, or error policies
Page-specific handlers duplicate request setup and accidentally diverge
Existing framework dispatch delegates need one intentional lifecycle
not_ideal_when: A tiny endpoint has no meaningful shared processing
The framework already provides the needed entry mechanism and another dispatcher would compete with it
The design assumes central request handling supplies authorization, rollback, or durable audit delivery
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with HTTP methods, request handlers, and response status codes
example_user_queries: Every page repeats the same locale setup and request logging code.
Our endpoints translate the same failure into different response formats.
I want one request lifecycle without putting every business operation in one giant controller.
Where should the shared dispatcher stop and the page-specific handler begin?
A direct URL reaches a page without passing through our common request checks.
We need unknown paths and unsupported methods to produce different outcomes.
Failed requests never reach our completion logging step.
A shared controller stores the current user and mixes data between requests.
Do we need a second routing layer when our framework already has a DispatcherServlet?
Does a single entry point mean every request must run on one server or one thread?

graphics.alt_text: Several web paths enter a shared front controller. It creates request-local context, chooses an allowlisted handler, and delegates path-specific work. Handler results or recognized routing failures return through common completion handling. Domain operations remain behind the handlers. Only paths mapped to this entry point participate.
graphics.caption: Centralize the request lifecycle while delegating action-specific work. The shared entry point is a logical boundary, not one mandatory server instance.

graphics.alt_text: An unknown path produces a 404 without calling a handler. A known path with the wrong recognized method produces a 405 with an Allow value. A selected handler that raises an exception produces a generic 500, with its request ID retained in internal diagnostics. All three cases reach the simulation's shared audit completion step.
graphics.caption: Routing misses and handler failures have distinct outcomes. Common completion processing also runs for the illustrated failures.

sources.title: Front Controller
sources.author: Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture catalog
sources.supports: Consolidates web request handling in one handler role, executes common behavior, and dispatches request-specific command work. Supports the central design move and differentiation from mere route selection.

sources.title: Core J2EE Patterns — Front Controller
sources.author: Core J2EE Patterns catalog, hosted by Oracle
sources.supports: Presentation-tier centralized entry, delegation, view/navigation responsibilities, and explicit allowance for several controller instances rather than a Singleton restriction. Primary basis for Presentation and UI State placement and logical versus physical centralization.

sources.title: DispatcherServlet
sources.author: Spring Framework reference documentation
sources.supports: Official concrete Front Controller implementation with shared request algorithm and configurable delegates; registration and mapping define the scope.

sources.title: DispatcherServlet — Processing
sources.author: Spring Framework reference documentation
sources.supports: Request attributes, locale resolution, mapping, execution, optional rendering, and exception resolution are separate processing responsibilities; framework configurations can differ.

sources.title: RFC 9110 — 405 Method Not Allowed
sources.author: IETF HTTP Semantics
sources.supports: A 405 response identifies an unsupported method for the target resource and must include the currently supported methods in Allow. The example is a bounded dispatch simulation rather than a complete HTTP server.

patterns.example_provenance: Original sequential request-dispatch simulation for an illustrative booking site. Inputs are already parsed exact paths and recognized GET/POST methods; language fr selects French while other values fall back to English. The controller copies allowlisted route configuration, creates a new frozen context per request, delegates callables returning Response, distinguishes 404 from 405 with Allow, translates handler exceptions or invalid response contracts into a generic 500, records exception class and local request ID internally, and appends a final audit status. In-memory sinks are assumed working. Local counters, lists, plain-text bodies, and exact route matching are teaching choices. No HTTP listener, URL canonicalization, authentication/authorization, template escaping, HEAD/OPTIONS synthesis, persistence, cross-process IDs, durable audit, transaction rollback, or concurrency guarantee is implemented. Spring is a sourced second context, not reproduced framework code.

patterns.title: Template View
patterns.short_description: Keep the shape of an HTML response in a template with markers for dynamic values, then render it with presentation data for the current request.
use_when: HTML structure dominates the output while request-specific values vary
Page layout needs to remain readable independently of data retrieval
Prepared presentation data can serve templates, partials, or shared layouts
not_ideal_when: A tiny fixed string is clearer as a direct formatter
The required output needs a different serializer or context-specific encoding
The template would hide substantial data access, authorization, or business workflows
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with HTML structure, strings, and context dictionaries
example_user_queries: Our request handler is full of HTML strings and punctuation that are hard to edit.
I want to change a page layout without rewriting how its data is retrieved.
A product name containing ampersands and angle brackets breaks the output.
Our template silently shows blank fields when the controller forgets required data.
How should zero values differ from missing template fields?
We keep mixing database queries and permissions into loops inside our markup.
Our HTML values are escaped twice and users see entity names on the page.
Can we reuse a parsed template without sharing the current user’s data?
Is string substitution enough to make values safe in HTML, scripts, and URLs?
Does the Template View pattern mean the same thing as GoF Template Method?

graphics.alt_text: A trusted HTML template contains name, availability, and units markers. A separate preparation step supplies raw display strings from application data. The renderer escapes those values for HTML text and substitutes them into the template, producing one HTML fragment. Template structure and request-specific data remain separate inputs.
graphics.caption: The template supplies structure; prepared data supplies values. In this example every dynamic slot is HTML text, and escaping happens at the rendering boundary.

graphics.alt_text: A product name containing an ampersand and angle brackets is encoded as HTML character references. The browser displays the original name as text rather than creating an extra element. Separately, omitting the required availability field raises a missing-field error before the buffered renderer returns HTML.
graphics.caption: Encoding preserves the intended text interpretation. A required-field failure is distinct from empty or zero-valued application data.

sources.title: Template View
sources.author: Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture catalog
sources.supports: HTML structure includes markers resolved with dynamic information; establishes the presentation output pattern rather than inheritance-based Template Method.

sources.title: string — Template strings
sources.author: Python documentation
sources.supports: Standard-library dollar-marked substitution, required-field KeyError behavior, and safe_substitute missing-placeholder semantics. This is simple string substitution, not HTML autoescaping or a full template language.

sources.title: html — html.escape
sources.author: Python documentation
sources.supports: Encodes ampersand, angle brackets, and optionally quotes for HTML text and quoted attribute use. The example deliberately restricts dynamic slots to HTML text.

sources.title: Template Designer Documentation
sources.author: Jinja / Pallets
sources.supports: Context variables, presentation expressions, repetition, conditional blocks, inheritance, and includes illustrate richer realizations without adding Jinja as a repository dependency.

sources.title: API — Environment, loaders, and autoescaping
sources.author: Jinja / Pallets
sources.supports: Reusable configuration and template loading, caching, and explicit HTML autoescape setup. Request-specific data should remain separate from shared environment configuration.

sources.title: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.author: OWASP
sources.supports: Output encoding depends on HTML text, attribute, JavaScript, CSS, or URL context; plain HTML escaping is not a universal injection defense. The example excludes dynamic attributes, URLs, scripts, and raw HTML.

patterns.example_provenance: Original product-card Template View with three complete files: trusted product.html, standard-library Python preparation/renderer, and demo. Nonblank raw names and nonnegative whole stock counts excluding booleans become display strings. A fixed template is loaded once relative to view.py; each rendering call makes a fresh HTML-escaped mapping and strict string.Template substitution. All markers are HTML text. Missing availability fails before a buffered string returns; zero stock is valid and displays Unavailable. Values are not recursively parsed as templates. No Jinja installation, template evaluation language, database, HTTP transport, streaming, dynamic attribute/URL/script context, authorization, rich HTML sanitization, rendered-page cache, or live-stock guarantee is supplied. The order-summary second context is explanatory, not a second runnable implementation.

patterns.title: Unidirectional Data Flow
patterns.short_description: Send interaction events to an explicit state owner, update state through a controlled path, and derive the UI from the resulting state.
use_when: Several UI elements must agree on shared feature state
Callbacks create difficult-to-reconstruct or out-of-order changes
Transitions need focused tests independently of widgets and service work
not_ideal_when: A local value already has one clear owner and a simple callback
The proposal sends every unrelated interaction through one global manager
The implementation assumes a one-way diagram supplies cancellation, ordering, authorization, or persistence
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with state, event callbacks, and asynchronous completion
example_user_queries: Older search results replace newer ones when responses arrive out of order.
Our spinner, error label, and result list disagree about the current request.
Callbacks keep mutating neighboring widgets and I cannot tell what caused a change.
I want to test state transitions without starting a browser or calling the network.
We need a clear owner for state shared by several components on one screen.
Does one-way data flow require putting all temporary application state in one global store?
Where should network requests happen if the state update function must stay pure?
An old completion repopulates the screen after the user clears the search field.
Rendering a component again accidentally starts another request.
Can replaying recorded UI actions reproduce state without re-running external effects?

graphics.alt_text: A user or service adapter supplies an event to the state owner. A controlled update produces a new UI state, which the view reads to render query, loading, results, and error consistently. The view sends subsequent interaction events back through the same entry path instead of directly changing shared state. Service work is outside the pure update in this example.
graphics.caption: Events request or report a change; state describes what the view should show. The feedback loop uses explicit transitions instead of competing UI mutations.

graphics.alt_text: Search ca becomes request 1, then search cat becomes request 2. A successful completion for request 2 installs cat results and ends loading. Request 1 then completes, but its identifier is stale, so the update returns the existing state and the cat results remain visible.
graphics.caption: Latest search intent wins because the update checks request identity and pending state. One-way flow alone does not choose this ordering policy.

sources.title: Redux Fundamentals — Concepts and Data Flow
sources.author: Redux official documentation
sources.supports: Recurring state, action, update, and rendering roles; explicit state transition path and immutable reducer realization. Redux is one design rather than a mandatory dependency for UDF.

sources.title: The Elm Architecture
sources.author: Official Elm guide
sources.supports: Model, Update, and View form a message-driven interactive architecture. Used as an established realization without assigning a sole inventor to broad unidirectional UI flow.

sources.title: UI layer — Manage state with Unidirectional Data Flow
sources.author: Android Developers architecture documentation
sources.supports: State flows toward UI elements, events toward the state holder; holders can have widget or screen scope, and application/domain data retain their own ownership.

sources.title: Side Effects Approaches
sources.author: Redux official documentation
sources.supports: Pure reducers exclude asynchronous work, timers, and other observable effects; middleware/adapters can run work and dispatch completion actions.

sources.title: createAsyncThunk — request identity and currentRequestId example
sources.author: Redux Toolkit official documentation
sources.supports: Request identifiers and pending/current checks are explicit reducer logic. Supports the example’s deliberate stale-result policy without implying UDF itself cancels work or chooses completion ordering.

sources.title: dataclasses — Frozen instances
sources.author: Python documentation
sources.supports: Frozen instances prevent ordinary attribute assignment; the example additionally limits nested state values to immutable primitives and tuples of strings. It is not a security boundary or automatic concurrent-store implementation.

patterns.example_provenance: Original sequential in-memory search-state simulation. Search intents create a new screen-local request ID, trim query text to at most 80 Unicode code points, and clear previous results/errors; an empty query invalidates older work without starting retrieval. A pure update accepts matching pending Loaded/Failed completions, ignores stale or duplicate terminal completions, validates IDs and current payload shapes, and returns frozen dataclass state containing immutable values. A pure text view reads the state. The composition owns assignment and manually supplies messages, including an older result arriving last. A real adapter would perform retrieval outside update and dispatch completion to the correct owner. Failed carries a prepared public display message. There is no network adapter, subscription/store framework, task cancellation, screen disposal implementation, cross-process IDs, concurrency synchronization, persistence, authorization, durable action history, or event-sourcing implementation. The settings-form second context is explanatory only.

patterns.title: Publish-Subscribe
patterns.short_description: Publish a message to a topic so independently interested subscribers can receive it without the publisher naming or calling each recipient.
use_when: Several independent applications react to the same published facts
Consumers need independent delivery progress and evolve separately
More worker capacity must be distinguished from more independent subscriptions
not_ideal_when: One receiver needs a direct immediate result
Workers should divide one task stream rather than each receive a copy
An ordered workflow, durable delivery, or exactly-once business effects are being assumed from fan-out alone
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with queues, asynchronous processing, and message contracts
example_user_queries: Our order service calls fulfillment, analytics, and notifications directly and every new consumer changes it.
Both applications need every event but our workers accidentally divide events between them.
Adding a second fulfillment worker caused each order to create two shipments.
We need each independent consumer to recover at its own processing pace.
Does a publish acknowledgment mean every subscriber completed the work?
A slow subscription fills its queue and blocks publication for other consumers.
We assumed reconnecting to a pub/sub channel would replay everything missed offline.
Our worker removed a message and crashed before applying its business change.
Do stable event IDs automatically prevent duplicate consumer effects?
How should creating, pausing, and deleting subscriptions affect their pending messages?

graphics.alt_text: OrderPlaced messages E901 and E902 fan out to fulfillment, analytics, and notifications subscriptions. Each subscription receives both messages as independent logical deliveries. Two fulfillment workers take a different message each from their shared fulfillment queue; they divide that workload rather than each receiving the full stream. Publisher acceptance does not mean subscriber work has completed.
graphics.caption: Create separate subscriptions for independent interests; add workers within a subscription to share its work. Delivery progress belongs to each subscription.

graphics.alt_text: Notifications has two pending messages and a capacity of two. A third publication is rejected before any queue changes, even though fulfillment has space. After notifications is unsubscribed and its backlog discarded, a later publication targets only fulfillment and analytics. This is the simulation's chosen capacity policy, not a universal broker guarantee.
graphics.caption: The bounded simulation rejects queue-full fan-out before enqueueing. One slow subscription can therefore block the publisher; deleting it explicitly discards its pending work.

sources.title: Publish-Subscribe Channel
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns
sources.supports: Original catalog fan-out mechanism and independent output subscriptions. The article distinguishes the idealized channel mechanism from infrastructure and end-to-end processing guarantees.

sources.title: Competing Consumers
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns
sources.supports: Workers sharing one delivery stream divide work, whereas separate pub/sub interests receive independent logical deliveries. Supports preserving the original three-interest/two-worker teaching distinction.

sources.title: Publisher-Subscriber pattern
sources.author: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center
sources.supports: Topic/filter routing, subscription lifetime, capacity, operational failure, and per-topic publisher/subscriber access controls. Not used to claim that all pub/sub systems retain offline messages.

sources.title: Redis Pub/Sub — Delivery semantics
sources.author: Redis official documentation
sources.supports: A concrete ephemeral at-most-once delivery contract without retry of lost deliveries. Contrasts with durable subscription implementations; the local Python queue model is not a Redis reproduction.

sources.title: Subscription overview
sources.author: Google Cloud Pub/Sub documentation
sources.supports: Acknowledgment deadline, possible redelivery, default at-least-once/no-ordering contract, retained-message replay prerequisites, and deletion losing the old subscription backlog.

sources.title: Fanout Amazon SNS notifications to Amazon SQS queues
sources.author: AWS official documentation
sources.supports: Managed topic-to-independent-queues implementation; preserves the earlier article’s sourced second context without pretending to implement AWS behavior.

patterns.example_provenance: Canonical data-publish-subscribe-distribution is revised in place, preserving its ID, order-distribution scenario, Data Engineering tags/verse, old title aliases, original primary asset path, and historical import provenance. Its primary collection moves to software-messaging-integration; the former capture collection retains an explicit cross-link. The original article and SVG are saved in ignored local review evidence. The new original sequential in-memory Python simulation stores separate bounded queues per named exact-topic subscription; two fulfillment workers destructively take different events from one queue. Frozen envelopes contain only string IDs and are shared as immutable values. Queue-full fan-out is preflight-rejected without queue changes under sequential execution, but is not crash atomic. Unsubscribe deletes queued backlog; no subscribers means no retained publication. Publish counts enqueues rather than completed effects. There are no network processes, acknowledgment/retry protocol, durable retention/replay, filters, producer/source transaction, consumer deduplication, authorization implementation, or concurrency guarantees.

patterns.title: Request-Reply
patterns.short_description: Pair a request message with a correlated reply so a caller can obtain an outcome without assuming that sending and receiving happen in one call stack.
use_when: A caller needs the outcome of a particular operation across a messaging boundary.
Several outstanding requests share a reply inbox and replies can arrive out of order.
Waiting must have an explicit deadline and pending-state owner.
not_ideal_when: A local function or short direct service call provides a simpler boundary.
A long-running job is better represented by an accepted job ID and later status or completion notification.
prerequisites: Understand messages, caller-owned pending context, and the distinction between transport acknowledgment and operation result.
example_user_queries: Our service replies arrive in a different order from the requests and get paired with the wrong screen.
We want several outstanding operations to share one callback queue.
How does a worker know where to send its answer without hard-coding every client?
A reply arrives after the caller has already stopped waiting.
A repeated server response completes the same application operation twice.
Our pending calls consume memory forever when a remote service does not answer.
Does a timeout mean the remote debit definitely did not happen?
We need to distinguish an unknown product response from a missing response.
An old reply matched a new request after the client restarted.
We publish work through a broker but need a particular result before continuing.

graphics.alt_text: The desk sends inventory requests desk:1 and desk:2 with the return address desk.replies. The inventory service sends replies to that inbox, copying each request ID into its reply correlation ID. Reply desk:2 arrives before desk:1; the desk selects the matching pending context by ID rather than arrival order.
graphics.caption: The return address selects the destination; the correlation ID selects the waiting request within it. Reply order need not match request order.

graphics.alt_text: A pending request has a local deadline of 500 milliseconds. A valid reply received at 499 milliseconds completes that request. If the request is still pending at 500 milliseconds, expiration removes its context. A later reply is ignored. The remote service can still have completed the work; local expiration is not remote cancellation.
graphics.caption: This example accepts replies only before the local deadline. Expiration releases pending state; it neither cancels remote work nor proves failure.

sources.title: Request-Reply
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns
sources.supports: Two-message conversation and blocking versus callback reception; messaging does not require a blocked sender thread.

sources.title: Return Address
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns
sources.supports: Reply destination carried in request metadata so the replier does not hard-code callers.

sources.title: Correlation Identifier
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns
sources.supports: A reply correlation identifier associates the answer with the outstanding request.

sources.title: RabbitMQ tutorial — Remote procedure call (RPC)
sources.author: RabbitMQ official documentation
sources.supports: Callback queue and correlation mechanism; duplicate replies after server redelivery; correlation is not server-side idempotency.

sources.title: Request-reply
sources.author: NATS official documentation
sources.supports: Request/reply over pub/sub using reply inboxes; ordinary request accepts the first answer, while collecting multiple answers needs a gathering policy.

sources.title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter
sources.author: AWS Builders’ Library
sources.supports: Timeout bounds waiting but does not imply that side effects did not happen; retry safety and overload costs.

patterns.example_provenance: Original checkout inventory conversation, not copied from the sources’ code. Sequential trusted-envelope simulation with a shared reply inbox, generated session-scoped IDs, two pending contexts, explicit nondecreasing local milliseconds, exact-deadline rejection, and manual expiration. Local acceptance once is not server idempotency. No networking, remote cancellation, payload validator, retry, broker, persistence, restart recovery, or synchronization. Session freshness and allowed return-address routing are explicit deployment responsibilities. Stock counts are observations rather than reservations.

patterns.title: Correlation Identifier
patterns.short_description: Carry an explicit identifier across related messages so a receiver can recover the correct conversation context regardless of arrival order or individual message identity.
use_when: Several operations share a reply path or messages arrive out of order.
Intermediaries replace message envelopes while the conversation must retain its identity.
Business identifiers or tracing identifiers are too broad to distinguish pending operations.
not_ideal_when: A local call stack or dedicated transport association already identifies the waiting context.
A value is being attached without defining its matching scope or lifecycle.
prerequisites: Understand messages, pending conversation context, and the distinction between message identity and business identity.
example_user_queries: Two quote requests for the same order overwrite one another in our pending map.
Our replies arrive out of order and the right result reaches the wrong operation.
A relay creates a new envelope and we can no longer associate the reply with the original caller.
Should the reply have its own message ID or reuse the original request ID?
We share one reply inbox across many outstanding conversations.
An old reply completed new work after our client restarted its counter.
A duplicate answer should not resume the same local continuation twice.
We have one trace ID for a checkout but several different requests pending inside that trace.
Does attaching a conversation value make retrying a remote write safe?
A reply from the wrong provider must not consume a valid waiting context.

graphics.alt_text: Economy and express quote requests for the same order O42 carry different correlation IDs, desk:C1 and desk:C2. A relay changes the express envelope message ID from desk:M2 to relay:M9 while preserving desk:C2. Replies have their own message IDs; the matcher uses correlation IDs to recover the economy or express context.
graphics.caption: Preserve the conversation value across envelope changes. Two operations on the same order need distinct matching contexts.

graphics.alt_text: The matcher receives a reply for desk:C2. An untrusted or unexpected source does not consume its context. A valid reply from the expected carrier completes the express quote and removes desk:C2. A duplicate then has no pending match. Explicit cleanup removes abandoned desk:C3 so its later reply is also ignored.
graphics.caption: Lookup and completion are separate decisions. This example checks the expected source before removing a pending context, and accepts one valid answer per context.

sources.title: Correlation Identifier
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns
sources.supports: The established request/reply correlation pattern: reply metadata identifies its originating request.

sources.title: Correlation and Conversations
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe
sources.supports: Conversation Identifier as an alternate name; independent conversation identity preserved across intermediaries that assign new envelope IDs.

sources.title: Return Address
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns
sources.supports: Reply destination is a separate concern from selecting a conversation within a shared inbox.

sources.title: RabbitMQ tutorial — Remote procedure call (RPC)
sources.author: RabbitMQ official documentation
sources.supports: Shared callback queues, matching correlation values, unknown responses, and duplicate replies after server redelivery. Local completion is distinct from server idempotency.

sources.title: Trace Context
sources.author: W3C Recommendation
sources.supports: A trace-id identifies a distributed trace, while parent context identifies its caller relationship. The article infers why a single whole-checkout trace ID can be too broad for distinct application conversations.

sources.title: Idempotent requests
sources.author: Stripe official API documentation
sources.supports: An explicit idempotency contract for retry safety is distinct from merely matching replies by correlation value; no implementation-specific retention or caching guarantee is generalized.

patterns.example_provenance: Original sequential two-quote teaching scenario for order O42. The matcher generates fresh-session correlation IDs independently of envelope message IDs, preserves a correlation value across a simulated relay rewrite, and recovers order/mode context on a validated reply from the expected source. Two pending contexts maximum; explicit owner cleanup; session freshness is an assumption. Source identity must come from a trusted adapter. No broker, reply routing, real authentication, timers, persistent workflow, server deduplication, retry, or concurrency synchronization. Prices are nonnegative integer US dollar cents, not reservations or production shipping calculations.

patterns.title: Content-Based Router
patterns.short_description: Inspect a message's data and select the appropriate output channel, keeping destination-selection rules out of the producer and downstream handlers.
use_when: Messages entering one channel require different processing paths selected from message fields.
Producers should not know concrete handler endpoints or routing exceptions.
Routing rules need explicit overlap, fallback, invalid-input, and replay policies.
not_ideal_when: Every message goes to the same fixed destination.
A local conditional inside one component is sufficient.
Every interested receiver needs its own copy rather than one selected route.
prerequisites: Understand message channels, schema validation, predicate ordering, and the difference between route selection and delivery.
example_user_queries: Checkout knows every fulfillment handler and each routing exception requires changing the producer.
We need expensive express orders to reach review before any shipment is started.
Two routing conditions match and both handlers process the same order.
An early broad routing rule hides the more specific rules below it.
We need a visible fallback for valid messages with an unfamiliar product category.
A missing amount was treated as zero and sent to ordinary fulfillment.
How can we prove whether a decision selected a channel or actually delivered the message?
Our replays reach different handlers after routing rules change.
We want a message header to select a route without letting the sender choose arbitrary endpoint URLs.
A router crashes after forwarding and we need to handle the resulting repeated delivery.

graphics.alt_text: A valid physical express order for 100000 US dollar cents enters an ordered routing policy. The high-value rule matches before the express rule, selecting manual-review only. A physical express order for 99999 cents reaches priority-fulfillment instead. The selected channel is a decision, not proof that a consumer completed the work.
graphics.caption: First match is a policy: a high-value express order selects review, not both review and priority fulfillment. The boundary is 100000 US dollar cents.

graphics.alt_text: An unfamiliar but structurally valid service order selects unclassified-review through the otherwise rule. A negative amount selects invalid-messages before business rules run. Selecting priority-fulfillment says nothing about enqueue acknowledgment or completed shipment; those are later boundaries with their own failure handling.
graphics.caption: Separate valid-but-unmatched messages from malformed input, and route selection from delivery and business completion. None of these paths silently drops a message in the model.

sources.title: Content-Based Router
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns
sources.supports: Established content-driven destination selection and maintainability of routing rules; not every Message Router is content-based.

sources.title: Recipient List
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns
sources.supports: Computing several intended recipients and forwarding to each differs from selecting one output path.

sources.title: Message Filter
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns
sources.supports: Passing or discarding through one output is distinct from the illustrated single-destination choice among outputs.

sources.title: Choice
sources.author: Apache Camel 4.22.x official documentation
sources.supports: Choice implements Content-Based Router with ordered first-match when predicates, otherwise fallback, and header-based selection. The article does not generalize first-match to every router or use startup precondition mode.

sources.title: Consumer Acknowledgements and Publisher Confirms
sources.author: RabbitMQ official documentation
sources.supports: Input consumer acknowledgments, output publisher confirms, eventual processing, and crash/requeue responsibilities are separate from computing a destination.

patterns.example_provenance: Original shop policy and threshold, not copied framework code. A pure sequential function validates an exact five-field schema, selects one allowed logical channel using ordered first-match predicates, retains valid unknown kinds for classification, and classifies malformed messages separately. Frozen decisions record rule name and orders-v1. Amounts are nonnegative integer US dollar cents; threshold 100000 means $1000. A high-value rule precedes all ordinary routes, including digital and unknown kinds. No enqueue, broker, actual review or fulfillment, acknowledgments, parser, transport retry, synchronization, or dynamic policy loading. Version labels record a decision; they do not pin replay behavior.

patterns.title: Message Translator
patterns.short_description: Convert a message into the representation another application expects while making field mappings, units, meaning, and unsupported cases explicit at the integration boundary.
use_when: Independent applications exchange incompatible message representations.
Partner-specific conversion is spreading into downstream handlers.
Codes, units, precision, and unsupported values need a named mapping owner.
not_ideal_when: Both applications already share a suitable contract.
Required meaning is unavailable without enrichment or a separate business decision.
A transformation is assumed reversible despite omitted data or lossy conversions.
prerequisites: Understand source/target schemas, semantic correspondence, message identity, and the difference between conversion and delivery.
example_user_queries: Every warehouse handler contains the same carrier-specific field conversions.
