Our partner sends kilograms as text but the receiver requires integer grams.
Renaming a measurement field left its numeric value in the wrong unit.
A new carrier status code was silently converted into a ready-for-pickup event.
The source has fractional grams that the target cannot represent without rounding.
We need to preserve source event identity when constructing a new message schema.
Does changing JSON to XML make the two applications agree about business meaning?
A payload failed conversion after some fields had already been changed in place.
We need to know which mapping rules produced a message during replay investigation.
Our integration needs packaging weight that is absent from the source message.

graphics.alt_text: Carrier schema 1 supplies event E901, parcel P42, gross_kg as the decimal string 1.250, and state R. Mapping carrier-a-v1/warehouse-v2 preserves event and parcel identity, converts kilograms to 1250 integer grams, and maps the documented carrier code R to ready_for_pickup. Warehouse schema 2 receives a newly constructed message with mapping provenance.
graphics.caption: Translate a declared contract, not just field names. The example preserves identity and gross-mass meaning while changing units and status representation.

graphics.alt_text: A known carrier status R and weight 1.250 kilograms produce a complete output with 1250 grams. Unknown state X produces a TranslationError without output. Weight 1.2505 kilograms would require 1250.5 grams, which the target cannot represent; it is rejected instead of rounded. Original input stays unchanged, and error retention belongs to the caller.
graphics.caption: Unknown meaning and unsupported precision are translation failures. This example emits no partial target and does not silently substitute a status or rounded weight.

sources.title: Message Translator
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns
sources.supports: Established messaging format-compatibility pattern and relationship to Adapter. Existing Reshape at Boundaries applies this mechanism to a narrower structural scope; it is retained as a related entry rather than replaced.

sources.title: Canonical Data Model
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns
sources.supports: Shared-model indirection and translators at its boundaries; a translator does not by itself require a canonical model.

sources.title: Content Enricher
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns
sources.supports: Missing information requires augmentation or computation with its own assumptions, rather than being invented through a representation conversion.

sources.title: Messaging Mapper
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns
sources.supports: Distinct mapping between domain objects and messaging infrastructure; avoids treating Messaging Mapper as an exact alias for Message Translator.

sources.title: Message Translator
sources.author: Apache Camel 4.22.x official documentation
sources.supports: Transforms, set-body operations, processors/beans, templates, and data formats as implementation choices. The article does not claim those tools establish semantic correspondence.

sources.title: decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic
sources.author: Python official documentation
sources.supports: Exact decimal strings and local arithmetic precision. The original example bounds lexical precision, sets local precision 20, and rejects fractional grams rather than rounding.

patterns.example_provenance: Original one-to-one carrier-a schema-1 to warehouse schema-2 parcel projection. Gross mass means the same thing on both sides by contract; state R means ready for pickup and D means dispatched in the teaching source. Exact decimal strings convert to whole integer grams in 1..50000 with fixed local precision; unknown codes and unsupported values raise TranslationError before target construction. Source namespace, event ID, parcel identity, and mapping provenance are retained. Identifiers follow a bounded ASCII grammar. No source authentication, network, broker, persistent quarantine, input parsing/size controls, external enrichment, rounding, deduplication, automatic replay pinning, concurrency, or reverse byte reconstruction. Existing narrower Data Engineering articles and the GoF Adapter remain intact.

patterns.title: Anti-Corruption Layer
patterns.short_description: Protect a local domain model by translating an external system's concepts, operations, and failures through an interface expressed in the local model's own terms.
use_when: An independently owned model would otherwise dictate local business concepts.
An external or legacy capability must be used without spreading its vocabulary and failures through the local domain.
A migration needs semantic compatibility while meaningful local operations remain stable.
not_ideal_when: The external model already fits and adopting it is an acceptable deliberate choice.
Only a mechanical interface conversion is needed.
A shared universal layer would erase useful distinctions between several local contexts.
prerequisites: Understand bounded contexts, semantic correspondence, explicit identity mapping, and the distinction between local policy and integration uncertainty.
example_user_queries: Our checkout code now contains supplier status codes and vendor-specific exceptions.
The supplier calls an inventory record active but that does not mean its units are sellable.
We need to integrate an external system without redesigning our business model around it.
External product identifiers do not map to our local SKU identifiers reliably.
A supplier timeout was converted into zero stock and treated as a business fact.
Renaming vendor response fields still leaves the vendor lifecycle in every domain operation.
We need local error meanings instead of leaking the external SDK throughout the application.
Our new service and the remaining monolith use different meanings for the same concepts.
Should the integration component decide order policy or only supply facts the domain understands?
A temporary migration adapter is becoming a permanent shared model for unrelated teams.

graphics.alt_text: The shop asks availability for local SKU-42. A shop-owned Anti-Corruption Layer maps it to supplier ITEM-9 and calls the supplier lookup. The supplier's active record reports quantity 10, committed 7, and damaged 2. The layer returns a local Availability with one sellable unit; the shop's own model decides whether a request for two units can be supplied.
graphics.caption: The boundary translates capability and meaning. Supplier active status does not become local availability, and the local supply rule remains in the domain model.

graphics.alt_text: A valid supplier snapshot with quantity 10, committed 7, and damaged 2 yields one sellable unit; a request for two is false under the local rule. A timeout yields StockUnavailable, not a zero-stock Availability. An unmapped local SKU fails before calling the supplier. These outcomes do not reserve or change stock.
graphics.caption: Insufficient stock is a known local result. Missing evidence is an integration failure, and must not be disguised as a business fact.

sources.title: DDD Reference — Anticorruption Layer
sources.author: Eric Evans, Domain Language
sources.supports: Original context-mapping pattern: an isolating layer presents upstream functionality through the downstream domain model and translates in one or both directions. Original spelling Anticorruption Layer; protection is about model independence, not a security access-control list.

sources.title: Anti-Corruption Layer pattern
sources.author: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center
sources.supports: Semantic model protection; local contracts; component or service implementation; avoiding business policy/orchestration in translation; validation, observability, consistency, and operational responsibilities.

sources.title: Anti-corruption layer pattern
sources.author: AWS Prescriptive Guidance
sources.supports: Domain semantics, migration in either calling direction, class-versus-service implementations, and latency, scaling, team, monitoring, and decommissioning considerations. The article does not generalize migration-specific retirement requirements to permanent domain boundaries.

sources.title: Bounded Context
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Independent coherent models can use familiar terms differently; explicit relationships and mappings are required. The inventory code and arithmetic assumptions are original teaching material, not source-provided stock rules.

patterns.example_provenance: Original supplier-stock integration protecting a shop-owned Availability model and StockUnavailable contract. Local SKU-42 maps explicitly to supplier ITEM-9. A version-1 active record contains 10 total units including 7 committed and 2 damaged; the declared coherent, disjoint-category contract yields 1 sellable unit. Active record status is not mapped to a supply Boolean. The domain owns can_supply; the boundary validates identity/schema/counts, maps TimeoutError to a local exception, and copies caller mappings. Unknown mappings and unusable data do not become zero stock. No network, authentication, persistent workflow, cache/freshness protocol, automatic retries, client lifecycle, synchronization, atomic reservation, or stock mutation. Messaging and Integration is the primary home for the integration boundary; Bounded Context and Ports and Adapters express overlaps through links only.

patterns.title: Splitter
patterns.short_description: Break a composite message into separately addressable messages so each meaningful part can be processed independently.
use_when: A composite message contains parts with independently meaningful processing responsibilities.
Children need separate destinations, retries, or work scheduling.
Child identity and parent context must survive replay without relying on SKU or position.
not_ideal_when: One small message can be handled coherently by one consumer and a local loop.
The parts share an invariant that independent processing would violate.
The only need is broadcasting the same publication to independent interests.
prerequisites: Understand immutable message identity, semantic part boundaries, bounded work, and the difference between construction, publication, and business completion.
example_user_queries: Our fulfillment consumer needs one order line but receives an order with many lines.
We want each document page to be processed independently while retaining its document identity.
Two lines contain the same SKU and our retry keys collapse them into one job.
Retrying a partially published batch repeats children that already reached the broker.
How do we retain parent context when splitting a composite event into child messages?
A malformed late element is discovered after earlier items have already been sent.
Our empty batch never produces a child result and the parent workflow waits forever.
Parallel workers finish order lines in a different order from their sequence numbers.
We need to distinguish fan-out of the same event from decomposition into separate work items.
A large parent message creates too many queued children and exhausts worker capacity.

graphics.alt_text: Order event E901 for O42 contains L1 with two BOOK units and L2 with one MUG unit. Splitter creates two immutable child messages, retaining parent E901 and order O42. Each child has its own line ID and one-based position within a two-part sequence.
graphics.caption: Each child contains one line and necessary parent context. Child identity follows the line; sequence position describes its place in this parent payload.

graphics.alt_text: A bounded input is fully validated before two children are returned. An invalid second line instead raises SplitError and returns no children. Later publication is a separate boundary: child L1 can be accepted while sending L2 fails, leaving a partial delivery that requires recovery.
graphics.caption: All-or-none construction is local to this function. It provides no atomic publication, rollback of external effects, or exactly-once processing.

sources.title: Splitter
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf
sources.supports: Established composite-to-part messaging, semantic items or subsets, and order-line motivation. Historical Sequencer.html URL is not used as a canonical name or alias.

sources.title: Message Sequence
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf
sources.supports: Group identity, position, and total size or end indicators. These fields convey sequence information rather than ensuring ordered completion.

sources.title: Aggregator
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf
sources.supports: Separate correlation, completeness condition, and aggregation algorithm; missing, delayed, and duplicate child-result concerns are distinct from splitting.

sources.title: Split EIP, Apache Camel 4.22
sources.author: Apache Software Foundation
sources.supports: Materialized and streaming execution, unknown initial streaming size, retained-memory tradeoffs, and explicit parallel/failure/unit-of-work options. The article does not equate Camel unit-of-work sharing with transactional rollback of arbitrary external effects.

sources.title: Consumer Acknowledgements and Publisher Confirms
sources.author: RabbitMQ
sources.supports: Publisher acceptance and consumer delivery acknowledgments are independent boundaries; neither is application-level confirmation that every child business effect completed.

patterns.example_provenance: Original bounded order-line splitter with strict decoded-input fields, ASCII identifiers, 0..100 lines and 1..1000 integer physical units per line. Two frozen child values retain immutable event/order/line identity, SKU, units, one-based position and size. Structured (parent event ID, line ID) keys distinguish repeated SKUs and survive replay and reordering; event IDs must be unique within the integration and immutable. Full validation precedes tuple construction. Empty input returns no children, invalid late elements return no partial tuple, and input is not mutated. No broker, publication, acknowledgments, deduplication store, aggregation, concurrent mutation, durable handoff, authentication, or external effects are implemented. Order-line motivation follows EIP; code, figures, bounds, fixtures, and policies are original.

patterns.title: Aggregator
patterns.short_description: Hold related messages as a group, decide when the group is ready, and combine its contents into one meaningful result.
use_when: Several independently arriving results must inform one downstream decision.
Expected members, a quorum, or a time-bounded release policy can be defined explicitly.
Duplicate, delayed, and reordered reports must not falsely complete a group.
not_ideal_when: One synchronous operation already holds all values and ordinary collection processing suffices.
Consumers should react independently rather than wait for a combined result.
Membership and completion semantics cannot be established reliably.
prerequisites: Understand correlation scope, distinct member identity, state ownership, monotonic deadlines, and the separate boundaries of local release and reliable publication.
example_user_queries: We need one status summary after several order-line workers report independently.
A repeated worker result is counted twice and completes the order group too early.
How do we know a result group is complete when replies arrive out of order?
One missing response keeps a message group in memory forever.
A late result from an earlier operation is entering the current order summary.
Should a deadline produce a partial result or an explicitly incomplete outcome?
Two copies of a worker result disagree about the number of packed units.
Several service instances can release the same message group concurrently.
A crash between saving completion and publishing the summary loses the output.
Closed groups are forgotten and delayed duplicate messages recreate old work.

graphics.alt_text: Operation E901 expects line results L1 and L2. L2 reports one packed unit, an identical L2 redelivery adds no new member, and L1 reports two packed units. Only the two distinct expected results release one complete summary totaling three physical units.
graphics.caption: Completeness depends on distinct expected members, not delivery count. This sum is independent of arrival order; other combination rules may require explicit ordering.

graphics.alt_text: A group is open while only L1 is known. Arrival of L2 before the fixed 100 millisecond deadline closes it as complete. If L2 arrives at exactly 100 milliseconds, the group instead closes as timed out with L2 missing and no total. Valid late results and later polls do not release a second outcome.
graphics.caption: This example uses an absolute deadline: now_ms must be less than 100 to contribute. Timeout reports missing evidence; it does not cancel a worker or prove that packing failed.

sources.title: Aggregator
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf
sources.supports: Established message-group pattern with correlation, completeness condition, aggregation algorithm, and alternate wait-all, time-bounded, first-best, and externally triggered policies. The packing example is original, following the established order-result context.

sources.title: Aggregator
sources.author: Spring Integration
sources.supports: Stored group progress, correlation and release strategies, per-group locking, shared ownership across servers, completion metadata, expiry and late arrivals. Specific framework defaults are not generalized to the Python example.

sources.title: Aggregate EIP, Apache Camel 4.22
sources.author: Apache Software Foundation
sources.supports: Explicit completion conditions, inactivity versus periodic timeout policies, persistent repositories, closed correlation keys and configurable timeout behavior. The example instead chooses a fixed absolute deadline and incomplete outcome.

sources.title: Consumer Acknowledgements and Publisher Confirms
sources.author: RabbitMQ
sources.supports: Separate publisher-to-broker and consumer delivery confirmation boundaries; neither establishes atomic progress storage plus summary publication or end-to-end exactly-once processing.

sources.title: Event Aggregator
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Event subscription indirection centralizes sources and forwards notifications; it is not used as an alias for stateful messaging group completion and reduction.

sources.title: DDD Aggregate
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Domain-object unit with a root guarding integrity, distinct from the message-group aggregator. Existing aggregate article and canonical ID are preserved.

patterns.example_provenance: Original one-group packing-result simulation. One operation ID has a fixed copied set of 1..100 distinct expected line IDs; ASCII identifiers are 1..64 characters. Authorized input reports 0..1000 packed physical units; complete means every expected member reported, not order fulfillment. Calls are sequential on a nondecreasing integer monotonic millisecond clock starting at zero. Identical open-group duplicates do not advance membership; conflicting open-group duplicates are rejected. The commutative sum is arrival-order independent. A fixed absolute deadline expires at now_ms >= deadline_ms; timeout records sorted missing members with total_units None. Each instance releases at most one frozen outcome and retains it, never reopening for valid late messages. The caller schedules polling and preserves state/configuration through the API. Empty work is handled upstream. No broker, durable state, restart recovery, global active-group bound, source authentication, concurrency control, automatic timer, cancellation, reliable output handoff, or exactly-once effect guarantee.

patterns.title: Idempotent Receiver
patterns.short_description: Make repeated deliveries of the same logical message leave the receiver's protected business state as if that message had been handled once.
use_when: A receiver can see repeated deliveries after lost acknowledgments, crashes, or replay.
A nonrepeatable local effect must be protected without suppressing distinct intended changes.
Shared workers need durable duplicate recognition coordinated with the business state they change.
not_ideal_when: Every effect is already safely repeatable at its destination and the additional ledger serves no need.
A local marker is expected to make an unrelated remote operation atomic.
Message identity, payload consistency, or the possible replay period cannot be established.
prerequisites: Understand stable logical message identity, receiver/source scope, transactional state changes, concurrency, and acknowledgment after commit.
example_user_queries: Our worker commits stock changes but gets the same message again after losing its acknowledgment.
Two consumers check the same event ID at once and both apply the inventory increment.
A receiver records a message as processed but crashes before making the business change.
Every retry gets a new request ID and our duplicate filter lets repeated effects through.
Different source systems emit the same event ID and one receipt is suppressed incorrectly.
We need to reject an event ID reused with a different quantity or SKU.
A deployment renamed the consumer and replayed already committed effects.
How long must we retain processed-message records if operators can replay old messages?
Our local deduplication flag does not stop a remote email or payment from being repeated.
Identical receipt contents sometimes mean a legitimate new delivery rather than a duplicate.

graphics.alt_text: Warehouse event E901 adds 40 mug units and records its processed identity in the same database transaction. The acknowledgment is lost. Redelivery with the same consumer, source, event ID, SKU, and quantity finds the committed record and leaves stock at 40. A distinct event E902 can legitimately add another 40.
graphics.caption: The receiver protects the stock change, not the number of deliveries. The same intended receipt is suppressed; a different receipt with identical contents remains legitimate work.

graphics.alt_text: Before database commit, a failed stock constraint rolls back both the processed-message row and stock change, so retry remains possible. After commit, losing acknowledgment leaves both records durable, so redelivery is a duplicate. An external email or remote API call sits outside this database boundary and has no protection from this transaction.
graphics.caption: The atomic boundary contains the processed record and inventory update. Acknowledgment follows commit; external effects require their own reliable handoff or idempotency contract.

sources.title: Idempotent Receiver
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf
sources.supports: Established receiver behavior: repeated deliveries preserve the effect of one message, through inherently idempotent semantics or explicit duplicate recognition.

sources.title: Idempotent Consumer
sources.author: Chris Richardson

sources.title: Transaction
sources.author: SQLite

sources.author: SQLite

sources.author: Spring Integration

patterns.example_provenance: Original file-backed SQLite stock receipt endpoint. A stable stock-receipts consumer, authorized source, and logical event ID form the processed key; stored SKU and units detect conflicting reuse. ASCII identifiers are 1..64 characters; each receipt carries 1..1000 physical units and stock has a 1000000-unit per-SKU constraint. BEGIN IMMEDIATE serializes writers before lookup. Processed identity/payload and stock increment share one transaction; return statuses occur only after commit. Caller owns initially idle dedicated connections and closes them; initialization failure closes before propagation. Reopening demonstrates replay after lost acknowledgment, and E902 remains distinct from E901 despite identical contents. The incrementing UPSERT alone is not idempotent. No broker, external effects, source authentication, ledger cleanup, multi-destination atomicity, automatic retry, or power-loss testing. The temporary demo directory is removed at the end. Existing Idempotent Writes remains a broader destination-focused article and is linked, not duplicated or rehomed.

patterns.title: Dead Letter Channel
patterns.short_description: Move messages that leave the normal delivery or processing policy to a separate recovery channel, preserving evidence and ownership until their outcome is resolved.
use_when: Messages cannot continue under normal delivery or retry policy but their unresolved obligation must remain recoverable.
Exhausted dependency failures need a separate, owned diagnosis and recovery path.
Normal processing can progress for independent work while failed work is retained safely.
not_ideal_when: A transient failure can recover within the normal bounded retry policy.
Every message fails because of a systemic defect that should instead pause processing.
No owner, durable handoff, retention window, or safe replay policy can be established.
prerequisites: Understand delivery versus processing failures, authoritative attempt semantics, safe handoff, retained evidence, replay identity, and per-key dependencies.
example_user_queries: One warehouse instruction keeps retrying and blocks unrelated work.
We need to preserve exhausted messages without pretending their business work succeeded.
A failed transfer to our error queue deleted the only recoverable source copy.
Our failure channel fills up and we need backpressure rather than silent message loss.
An unsupported message and a valid message facing an unavailable dependency need different recovery.
Nobody owns messages after they leave the normal queue and the oldest failures are expiring.
Replaying the whole failure backlog overloads a destination that just recovered.
Redriven messages get new transport IDs and repeat effects already committed earlier.
Skipping one failed command breaks later commands for the same document.
We need original bytes and consumer-version context to investigate why delivery stopped.

graphics.alt_text: Instruction E901 remains on the normal orders path while classified dependency failures are within a three-failure budget. At the third failure, a safe handoff preserves the original instruction and failure context in the dead letter channel. Diagnosis and repair precede controlled redrive through the normal idempotent receiver.
graphics.caption: A parked instruction remains unresolved work. Redrive is an explicit recovery decision after repair, not an automatic loop that resets the retry budget.

graphics.alt_text: One local SQLite transaction inserts the complete failure record and deletes the pending record. Commit leaves the instruction in the dead letter channel. A full destination or an error before commit leaves the source instruction intact. Broker acknowledgments and remote processing effects are outside this database simulation.
graphics.caption: The example models a transactional local move. A real broker-to-store transfer needs its own documented safety contract; moving a message cannot undo earlier business effects.

sources.title: Dead Letter Channel
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf

sources.title: Invalid Message Channel
sources.author: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf

sources.title: Dead Letter Exchanges
sources.author: RabbitMQ
sources.supports: Distinct triggers, routing metadata, dead-letter cycles, default republishing without internal confirms and potential loss, and configurable quorum at-least-once transfer. Naming a DLX does not guarantee safety.

sources.title: Using dead-letter queues in Amazon SQS
sources.author: Amazon Web Services
sources.supports: maxReceiveCount counts receives, not confirmed handler executions; retention differs between standard and FIFO; original enqueue time matters for standard queue expiry; removing a message can break exact FIFO ordering.

sources.title: Configuring dead-letter queue redrive
sources.author: Amazon Web Services
sources.supports: Controlled redrive velocity, gradual recovery under load, transport-ID/enqueue-time changes, and interleaving with live messages. The example does not implement an AWS broker or redrive API.

sources.title: Transaction
sources.author: SQLite
sources.supports: Explicit BEGIN IMMEDIATE writer serialization and atomic local insert/delete transaction; failure before commit preserves source state. Local safety is not generalized to remote messaging transfers.

sources.title: sqlite3 — Transaction control and connection context manager
sources.author: Python documentation
sources.supports: isolation_level=None permits explicit BEGIN in legacy transaction mode, the context commits or rolls back an open transaction, and caller-owned closure remains separate. Initialization errors close the connection before propagation.

patterns.example_provenance: Revision of the existing Dead-Letter Queues article, preserving canonical ID data-dead-letter-queues, its original asset path, Data Engineering verse membership and tags, and the recovery/ownership perspective. No duplicate Dead Letter Channel article is created. Original bounded file-backed SQLite disposition simulation: trusted caller supplies a classified DEPENDENCY_UNAVAILABLE failure count; fewer than 3 failures leave pending work untouched. At 3 or more, BEGIN IMMEDIATE coordinates an insert of original bytes/identity/timestamps/failure metadata and source deletion in one transaction. A one-record failure channel exposes capacity failure without losing the source. Receipt IDs are immutable and unique for the store lifetime; event IDs preserve business intent independently. Counts are 1..1000, source bodies are BLOBs up to 4096 bytes, and failure timestamps are nonnegative signed-64-bit integer milliseconds not preceding enqueue. Reopening recognizes already parked receipt IDs without rewriting evidence. This is not a handler, counter, scheduler, broker, remote handoff, redrive implementation, external-effect rollback, authentication, or power-loss test. Existing exact-pattern article is reused; primary collection moves to Messaging and Integration while its former Data Engineering collection retains a cross-reference.

patterns.title: Database per Service
patterns.short_description: Keep each service's persistent data private to its owner, exposing business contracts instead of allowing other services to depend on its tables.
use_when: Service teams need private authority over persistent state and independently evolving storage.
Direct cross-service SQL reads or writes force coordinated releases or bypass the owning service contract.
Different capability owners require explicit data-access, transaction, and lifecycle boundaries.
not_ideal_when: One owner and a coherent local transaction already meet the application’s needs.
Table-by-table splitting would fragment an invariant without useful service autonomy.
The operational and consistency costs of additional stores and contracts cannot be supported.
prerequisites: Understand service capability ownership, published contracts, ordinary versus owner/admin privileges, local transaction scope, and explicit consistency and recovery for cross-owner workflows.
example_user_queries: Orders queries Inventory tables directly and every stock schema change requires coordinated releases.
We have separate deployments but all services still share one database login.
Does each service need its own physical database server or can private schemas share a host?
A read-only integration is coupling another team to our internal table layout.
How do we stop application roles from bypassing the service that owns stock?
A local order failure does not undo the inventory change already committed by another service.
Our report needs customer and order data owned by different services without direct database joins.
We need copied facts for a projection while preserving one authoritative owner.
Shared database maintenance still affects several services despite private schemas.
We are splitting one database per table but cannot explain the business capability boundaries.

graphics.alt_text: Orders and Inventory use separate runtime roles and each issues SQL only to its own private schema. The two schemas share one PostgreSQL server. An inter-service API request connects the services above the storage boundary, rather than granting Orders direct access to Inventory tables.
graphics.caption: Logical ownership can share physical hosting. The conceptual API arrow is not implemented by the SQL example, which demonstrates runtime storage privileges.

graphics.alt_text: Inventory commits a two-unit local adjustment, leaving three available units. A later Orders transaction rejects an order with zero requested units, leaving no order row. Inventory remains at three. Direct cross-service SQL is denied; a real workflow must resolve partial progress through a service contract and explicit recovery.
graphics.caption: Private stores give each service a local commit boundary. The deliberate rejection exposes partial progress; this is a permissions and transaction demonstration, not a checkout workflow.

sources.title: Database per Service
sources.author: Chris Richardson
sources.supports: Established private persistent state accessible through the owning service contract, local transaction boundary, private-table/private-schema/separate-server variants, privilege barriers, and coordination/query costs. The article does not turn the catalog’s distributed-transaction discussion into a universal CAP-based prohibition.

sources.title: Data considerations for microservices
sources.author: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center
sources.supports: Independent data ownership and schema evolution, permitted shared physical hosting, authoritative versus replicated facts, explicit consistency requirements, and cross-service coordination.

sources.title: Schemas
sources.author: PostgreSQL documentation
sources.supports: Schemas group objects within a database; roles are cluster scoped, schemas are not rigidly separated when grants allow access, schema ownership/qualification and search-path privilege concerns matter.

sources.title: Privileges
sources.author: PostgreSQL documentation
sources.supports: Object ownership, table privileges, inherited permissions, PUBLIC grants, and the distinction between schema ownership and ordinary runtime permissions. Administrator bypass remains explicitly outside the service-runtime boundary.

sources.title: GRANT
sources.author: PostgreSQL documentation
sources.supports: Schema USAGE, table SELECT/INSERT, column-specific UPDATE, and cumulative role/PUBLIC grants. The example grants no cross-owner schema access or owner-role membership to runtime roles.

sources.title: SET ROLE
sources.author: PostgreSQL documentation
sources.supports: Permission checks use the selected current role; SET LOCAL ROLE lasts within its transaction. Switching roles from a privileged administrator session is a demonstration, not separately authenticated production service sessions.

patterns.example_provenance: Original executable PostgreSQL SQL example of private Orders and Inventory schemas on one shared database. Four NOLOGIN owner/runtime roles are provisioned in a fresh isolated cluster; public CREATE is revoked, new private schemas have no PUBLIC access, runtime roles get only own-store USAGE/SELECT plus Orders INSERT or Inventory UPDATE(available_units). The provisioning administrator uses SET ROLE/SET LOCAL ROLE for permission checks; production separate authentication is not modeled. Inventory starts with five physical units and commits a two-unit local adjustment. A deliberate zero-unit Orders insert raises check_violation, leaving no order while Inventory remains at three. Two live cross-service SQL attempts must raise insufficient_privilege. Exception blocks catch only the expected SQLSTATE class and fail on unexpected success. No API, network, reservation lifecycle, retries, reconciliation, authentication setup, distributed transaction, or production checkout workflow. The host has PostgreSQL clients but no server, so the SQL is verified in an isolated ignored PGlite 0.5.13 runtime using its PostgreSQL 18.6 engine, without project dependency changes. PGlite is single-connection verification and is not a concurrency or production deployment test.

patterns.title: CQRS
patterns.short_description: Separate the model that handles business changes from the model that answers queries, so each can serve its own responsibilities without forcing one representation to do both.
use_when: A behavioral model for business changes and consumer-specific query representations are forcing one conceptual model to serve incompatible needs.
Commands need authoritative validation while queries benefit from a thin, independently shaped read layer.
One bounded area justifies separate read/write optimization with explicit consistency and lifecycle choices.
not_ideal_when: Straightforward CRUD and ordinary query methods remain clear and sufficient.
Read traffic can be addressed by simpler indexes or caching without model segregation.
Two stores, queues, or Event Sourcing are being added only to match a presumed mandatory CQRS architecture.
prerequisites: Understand business command intent, query DTOs, model versus deployment boundaries, authoritative write validation, immutable observations, concurrency, and read consistency.
example_user_queries: Our booking domain model is becoming full of fields and methods needed only to render cards.
Do separate read and write models require separate databases or services?
We want a query DTO without loading the behavioral domain model for every screen.
A page still shows available seats after another user books them and the command must revalidate.
We are unsure whether CQRS requires Event Sourcing or asynchronous message queues.
Command success is being confused with an asynchronous read projection having caught up.
We need to define what an observed version means for read-your-writes behavior.
Our business actions are exposed as generic state setters rather than meaningful commands.
We need to distinguish method-level command-query separation from separate conceptual models.
Simple CRUD is growing into two stores and an event pipeline without a clear benefit.

graphics.alt_text: A Book Seats command goes through a SeatPool model that checks capacity and changes booked seats. An Availability query uses SQL to return an immutable title, remaining count, status, and observed version. Both paths access one shows table; the query does not load the command model or perform booking.
graphics.caption: The separation is between responsibilities and representations. This example shares storage and derives its read DTO on demand; it has no asynchronous projection or event log.

graphics.alt_text: An availability DTO reports two remaining seats at version zero. A later booking command commits both seats and advances the stored version to one. The old DTO still reports two. A new command for one seat validates current state and rejects it; a fresh query reports zero, sold out, version one.
graphics.caption: Even without an asynchronous read store, a returned answer can become outdated. The command enforces capacity from current state; the displayed remaining count is not write authority.

sources.title: CQRS Documents
sources.author: Greg Young
sources.supports: Original author’s CQRS material, especially printed pages 17–23: origins in method-level CQS, split model responsibilities, behavioral commands, and a thin read layer projecting DTOs without loading the domain model. Event Sourcing is treated separately.

sources.title: CQRS
sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Different conceptual update/read models, possible shared database or separate stores, no required separate deployment, optional Event Sourcing, and selective applicability with significant complexity costs.

sources.title: Command Query Separation

sources.title: CQRS pattern
sources.author: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center
sources.supports: Task-oriented commands, separate data models over one store or separate stores, read DTOs, explicit concurrency and consistency choices, asynchronous propagation concerns and optional Event Sourcing.

sources.title: Transaction
sources.author: SQLite
sources.supports: BEGIN IMMEDIATE serializes writers before authoritative-state validation; open read transactions can preserve older snapshots; local commit and rollback behavior are separate from model-level CQRS choices.

sources.author: Python documentation
sources.supports: File URI mode=ro read connections, explicit transaction control with isolation_level=None in legacy mode, open-transaction commit/rollback through the connection context, and caller-owned connection closure.

patterns.example_provenance: Original shared-SQLite-store CQRS seat-booking simulation. Immutable SeatPool(capacity, booked) holds the command-side capacity policy; immutable Availability(title, remaining, status, version) is separately projected by parameterized SELECT without loading SeatPool. One owner and one shows table, no asynchronous projection or event log. An initially idle write connection uses BEGIN IMMEDIATE to serialize loading current state and atomically updating booked/version; the public book_seats command returns no value and completes normally only after commit. A mode=ro URI connection issues fresh autocommit read statements. Show IDs are 1..64 ASCII characters, command quantities 1..1000 integer physical seats, and seeded capacity is 1..1000 with database count constraints. An old DTO with 2 remaining/version 0 survives a two-seat commit; another one-seat command rejects current sold-out state and leaves version 1 unchanged; fresh query reports zero/sold out/version 1. Version is observational, not an expected-version concurrency precondition. Caller owns dedicated connection closure. No individual booking ledger, payment, command deduplication, authentication, network, asynchronous projector, event history, recovery/cancellation lifecycle, or deployment-level read-only privilege boundary.

patterns.title: Event Sourcing
patterns.short_description: Make accepted business events the authoritative record and reconstruct state by applying them in order, keeping replay separate from repeated external actions.
use_when: Accepted business changes must explain how current state arose.
Earlier states or new projections must be rebuilt from sufficient retained facts.
A selected business boundary justifies durable history and long-term event compatibility.
not_ideal_when: Current-state CRUD and an ordinary audit trail meet the need.
Events are only being published for integration, without a need for event-authoritative persistence.
The team cannot maintain replay compatibility, restoration procedures, or sensitive-data retention policies.
prerequisites: Understand business commands versus accepted facts, deterministic replay, stream revision checks, transaction ownership, and projection consistency.
example_user_queries: We can see current availability but cannot explain which accepted changes produced it.
We need to rebuild an earlier state from business facts rather than guess from update logs.
How can we add a new projection of historical decisions without making it the source of truth?
Two reservations read the same event stream and both try to append a valid-looking change.
Replaying our history accidentally resends old confirmation emails.
Our old events no longer deserialize after a schema change.
We are unsure whether publishing events alongside a normal database counts as event sourcing.
Long histories are making reconstruction slow and we need safe replay checkpoints.
A lost response makes us unsure whether a retried command should append another event.
We need to distinguish recorded stream position from business-effective time.

graphics.alt_text: An authoritative stream contains Opened 20 at revision one, Reserved R1 three at revision two, and Released R1 one at revision three. Applying the first two events yields seventeen available seats; applying all three yields eighteen. Neither reconstruction sends a confirmation.
graphics.caption: One-based stream revisions establish order. Replay reconstructs capacity 20 and R1 holding two seats, leaving 18 available; the derived state can be discarded and rebuilt.

graphics.alt_text: A release command based on revision two reaches a stream already at revision three and is rejected without adding an event. The caller must reload and reconsider. The accepted stream remains at revision three and replay still reports eighteen seats.
graphics.caption: Checking expected revision and appending occur in one transaction. A stale proposal adds nothing. Stream order protects this pool, without implying global ordering or retry deduplication.

sources.author: Martin Fowler
sources.supports: Authoritative event history, reconstruction, temporal queries, external interactions, and changing interpretations.

sources.title: Event Sourcing pattern
sources.author: Microsoft

sources.title: Writing Events

sources.title: Snapshots

sources.title: sqlite3

patterns.title: Transactional Outbox
patterns.short_description: Save an outgoing message with its business change in one database transaction, then relay committed messages with duplicate handling.
use_when: A committed business change must retain its obligation to notify another system.
The database and broker have independent failure and commit boundaries.
Temporary broker outages should delay asynchronous delivery without losing locally accepted intent.
not_ideal_when: All work fits inside one ordinary database transaction.
Loss of an optional notification is acceptable and durable retry machinery is unwarranted.
The implementation assumes an outbox alone supplies consumer exactly-once effects or client-command deduplication.
prerequisites: Understand local atomic commit, serialized payloads and stable event identity, asynchronous delivery, acknowledgment scope, duplicate handling, and relay ownership.
example_user_queries: Our order commits but a crash before publication leaves fulfillment unaware of it.
Publishing first creates events for database changes that later roll back.
We want to accept local orders while the message broker is temporarily unavailable.
The relay resends a message after losing the broker acknowledgment.
Should a dispatch flag be written before or after publishing a pending event?
Our relay rebuilds old notifications from current business state and sends the wrong payload.
Parallel relay workers can publish an order cancellation before its placement.
We need to choose between polling pending messages and following committed database changes.
The pending-message backlog keeps growing even though database writes succeed.
We need a retention policy that does not delete pending intent or forget duplicates too early.

graphics.alt_text: One source database transaction inserts order O42 and outbox event E901 together. A rollback preserves neither. After commit, a relay reads the pending event and publishes it to a separate broker; broker acceptance is outside the source transaction.
graphics.caption: The atomic boundary covers the order and publication intent, not the broker or consumer. Committed intent survives temporary delivery failure.

graphics.alt_text: E901 is pending after the order commits. A broker accepts it, but acknowledgment is lost, so the source still says pending. After restart the relay sends the same E901, gets acknowledgment, and marks it dispatched. The broker test log contains two acceptances; the order remains a single row.
graphics.caption: Retried publication retains E901. Two acceptances of one message are possible even when the business transaction ran once; receiver-side repeat protection remains necessary.

sources.title: Transactional Outbox

sources.title: Polling Publisher

sources.title: Transactional outbox pattern

sources.title: Outbox

sources.title: sqlite3
sources.author: Python documentation

patterns.title: Saga
patterns.short_description: Coordinate a business operation as locally committed steps, with explicit recovery and compensating actions when the overall operation cannot complete.
use_when: One business operation spans independently committed participant data.
Visible intermediate states and explicit business recovery are acceptable.
A plan can identify each step’s remedy, retry identity, progress, and unresolved outcome ownership.
not_ideal_when: One ordinary local transaction can enforce the complete rule.
Temporary inconsistency or irreversible consequences have no acceptable business remedy.
The design assumes compensation supplies automatic isolation, rollback, exactly-once delivery, or guaranteed eventual success.
prerequisites: Understand local transaction boundaries, scoped compensation, business refusal versus uncertain outcome, stable operation identity, progress durability, and ownership of intermediate state.
example_user_queries: Inventory committed but the carrier refused our order and the reservation is still held.
Our workflow changes several service databases and cannot use one local transaction.
Restoring an old stock count during recovery would erase another order’s reservation.
A participant timed out after possibly committing and we do not know whether to compensate.
A compensation failed and we need to retain the remaining recovery work.
We need to choose between a central workflow coordinator and events between participants.
Customers can see partially completed orders and we need a clear pending outcome.
Retrying a participant action creates duplicate reservations unless we retain operation identity.
A late reserve request might recreate a reservation that was already cancelled.
We are treating a long business workflow like a database rollback and losing track of committed effects.

graphics.alt_text: Inventory reserves two mugs for O42, Packing reserves one slot, and Carrier declines delivery without committing it. Compensation releases the packing slot and then the Inventory reservation. Each effect belongs to its participant; there is no shared rollback.
graphics.caption: Forward steps commit separately. This example compensates Packing before Inventory; the order follows its declared plan, not a universal requirement for every business workflow.

graphics.alt_text: Inventory starts with five mugs. O42 reserves two, and another order O99 reserves one, leaving two available. O42's carrier declines. Packing is released, Inventory release temporarily fails, and a later retry releases only O42's two mugs. Four remain available; O99 still holds one.
graphics.caption: Compensation reaches an acceptable new state, not the original snapshot. The retry uses the same in-memory coordinator state; this simulation does not recover across process crashes.

sources.title: Saga
sources.author: Chris Richardson

sources.title: Saga design pattern
sources.author: Microsoft

sources.title: Saga pattern

No database, network, threads, durable log, scheduler, or process-crash recovery.

patterns.title: API Composition
patterns.short_description: Answer a cross-service query by calling the APIs that own the required data and joining their responses into one result.
use_when: A selective query needs data from several independently owned services.
Owner APIs can supply bounded batches and the result tolerates separately observed versions.
An occasional read does not justify maintaining a new stored projection.
not_ideal_when: An ordinary query or batch endpoint within one owner is sufficient.
The query requires broad scans, large joins, or expensive repeated dashboard assembly.
A display join is being treated as a cross-service snapshot or authoritative business invariant.
prerequisites: Understand data ownership, join identities/cardinality, validated DTO contracts, required versus optional data, owner-local revisions, bounded query work, deadlines, cancellation, and authorization context.
example_user_queries: Our order dashboard needs totals from Orders and labels from Customers without reading their private tables.
A screen with fifty orders is making fifty separate customer lookups.
Two owner APIs return rows in different orders and our cards are being joined incorrectly.
We need a clear policy when one required service is unavailable or omits a referenced record.
A cross-service dashboard silently drops rows when customer information is missing.
We want one selective combined answer without maintaining a replicated read database.
The order and customer versions in our combined response do not come from one snapshot.
Our per-call timeouts add up and the whole composed request takes too long.
We need to propagate caller permissions safely while assembling fields from several services.
We are unsure whether to join live API responses or maintain a materialized read model.

graphics.alt_text: An API Composer receives order IDs O42, O43, and O44. It calls Orders once, derives distinct customer IDs C2 and C7, calls Customers once, and joins returned rows by customer ID. The three cards retain requested order; O42 and O44 reuse the same C7 result.
graphics.caption: The composer uses owner APIs rather than private tables. Two batch calls answer three cards; matching follows identity, not response position. The customer call depends on the order response.

graphics.alt_text: Orders returns O42, O43, and O44 with customer references C7, C2, and C7. Customers returns C2 but omits required C7. The composer rejects the whole result as incomplete; it does not silently drop O42 and O44 or invent a customer label.
graphics.caption: This example requires both services and every requested identity. Missing data is a visible composition error. A deliberately partial product would need a different, explicit response contract.

patterns.title: Leader Election
patterns.short_description: Select one participant to hold a coordination role for an authority term, with explicit rules for replacement and for rejecting obsolete authority.
use_when: Replicas need a single active coordinator for a defined scope with replaceable ownership.
The system can tolerate handover pauses and has a dependable authority service or protocol.
Obsolete owners and delayed mutations need an explicit destination enforcement boundary.
not_ideal_when: Independent task claims or repeat-safe duplicate execution eliminate the need for a leader.
A simpler local transaction can coordinate the complete workload.
A local is_leader flag, heartbeat timeout, or reachable-minority vote is being treated as proof of exclusive external authority.
prerequisites: Understand election versus consensus, fixed membership, majority intersection, retained voting terms, safety versus liveness, coordinator failure assumptions, trusted scope, destination fencing, and durable restore.
example_user_queries: Several scheduler replicas can publish conflicting manifests and we need a replaceable coordinator.
A heartbeat stopped but the old leader may only be paused or partitioned.
One isolated replica is treating itself as a majority of the reachable nodes.
We need to distinguish an election result from permission to write forever.
A replacement leader was elected but a delayed old publication still overwrote its work.
We are deciding whether to use a coordination service instead of implementing our own election protocol.
Restarting a voter could forget its earlier vote and allow conflicting leaders in the same term.
A destination restore may forget which ownership generation it must reject.
We need to choose a leadership scope without creating one global throughput bottleneck.
A workflow needs one active executor but also requires durable progress and retry protection.

graphics.alt_text: In a fixed three-member group A, B, and C, an isolated C receives only its own vote and cannot win. A receives A and B's votes in term one and wins with two of three. Each voter can choose only one candidate per term, so another candidate cannot assemble a different majority in that term.
graphics.caption: The quorum is calculated from all three configured members, not just reachable members. Majority intersection and retained one-vote-per-term state prevent different winners in one term under this model's assumptions.

graphics.alt_text: A wins term one and publishes manifest-A. After a partition B wins term two with B and C. A's old election result still exists. B installs term two at the destination and publishes manifest-B; the destination rejects A's later term-one write and retains manifest-B.
graphics.caption: Election and destination handover are separate boundaries. The register rejects obsolete writes after installing the newer authority. It does not stop the old process, authenticate callers, or establish publication correctness by itself.

patterns.title: Lease
patterns.short_description: Grant a scoped right for a limited time, renew it explicitly, and allow reassignment when that grant expires.
use_when: A scoped ownership or registration right must lapse without cooperation from an unreachable holder.
Workers need explicit renewable claims and eventual reassignment after a pause or failure.
Coordination service timing, client uncertainty and external effects need distinct lifecycle rules.
not_ideal_when: One transaction or conditional update already covers the complete operation.
Repeat-safe duplicate execution removes the need for exclusive ownership.
Expiry is being treated as proof of process death, automatic cancellation, or permission for unconditional external writes.
prerequisites: Understand atomic conditional acquisition, scoped acquisition identity, TTL versus authority deadline, clock assumptions, uncertain RPC outcomes, conservative failover recovery, and external enforcement.
example_user_queries: A crashed worker leaves a partition claimed forever and someone has to clear it manually.
We need an ownership record to lapse when its holder cannot contact the coordinator.
A delayed cleanup request removed a newer claim for the same worker name.
Our renewal request timed out and we cannot tell whether the server accepted it.
We are choosing a claim duration that balances takeover delay against renewal traffic.
A paused worker resumed after its claim expired and continued writing to an external service.
Our registry keeps advertising instances that disappeared without unregistering.
Restarting the coordinator could forget rights it already granted to clients.
We need to distinguish a local timer from the server’s actual authority deadline.
Two workers both saw an expired record and tried to take ownership at once.

graphics.alt_text: At authority time zero A acquires the partition for 3000 milliseconds. At 2000 milliseconds A renews, moving expiry to 5000. B is denied at 4999. At exactly 5000 A's grant is expired and B can acquire a new grant.
graphics.caption: All times are milliseconds on one authority clock in the teaching model. The valid interval excludes its expiry boundary. Renewal sets a new deadline from acceptance time; it does not add another duration to the old deadline.

graphics.alt_text: A sends a renewal request but receives no reply. The authority may have renewed it, so A's local knowledge is uncertain. Separately, an expired grant can be replaced while A's process still runs. External writes need enforcement at their destination.
graphics.caption: A timeout does not establish whether renewal succeeded. Authority expiry, client knowledge, and external effects are separate boundaries; this illustration does not prescribe a distributed clock algorithm.

patterns.title: Reactor
patterns.short_description: Wait for readiness across registered event sources, then dispatch short handlers that perform nonblocking work and return control to the loop.
use_when: Many connections spend time waiting for I/O and each can make short nonblocking progress.
Readiness detection and dispatch should be shared while parsers retain independent per-connection state.
Resource registration, callback work limits, and cleanup need explicit ownership.
not_ideal_when: A few simple blocking workflows are clearer with threads.
Handlers require CPU-heavy or blocking operations without an offload strategy.
Completion of initiated asynchronous I/O is being confused with readiness to attempt I/O.
prerequisites: Understand stream framing, readiness versus completion, nonblocking would-block behavior, per-connection state, callback budgets, backpressure, and unregister-before-close lifecycle.
example_user_queries: One slow connection holds up every other device while we wait for its complete message.
We need to handle many mostly idle sockets without dedicating a thread to each one.
Our callbacks block on a database call and the whole event loop becomes unresponsive.
A readable socket delivered only half a record and our parser assumed it was complete.
We need to keep independent parsing state for several connections across callbacks.
The server keeps waking on writable sockets even when there is nothing queued to send.
A peer closed in the middle of a record and we need a clear cleanup policy.
We are confusing an I/O readiness notification with completion of an asynchronous operation.
One busy connection drains an unlimited amount of input before any other handler runs.
We need to unregister socket resources safely when a connection fails or the service shuts down.

graphics.alt_text: Two sockets are registered with the Reactor. The dispatcher waits on the selector, receives readable socket handles, and invokes each handle's registered handler. Each handler attempts nonblocking reads, retains unfinished state, and returns control to the dispatcher.
graphics.caption: Readiness identifies which operation to attempt; it does not supply a complete application record. The selector waits, the dispatcher chooses the registered callback, and the handler performs I/O.

graphics.alt_text: A first sends hel without a newline, so its handler retains three bytes and returns. B sends ok followed by a newline and completes independently. A later sends lo followed by a newline, completing hello. A final incomplete record at EOF is rejected and its socket is unregistered before closing.
graphics.caption: This is an explanatory trace, not a promise about selector ordering. Each callback consumes at most four bytes in the example. Record state belongs to its connection; EOF never turns an unfinished record into a valid one.

patterns.title: Proactor
patterns.short_description: Initiate asynchronous operations with request context, then dispatch their completion results to handlers that decide the next step.
use_when: An I/O facility or library executes initiated operations asynchronously and delivers operation-level completion results.
Request identity, buffers, status and transferred byte counts must survive until completion dispatch.
The application needs explicit cancellation, shutdown, completion-order and outstanding-work policies.
not_ideal_when: A few sequential blocking operations are clearer and sufficient.
An existing readiness library already solves the workload without completion machinery.
A callback, future, or async keyword is being treated as proof of native asynchronous completion I/O.
prerequisites: Understand readiness versus completion, submission versus terminal outcome, partial transfers, request-scoped ownership, buffer lifetime, cancellation races, dispatcher threading, and admission bounds.
example_user_queries: We submit several reads and need to match each completed result to its original connection.
An operation finished with fewer bytes than requested and our transfer was incorrectly marked complete.
A cancellation request returned but the I/O operation still completed successfully.
We reused a read buffer before an outstanding operation had actually finished.
Our event handlers should consume completed I/O results instead of performing readiness-triggered reads themselves.
We need to distinguish acceptance of an asynchronous request from its successful completion.
Completions arrive out of submission order and our shared connection context gets mixed up.
Immediate completion and a later notification both released the same request resources.
We need a shutdown policy that observes outstanding operation results before freeing resources.
The service accepts too many outstanding requests and undelivered completions consume all its memory.

graphics.alt_text: The initiator submits a read request with an identity, buffer, and handler. The operation processor performs the read and places its result on a completion queue. The dispatcher retrieves that result and invokes the matching handler with transferred bytes and status.
graphics.caption: Submission is not completion. The processor performs the operation; the handler consumes its result. A completed read can still provide only part of an application record.

graphics.alt_text: A and B occupy two request slots. B finishes first, but its queued completion still retains a slot. Cancellation is requested for A without freeing its context. The backend reports A successful with three bytes. Dispatch consumes B and A's actual outcomes and releases their request slots.
graphics.caption: The model retains each request through completion dispatch. Cancellation is a request, not a terminal result; A's successful short read remains distinguishable from a canceled operation.

patterns.title: Active Object
patterns.short_description: Turn method invocations into queued requests and execute them through an object's scheduler, keeping its state under one execution owner and returning results separately.
use_when: Callers should hand work to an independently executing owner of mutable state.
Methods on one servant need deliberate scheduling, bounded admission and deferred result handling.
Slow operations should run away from request-handling threads with explicit queue and shutdown policies.
not_ideal_when: A short passive method with a lock is simpler and caller waiting is acceptable.
An existing event loop already supplies the required execution ownership.
Every object would receive a worker regardless of workload, or callers can bypass the proxy and mutate servant state.
prerequisites: Understand invocation versus execution, state confinement, immutable request arguments, FIFO admission order, bounded queues, future running/canceled states, callback deadlocks, graceful draining, and non-daemon join.
example_user_queries: Several request threads update the same object and every access path needs the same synchronization rules.
We want callers to submit work without executing a slow stateful method on their own threads.
A generic worker pool runs two methods on the same mutable object at once.
We need a clear owner for a device session and a bounded backlog of requests.
Queued methods should return a result or exception to the correct caller later.
The service accepts too many method calls while its worker is busy and the queue grows indefinitely.
A canceled request is still in the queue and we need to skip its execution safely.
Shutdown races with callers submitting new methods and accepted work gets stranded.
A completion callback waits for another request on the same worker and deadlocks.
Callers keep references to mutable state and bypass the intended worker ownership.

graphics.alt_text: Clients invoke the stock proxy, which creates requests containing an immutable quantity change and a future. A bounded activation queue passes requests to one worker scheduler. Only that worker accesses the stock quantity and resolves each future with a result or error.
graphics.caption: Invocation happens on a caller thread; stock execution happens on the owner thread. The queue transfers a request, not permission for callers to access the servant's state directly.

graphics.alt_text: Three admitted changes execute in order. Adding three units returns three. Removing five fails before mutation and returns an error, leaving three units. Adding two then returns five. Shutdown rejects new invocations, drains accepted requests, and joins the worker.
graphics.caption: Serialization protects this servant's check-and-update rule. A failed request does not stop later requests here, and only the example's pre-mutation validation preserves quantity on failure; there is no general rollback guarantee.

patterns.title: Monitor Object
patterns.short_description: Encapsulate shared state behind synchronized methods, using a monitor lock for exclusive access and condition waiting for state-dependent progress.
use_when: Multiple threads need a cohesive synchronous object with shared invariants and state-dependent waiting.
Predicate checks and mutations must remain under one lock while waiting releases that lock for progress.
Bounded buffer or local resource lifecycle requires clear notification, closure, and drain rules.
not_ideal_when: Mutual exclusion alone is sufficient and no condition waiting is needed.
An existing synchronized queue already provides the required contract.
A method would block an event loop, perform slow I/O under the monitor, or span multiple objects without a lock-order protocol.
prerequisites: Understand caller-thread execution, shared monitor locks, protected invariants, condition wait release/reacquire, while-predicate loops, notification versus handoff, plain-lock reentrancy limits, and shutdown/draining semantics.
example_user_queries: Several producers can overfill a shared buffer because the capacity check and insert race.
A consumer waits for data while holding the lock that producers need to add it.
Our condition wait wakes up but the item it expected is no longer available.
We used one if check around wait and sometimes remove from an empty buffer.
We need shared object methods to preserve invariants without giving the object its own worker thread.
Closing a buffer leaves producers or consumers blocked forever.
A notification happens while the producer still holds the lock and we expected the consumer to run immediately.
We need already accepted items to drain while new puts are rejected after closure.
Public methods call each other under a nonreentrant lock and deadlock.
Different state access paths use unrelated locks and our checks are no longer atomic.

graphics.alt_text: Producer and consumer caller threads enter synchronized put, get, and close methods through one shared monitor lock. The protected inbox contains a bounded deque and a closed flag. A condition wait releases that same lock; a returning waiter reacquires it and rechecks the state predicate.
graphics.caption: The lock protects the complete check-and-update operation. Waiting temporarily leaves the protected region; the method invocation remains pending on its caller's thread.

graphics.alt_text: A consumer finds an empty inbox, waits, and releases the lock. A producer acquires it, inserts one item, and notifies while retaining the lock. Only after the producer releases can the consumer reacquire. The consumer rechecks the predicate before removing an item, or waits again if it is still false.
graphics.caption: Notification makes a waiter eligible to run; it does not reserve an item. Rechecking under the lock handles changed state and extra wakeups without violating the buffer invariant.

One Condition over a plain Lock protects deque, closed flag, predicates, and mutations. While loops recheck state after every wait. notify_all serves producers, consumers, and closure. patterns.title: Producer-Consumer
patterns.short_description: Separate work creation from execution through a synchronized buffer, with explicit capacity, ownership, and completion rules.
use_when: Work creation and processing have different timing and should progress independently.
Bursts need bounded waiting storage and upstream blocking or an explicit overload policy.
Independent jobs can be distributed across a stable group of consumers with recorded outcomes and coordinated completion.
not_ideal_when: A cheap sequential loop already meets timing and resource needs.
Unpausable upstream input has no overload or loss policy.
Business ordering, durable delivery, or crash recovery is expected from a local FIFO queue alone.
prerequisites: Understand synchronized queue admission/removal, immutable ownership handoff, waiting versus active capacity, competing consumption, task accounting, handled failures, all-producer completion before stops, and thread joining.
example_user_queries: My input loop waits for slow processing before it can receive the next record.
Creating a new thread for every incoming job exhausts resources during bursts.
Our pending job list grows without a limit when processing falls behind.
I want several reusable workers to divide independent jobs from one shared buffer.
We need to slow a pausable producer when all waiting places are occupied.
A bad input kills a worker and leaves the rest of the batch unfinished.
The queue is empty but some workers are still processing and the report is incomplete.
Multiple workers finish out of order even though the input queue is FIFO.
One producer sends stop markers while another producer still has jobs to submit.
Our shutdown waits forever because a failed job never decremented the unfinished count.

graphics.alt_text: A producer holds record 4 while two queue places contain records 2 and 3. Two consumers already process records 0 and 1 outside the queue. Removing a queued record frees a waiting place before processing finishes. Outcomes are collected separately.
graphics.caption: Capacity counts waiting entries, not active processing. With two queue places and two consumers, up to four accepted records can be queued or executing; the producer's current record, input batch, and collected outcomes are additional storage.

graphics.alt_text: The coordinator first finishes all producers, then enqueues one stop marker per consumer behind accepted jobs, waits for queue task accounting, and joins the consumer threads. Consumers keep removing and handling jobs during shutdown, recording either a measurement or a rejection before task_done; each exits after its own stop marker.
graphics.caption: Stop markers follow the last accepted jobs. Consumers remain active while the coordinator sends markers and waits. Queue completion counts handled entries, including failures; joining threads confirms termination.

patterns.title: Thread Pool
patterns.short_description: Reuse a managed group of worker threads to execute submitted tasks, separating task lifetime from thread creation and shutdown.
use_when: Many independent finite tasks should share reusable managed thread capacity instead of creating a thread per task.
Blocking I/O can overlap while worker count and downstream resources need explicit limits.
Submitted task outcomes and pool shutdown need an owner, with admission bounded separately from worker count.
not_ideal_when: A cheap direct loop already meets timing and resource needs.
Tasks are long-lived dedicated activities or depend synchronously on child tasks in a saturated pool.
CPU-heavy conventional CPython tasks, durable jobs, forced interruption, security isolation, or thread confinement are expected from a thread pool alone.
prerequisites: Understand callable submission, worker reuse, futures, execution versus admission bounds, immutable/stable inputs, shared-state safety, result observation, resource cleanup, and owned shutdown.
example_user_queries: Creating one thread per incoming task uses too many stacks and scheduling resources.
We need a reusable group of threads to overlap independent blocking file reads.
The worker count is limited but our submitted backlog keeps growing.
I want to cap jobs awaiting result collection, including completed futures I have not read yet.
How do I collect individual task errors without abandoning the remaining batch?
We need every file handle closed and all workers stopped before deleting temporary input files.
Our jobs finish out of order even though we need an index-ordered report.
All workers wait for child tasks submitted to the same executor and nothing can progress.
Creating a new executor for every small request defeats thread reuse.
A result wait timed out but the running task still owns its resources.

graphics.alt_text: A coordinator admits at most four jobs awaiting result collection. The pool has up to two reusable threads; in the illustrated snapshot two jobs execute while two wait. A thread finishes one job and takes another instead of being recreated. Completed futures still occupy the coordinator's admission window until collected.
graphics.caption: Two worker threads limit simultaneous task execution. A separate four-job window limits submitted work awaiting collection, including queued, running, and completed-but-uncollected jobs. These are different resource limits.

graphics.alt_text: In one possible schedule, worker A runs job 0 and later job 2 on the same thread. Worker B runs job 1 and later job 3. Each future becomes a result or exception, which the coordinator collects before freeing an admission place. After the final submitted tasks finish, the owner shuts down and joins the pool workers before removing temporary files.
graphics.caption: A future belongs to a task; a reusable thread outlives individual tasks. Result collection frees an admission place. Pool shutdown, rather than one task's completion, ends the owned worker lifetime. Assignments are illustrative.
