patterns.title: Resource Pool
patterns.short_description: Manage reusable resources behind a borrowing boundary, returning each to circulation only after exclusive use and required cleanup.
use_when: Reusable resources are expensive to initialize or their available count is constrained.
Compatible borrowers need exclusive temporary use with a reliable cleanup/reset baseline.
Resource creation, availability, exhaustion and closure need an owner distinct from individual borrowers.
not_ideal_when: Ordinary allocation is cheap enough and no scarcity or measured reuse benefit exists.
Only concurrent-operation count matters, so a semaphore is sufficient without retaining instances.
No safe reset, compatibility, ownership or resource-failure retirement policy is available.
prerequisites: Understand exclusive scoped borrowing, physical-resource versus handle lifetime, reset/validation before availability, thread-safe pool coordination versus borrowed-object safety, exhaustion, close-with-active-borrows, and resource-specific failure handling.
example_user_queries: Opening a new connection for each request repeats expensive authentication and initialization.
Giving every request its own resource exhausts the downstream server.
Two callers accidentally use the same reusable object at the same time.
A returned connection still carries the previous tenant or session settings.
A failed job leaves its borrowed resource unavailable forever.
We need to wait when every reusable instance is in use instead of creating more.
An old handle can still access an object after it has been returned to another caller.
Pool shutdown must reject new borrows while allowing active users to finish.
A resource fails validation on return and must not be recycled as healthy.
Our pool caps idle retention but still creates unlimited instances under load.

graphics.alt_text: A pool manages two resources. One belongs exclusively to caller A while another is idle and available to caller B. Caller C must wait if both are borrowed. Use takes place outside the pool's coordination lock, and a resource becomes available again only after return cleanup.
graphics.caption: The pool owns resource lifetime; borrowers own temporary use. A capacity limit counts resources in use and being reset as well as idle resources. Waiting policy and creation policy are separate choices.

graphics.alt_text: A borrow owns a buffer until its scope ends, including on a job exception. Scope exit invalidates the old handle and resets all eight bytes before publishing the buffer as idle. If the pool has closed, the returned buffer is dropped instead. The next borrow receives a new handle; the old handle remains invalid.
graphics.caption: Ending a borrow and destroying a resource are different operations. Reset precedes reuse. Pool closure stops admission and changes the return path; it does not interrupt an active borrower.

A Condition protects idle availability and closed state; a while loop blocks when all resources are held or resetting. Each scoped borrow gets a fresh guarded handle, with public read/write rejecting an ended borrow. Immutable 0–8-byte writes pad to eight bytes and reads return copies. patterns.title: Scoped Locking
patterns.short_description: Bind an acquired lock's release to a scope so normal exits, early returns, and exceptions cannot omit the matching unlock.
use_when: A critical section has a clear scope whose exits must always release the successful acquisition.
Returns, rejection branches or exceptions make manual unlock bookkeeping fragile.
All competing accesses can share a coherent lock protocol over a complete invariant.
not_ideal_when: Data is confined to one execution context and no shared-state lock is necessary.
The required protocol deliberately waits/releases/reacquires and a simple uninterrupted lock scope is assumed to cover it.
Rollback, deadlock freedom, fairness, async-task synchronization or process-failure recovery is expected from scope cleanup alone.
prerequisites: Understand mutual exclusion, one shared lock per protected invariant, lexical scope/context-manager cleanup, acquisition success, state consistency, nonreentrancy, lock ordering and short critical sections.
example_user_queries: An early return forgets to unlock and later callers stop progressing.
An exception escapes a critical section before the manual release call.
Every new branch requires another unlock and we keep missing one.
How can I make release happen before a method returns a value?
I used a new lock on every call and concurrent updates still race.
An unlocked reader sees state between a protected check and update.
A scope released the lock after an exception but the data changes were still there.
A temporary C++ locking guard was destroyed before the statements it should protect.
I assumed nested scoped locks would prevent deadlock without an acquisition order.
I want snapshot reads and reservation updates to use the same protection interval.

graphics.alt_text: After lock acquisition succeeds, control enters the protected body. Normal completion, an early return, or an exception all reach the same scope-exit release. Only after that release does the caller continue, receive the return value, or observe the exception. Failed acquisition does not enter the protected body.
graphics.caption: Each successful acquisition has one scope-owned release. The illustration concerns structured control flow; it does not promise cleanup after process termination or restoration of changed data.

graphics.alt_text: With five initial items, reserving two changes the protected state to three available and two reserved, then returns after release. A request for four raises before changing that state and still releases. Another caller can then reserve the remaining three and obtain zero available and five reserved. All displayed states preserve a total of five items.
graphics.caption: The rejection preserves stock by validating before mutation. Scoped cleanup makes the lock available on both success and rejection; it does not itself implement transaction rollback.

patterns.title: Scoped Resource Management
patterns.short_description: Give each acquired resource a deterministic owner that releases it when its scope ends, including during failure and partial acquisition.
use_when: Acquired resources require paired release across returns and exceptions.
Several resources have dependency-ordered lifetimes or setup can fail after earlier acquisitions.
An API can express a clear owning scope while borrowers stay within that lifetime.
not_ideal_when: Ordinary immutable values have no release obligation.
Background users outlive the proposed scope without explicit ownership transfer.
Crash recovery, rollback, bounded execution time or guaranteed cleanup success is being inferred from scope unwinding.
prerequisites: Understand owning versus borrowing, successful acquisition, reverse dependency cleanup, structured scope exit, entry failures, exception propagation and live-handle escape.
example_user_queries: An exception skips the close call at the bottom of my import function.
Opening a second resource fails and the first one stays allocated.
My decoder closes but the underlying file is still open.
Temporary directory removal fails because a reader still holds a file inside it.
A function returns an open stream from a with block and the caller finds it closed.
I need conditional acquisitions to unwind in reverse order without nested error branches.
An early return bypasses manual cleanup of a socket or file.
How do I distinguish a borrowed handle from the object responsible for closing it?
A background operation still uses a buffer when its surrounding scope ends.
A cleanup error masks a decoding error and I need to understand the ownership boundary.

graphics.alt_text: One scope owns a temporary directory, then an open file in that directory, then a gzip decoder that borrows that file. Acquisitions are registered as they succeed. On exit, the decoder closes before the file, and the file closes before the directory is removed. A returned byte value is independent of all three resources.
graphics.caption: Register ownership as each acquisition succeeds. Unwind dependents before their dependencies. The scope owns cleanup responsibility; merely wrapping another object does not prove ownership of that object's underlying resource.

graphics.alt_text: On a successful read or body exception, cleanup closes the decoder, closes the raw file, and removes the directory. If opening the raw file fails, cleanup removes only the already-owned directory; no file or decoder exit is registered. A resource whose own entry fails remains responsible for its internal partial acquisition.
graphics.caption: Cleanup follows successful ownership registrations, not the list of resources the function hoped to acquire. Cleanup is attempted before an outcome leaves the scope; release failures can still change that outcome.

patterns.title: Timeout
patterns.short_description: Limit how long an operation may wait, then take an explicit failure path without assuming that the underlying work stopped or had no effect.
use_when: Waiting can exceed a caller’s useful latency budget or retain scarce capacity.
Nested dependency calls need one operation-wide deadline rather than renewed per-call allowances.
An expiry outcome and ownership of cancelled or late work can be specified explicitly.
not_ideal_when: Predictable bounded local work has no meaningful waiting boundary.
A long-running job needs acceptance and status lookup rather than a continuously open request.
A timer is expected to kill arbitrary work, roll back remote effects or replace concurrency admission limits.
prerequisites: Understand elapsed-time clocks, duration versus deadline, total versus phase/idle budgets, cooperative cancellation, task ownership, cleanup, uncertain remote outcomes and safe retry identity.
example_user_queries: A slow downstream service keeps all our request slots occupied.
Each dependency gets a full wait allowance and the whole request takes far too long.
Our read timer resets whenever bytes arrive, so a response can trickle forever.
How do I include connection setup and queue waits in one operation budget?
A caller gave up but the server may already have changed state.
Cancelling a local coroutine should release its resources before I report failure.
My event loop is blocked and its expiry callbacks are not running.
A timed thread join returned but the worker is still executing.
How can I reject work when the operation has no budget left?
Retries after slow responses are increasing load and making the outage worse.

graphics.alt_text: A quote has one 300 millisecond budget. Inventory consumes the first 120 milliseconds, leaving shipping 180 milliseconds until the same deadline. Giving shipping a fresh 300 milliseconds would extend the operation to 420 milliseconds. Queueing and setup must be explicitly included or excluded from the chosen boundary.
graphics.caption: One operation, one deadline: later stages inherit the remaining allowance. The numbers are illustrative budget accounting, not benchmark results or a recommended production setting.

graphics.alt_text: When a deadline expires, the caller takes a timeout path and may request cancellation. A cooperative local dependency releases its resource before reporting timeout. A remote service can commit before cancellation or a late reply arrives; the caller must reconcile that outcome rather than infer rollback.
graphics.caption: The timeout boundary governs the caller's willingness to wait. Cancellation, local cleanup, and confirmation of a remote business outcome are distinct events.

patterns.title: Exponential Backoff with Jitter
patterns.short_description: Increase retry wait limits after eligible failures and randomize each wait, spreading recovery traffic while keeping attempts and total elapsed time bounded.
use_when: Documented transient failures can recover and repeating the operation is safe.
Clients fail together and deterministic waits produce repeated synchronized retry bursts.
A finite total deadline, explicit attempt count and owner of retry admission can be established.
not_ideal_when: The failure is permanent or a useful response cannot fit within the remaining budget.
An uncertain state change lacks duplicate protection or a version/reconciliation contract.
Independent jitter is expected to enforce aggregate rate, fairness, forced cancellation or durable resumption.
prerequisites: Understand transient versus permanent failure classification, idempotent effects versus identical responses, full-jitter windows, inclusive attempt counts, monotonic budget accounting, resource release and layered retry amplification.
example_user_queries: Hundreds of workers retry together whenever our metadata service recovers.
We doubled each retry delay but the requests still arrive in bursts.
How can I spread retries without waiting the entire maximum delay every time?
A capped wait loop keeps retrying for hours during a permanent outage.
Our application and SDK both repeat requests and multiply downstream traffic.
A request may have committed before its reply disappeared; is repeating it safe?
The server asked us to wait thirty seconds but the operation has only twenty seconds left.
A shorter later random wait looked wrong even though its retry window was larger.
Sleeping retries keep scarce connections or transaction locks occupied.
I need to distinguish four attempts total from four additional retries.

graphics.alt_text: Four clients without jitter retry at elapsed times one, three, and seven seconds. Independent full-jitter draws spread their retry times within the same successive one, two, and four second waiting bounds. Request durations are omitted and the times are illustrative.
graphics.caption: Backoff widens the interval between opportunities; jitter breaks repeated alignment. Squares mark retry starts, not successful completions. Both panels use the same elapsed-time scale.

graphics.alt_text: After an eligible failure, retry only when an attempt remains and the total budget permits the sampled wait. A first full-jitter window is zero through 100 milliseconds, then zero through 200, then zero through 400. Four total attempts permit at most three waits. Permanent failure, exhausted attempts, or exhausted budget ends the operation.
graphics.caption: Error classification, attempt limits, and the total deadline govern admission. Jitter chooses when an admitted retry may run; it does not make an unsafe operation safe.

patterns.title: Circuit Breaker
patterns.short_description: Temporarily reject new calls to an unhealthy dependency, then admit limited recovery probes before allowing normal traffic again.
use_when: Sustained dependency failure or slowness can exhaust caller resources and local rejection is preferable to repeated exposure.
Recent classified outcomes can drive an explicit admission and limited recovery-probe policy.
Rejected business work has an owner, a durable disposition or an honest unavailable/fallback outcome.
not_ideal_when: Most failures are invalid requests rather than a shared dependency-health condition.
A single bounded attempt plus existing platform isolation already protects the boundary adequately.
The breaker is expected to store work, terminate in-flight calls, roll back writes or enforce a fleet-wide concurrency limit.
prerequisites: Understand health classification, retained instance scope, sample windows, cooldown versus health proof, probe ownership, local rejection versus uncertain writes, resource cleanup and concurrent state transitions.
example_user_queries: A slow warehouse consumes all our connections even while almost every write fails.
We need to stop calling an unhealthy service temporarily and test recovery cautiously.
A newly created wrapper on each request never accumulates enough failures to protect us.
Bad input records are making our entire healthy integration shut down.
One failed supplier endpoint blocks two unrelated suppliers behind a shared health flag.
The waiting period ended but we do not know whether full traffic is safe again.
A successful lightweight health check did not mean the actual write path had recovered.
Every process sends its own recovery probe and together they overload the repaired service.
Calls rejected locally must retain their batches without pretending a write succeeded.
Our state-check shortcut prevents the dependency from ever receiving a recovery trial.

graphics.alt_text: Closed admits calls and observes classified outcomes. A threshold opens the breaker and rejects new calls. After a cooldown, a subsequent call may enter half-open as a limited probe. A successful qualifying probe closes the breaker; a failed probe reopens it and restarts the cooldown.
graphics.caption: Admission changes with state. The general pattern allows different sampling and probe policies; the worked model uses two counted failures and one recovery probe. Open-state rejection is not buffering or cancellation of earlier calls.

graphics.alt_text: Six sequential calls use one retained breaker. Two failures at time zero open it; a third call at zero is rejected locally. A probe fails at 100 milliseconds and reopens until 200. A call at 199 is rejected; a successful probe at 200 closes the breaker. Only four calls reach the simulated dependency.
graphics.caption: Local rejection never invokes the protected action. A failed probe restarts the cooldown from its completion; the next probe is admitted at the exact boundary. Times and outcomes belong to the sequential teaching model.

patterns.title: Bulkhead
patterns.short_description: Partition constrained capacity into separately enforced compartments so overload in one workload or dependency cannot consume every compartment's allowance.
use_when: A workload or slow dependency can consume capacity needed by independent work.
Workload/dependency classes have different deadlines or failure behavior and can be routed through enforceable resource boundaries.
Protected capacity can be provisioned, saturation outcomes owned and the shared downstream bottlenecks addressed explicitly.
not_ideal_when: A bounded shared pool adequately serves similar work without a separate protection requirement.
Permits or separate queue names are being mistaken for reserved execution threads, CPU, memory or data correctness.
A process-local cap is expected to enforce a fleet-wide rate, security sandbox, deadline or cancellation guarantee.
prerequisites: Understand resource-scoped isolation, concurrency versus rate/bytes, fixed allocation and borrowing, reliable routing, admission versus execution capacity, complete action lifetime, cleanup, shared bottlenecks and local versus fleet scope.
example_user_queries: A historical backfill uses every worker and our live ingestion misses its deadline.
One slow API consumes connections needed by an unrelated feature.
We created separate queues but both still feed the same unrestricted worker pool.
Higher priority did not help because all workers were already running long jobs.
I need excess repair work to be refused without using live work’s allowance.
A caller stopped waiting but its action still runs, so releasing its slot would over-admit work.
Four tasks each open ten database connections and exceed the downstream budget.
Our per-process concurrency cap multiplies when we add more replicas.
A production query depended on idle borrowed capacity that vanished when neighbors became busy.
I want to test that interactive work still runs while another class is saturated.

graphics.alt_text: A fixed allocation divides twenty worker permits into twelve for live processing, four for backfills, and four for exploration. Backfills at their four-permit limit cannot take the live allowance. Each class has its own admission boundary; all still depend on shared systems that need separate limits.
graphics.caption: Separate enforced allowances contain interference in the named resource. The 12/4/4 allocation is illustrative. Worker permits are not automatically reserved CPU, memory, or database connections.

graphics.alt_text: A backfill action acquires its one permit and waits on an event. A second backfill call is rejected without invocation, while a live call uses its independent permit. After the event is released, the first backfill finishes, returns its permit, and permits another backfill call.
graphics.caption: The permit follows the synchronous action's lifetime. Saturation changes admission in that compartment; it does not consume the other compartment's allowance or terminate the action already running.

patterns.title: Queue-Based Load Leveling
patterns.short_description: Buffer bursty requests in a queue and control the aggregate drain so downstream work proceeds within a sustainable budget.
use_when: Temporary bursts exceed a downstream service’s safe processing budget but the total work can drain within a business deadline.
Callers can accept a job receipt and retrieve an eventual outcome instead of holding a synchronous connection.
Waiting capacity, aggregate consumption, durable acceptance and failure recovery have explicit owners.
not_ideal_when: The caller requires the completed result immediately or traffic is low and steady.
Sustained arrival volume exceeds safe capacity with no policy to reduce admission or add sustainable capacity.
A queue alone is expected to impose a fleet-wide drain rate, successful processing or exactly-once effects.
prerequisites: Understand admission versus completion, waiting versus in-flight work, concurrency versus rate, queue/byte/retention limits, aggregate consumer/retry budgets and duplicate-safe acknowledgment protocols.
example_user_queries: A burst of report requests overwhelms the database even though it can handle the daily total.
Customers can wait for an export but our API currently holds every connection until it finishes.
Our workers autoscale from queue depth and overload the service they call.
The request was accepted quickly but the oldest job has been waiting for hours.
I need to absorb a short traffic spike without allowing unlimited pending work.
Doubling the buffer delayed overload but did not let the service catch up.
A job was completed before the worker crashed, then the broker delivered it again.
Our concurrency cap still permits too many fast downstream requests each second.
I need an explicit outcome when a waiting queue reaches its limit.
I want to calculate how long a burst takes to drain while new jobs keep arriving.

graphics.alt_text: Bursty producers enqueue jobs into a six-place waiting buffer. A controlled handler transfers work toward the target using a two-job budget per one-second model tick. Confirmed admission and completed work are distinct outcomes. Queue capacity, drain budget, and target capacity are separate controls.
graphics.caption: The queue separates arrival from execution. Arrows mean work transfer; the handler's aggregate drain must fit downstream capacity. The six-place buffer and two-job tick budget belong to the teaching model.

graphics.alt_text: Four one-second ticks show arrivals of six, two, zero, and zero jobs. All are admitted without rejection. Each tick completes two jobs, leaving four, four, two, and zero waiting. Accepted jobs total eight, completed jobs total eight, and the final backlog is empty.
graphics.caption: This trace matches the runnable simulation. Arrivals are admitted before draining; waiting is sampled at the end of each tick. Two completions per tick smooth the initial six-job burst across four ticks.

patterns.title: Backpressure
patterns.short_description: Slow or pause upstream admission when downstream work cannot keep up, using feedback to bound buffering instead of letting queues grow without control.
use_when: An incremental producer can wait while a slower receiver finishes work.
Buffers or unfinished asynchronous operations grow because intake ignores downstream readiness.
The system needs explicit capacity feedback across cooperative stage boundaries and a declared policy where production cannot pause.
not_ideal_when: A direct loop already waits for real completion before fetching the next item.
A non-pausable source has no deliberate overflow, retention or loss policy.
Flow-control permission is being mistaken for durable completion, exactly-once effects, total memory bounds or a fixed rate quota.
prerequisites: Understand waiting versus in-flight capacity, demand permission versus acknowledgment, incremental source behavior, async callback lifetime, buffer/byte units, cooperative cancellation, upstream retention and scope-owned cleanup.
example_user_queries: My reader keeps fetching while the destination is stalled and memory grows.
A bounded input queue did not help because we launch unlimited asynchronous writes after taking items out.
I need the next source read to wait until the previous write actually finishes.
The stream says it cannot accept more work, but our sender keeps pushing.
We increased the buffer size and only delayed the crash.
The source is waiting for output capacity but the real bottleneck is several stages downstream.
Our consumer memory is stable while the broker backlog grows past its retention window.
A Node write returned false and I need to know whether that chunk was rejected.
I need cancellation to stop further reads and close the source without claiming remote work was undone.
A live sensor cannot pause, so I need an explicit policy when its receiver has no capacity.

graphics.alt_text: Without feedback, a source offering five thousand records per second feeds a sink processing two thousand; a buffer with six thousand free places fills in two seconds. With feedback, downstream capacity limits upstream admission. Data moves downstream while a separate capacity signal travels upstream; excess work remains outside the controlled boundary.
graphics.caption: Steady rates of 5,000 in and 2,000 out add 3,000 queued records per second. With 6,000 free places, filling takes two seconds. Feedback changes admission, not processing capacity; remaining work needs an explicit home.

graphics.alt_text: The transfer reads the first chunk and awaits its sink write. While the write is blocked, it does not request chunk two. Completion permits the next read. After all three chunks complete, the generator is closed and the result reports three chunks and six bytes. Failure or cancellation exits through source closing instead of requesting further chunks.
graphics.caption: Awaited completion gates the next read in this example. It permits at most one unfinished callback invocation and creates no per-chunk task queue. The sink owns its cleanup; source closing belongs to transfer.

patterns.title: Load Shedding
patterns.short_description: Refuse selected work before expensive processing when an admission policy says available capacity cannot safely accommodate it.
use_when: Excess offered work threatens useful completions and clients cannot wait indefinitely for capacity.
Admission can be decided before an expensive operation using a trustworthy budget or resource signal.
Refusal outcomes, retry budgets and aggregate client-observed service loss are explicit.
not_ideal_when: Low predictable demand is adequately protected by existing bounded server settings.
All work must be retained durably, so an explicit acceptance/storage contract is needed instead of silent discard.
A static per-process cost estimate is expected to reserve hardware, enforce a fleet-wide rate or implement trusted priority automatically.
prerequisites: Understand early admission versus incurred costs, occupancy versus timed rates, variable request cost, trusted classification, rejection overhead, callback resource lifetime, local versus fleet scope and duplicate-safe bounded retries.
example_user_queries: A traffic rush makes every request time out even though we could still serve a useful subset.
Our service accepts work before discovering that there are no database resources left.
I need an explicit refusal instead of adding another request to an already delayed queue.
One expensive search costs much more than a small lookup, so a request-count cap is misleading.
The service looks fast when I graph only successful accepted requests, but most clients are being rejected.
We keep retrying overload errors and create even more demand.
I need to distinguish a temporary occupancy refusal from an invalid request cost.
The admission gate protects handlers but is itself overwhelmed by rejection traffic.
We want to drop optional recommendations before losing checkout operations.
A client stops waiting while its operation continues, so returning its budget early would admit too much work.

graphics.alt_text: A request reaches a cheap admission decision before expensive work. If its trusted work cost fits the remaining budget, that cost is claimed and the operation runs. If it does not fit, the service returns an explicit overload result without invoking the operation or adding it to an internal waiting queue. Claimed budget returns after local completion and cleanup.
graphics.caption: Refusal happens before the protected operation. Admission bookkeeping still costs resources, and this boundary cannot recover costs already incurred upstream. A shed request is not silently accepted for later processing.

graphics.alt_text: With capacity three, a running heavy search occupies two units. A second two-unit search would require four and is refused without invocation. A one-unit lookup fits exactly alongside the running search. After local work finishes and releases its units, a later heavy search can run. Policy units do not reserve execution threads or predict actual resource consumption.
graphics.caption: Two occupied units plus a two-unit request exceed three; two plus one fit. Equality is admitted. The light call has an already available caller thread. The code enforces the declared weighted budget, not a rate, CPU allocation, fairness policy, or fleet-wide limit.

patterns.title: Health Endpoint
patterns.short_description: Expose a small, explicit health contract that an external observer can use to make routing, startup, or recovery decisions.
use_when: An external monitor, router or orchestrator needs a declared instance-health signal for a particular decision.
A process and port can remain present while required serving capability is unavailable.
Startup, traffic eligibility and local recovery need distinct contracts with explicit timing and consumers.
not_ideal_when: An existing platform health group already supplies the required interface and only needs its membership configured.
A simple process-existence check is the only operational question actually being managed.
A shallow success is being used as proof of full business correctness, guaranteed future success or universal traffic removal.
prerequisites: Understand local progress versus traffic readiness versus initialization, observer-owned actions and thresholds, dependency criticality, shared-failure coupling, cached-state freshness, probe cost, serving-path reachability, minimal disclosure and resource-owned cleanup.
example_user_queries: The process is running but its database pool is unusable and the load balancer still sends it requests.
A slow-starting instance gets restarted before it can finish loading its index.
A shared database outage makes every application instance restart at once.
I need to stop new traffic before shutting down an instance while existing requests finish.
Our management listener looks healthy while the real application port cannot accept work.
A green health check keeps serving an old cached dependency result.
I need to separate liveness, startup completion and readiness instead of sharing one generic status.
Our health endpoint redirects to a login page and the probe treats it as success.
A dependency check on every probe overloads the dependency during an incident.
All targets are marked unhealthy but the load balancer still routes traffic, so I need to understand its policy.

graphics.alt_text: An external prober calls an instance's health endpoint. The handler reads declared local lifecycle and dependency observations and returns a small status. The observer applies configured timing and thresholds before changing routing, startup gating, or restart behavior. The endpoint does not perform those actions itself.
graphics.caption: A reported observation and an operational action are separate steps. Define what is checked, where the probe runs, and which consumer owns the response to failure.

graphics.alt_text: Five lifecycle phases show liveness, startup, and readiness responses. Starting gives 200, 503, 503; ready gives three 200 responses; a required dependency outage gives 200, 200, 503; recovery gives three 200 responses; draining gives 200, 200, 503. Readiness loss does not imply a liveness failure or an automatic restart.
graphics.caption: These are the example's status decisions, not a universal health schema. Each request reads its own snapshot; independent probes can straddle state transitions. No router or restart controller is implemented.

patterns.title: Cache-Aside
patterns.short_description: Let application code check a disposable cache first, load misses from the authoritative store, and manage invalidation after writes.
use_when: Expensive source reads repeat for a subset of data with an explicit acceptable-staleness contract.
Application code must manage cache hits, source loads, expiration and invalidation.
Demand-driven population is preferable to caching every source record in advance.
not_ideal_when: Direct indexed reads already meet the budget or repeated keys are rare.
A sensitive operation must consult current authoritative state without an established stronger cache protocol.
A native read-through provider or local bounded memoization already owns the required loading contract.
prerequisites: Understand source ownership, complete cache identity and current authorization, TTL versus source freshness, cold-cache capacity, invalidation failure and stale in-flight fills.
example_user_queries: Our product pages keep reading the same records from the database and response times are rising.
I need to load only requested records into a cache instead of copying the entire database.
A database update succeeds but users keep seeing the old cached value.
A slow reader puts an old value back after another request deletes the cached key.
I need to choose where cache-miss loading and invalidation should live in the application.
Our service works with a warm cache but overloads its database after a deployment.
I need expiration and a memory limit without treating zero as a missing value.
Two customers can receive different prices so a shared product-only cache key is unsafe.
A cache outage sends all traffic to the database and causes a second outage.
I want to distinguish lazy cache loading from read-through, write-through and memoization.

graphics.alt_text: Application code checks the cache first. A usable hit returns without reading the store. A miss or expired entry causes a store read and cache fill before returning. A separate write path commits the source update and then invalidates the cached key.
graphics.caption: The application coordinates both systems. Arrows show ordered operations, not an atomic transaction spanning cache and store.

graphics.alt_text: Four ordered events show a late cache fill: reader A obtains 1200 on a miss; writer B commits 1300; B invalidates the key; A installs its older 1200. The authoritative store remains 1300 while a subsequent cache hit can return 1200.
graphics.caption: Commit then invalidate is necessary ordering for this design, but it does not reject a fill that began before the write. TTL starts at installation and does not establish source age.

patterns.title: Memoization
patterns.short_description: Remember a function’s completed results under equivalent inputs so later calls can reuse them instead of repeating the calculation.
use_when: Expensive deterministic function evaluations repeat under equivalent complete inputs.
An acyclic recursive problem repeats overlapping subproblems.
A computation-owned immutable snapshot makes cache identity and lifetime explicit.
not_ideal_when: The calculation is cheap or almost every call has a unique input.
A hit would skip a required side effect or hide mutable dependencies and changed permissions.
An iterative pass or a better recurrence avoids the repeated work with less memory or recursion.
prerequisites: Understand complete input equivalence, hash/equality behavior, immutable values, recursion, acyclic dependencies, retention ownership and the distinction between completed-result reuse and in-flight coordination.
example_user_queries: My recursive project estimate keeps calculating the same shared dependency more than once.
An expensive function receives the same arguments repeatedly and I want to reuse its answers.
I added a wrapper but internal recursive calls still repeat all the work.
A cached function reads mutable configuration and starts returning old answers.
Two versions of a project use the same task indices but produce different results.
A long-lived function cache holds onto large inputs and results until memory grows.
My cached function returns a list and one caller changes what the next caller sees.
Two threads both execute a function even though its cache bookkeeping is thread-safe.
Filtering an unchanged document runs again whenever unrelated screen state changes.
I need to compare a recursive cache with an iterative dynamic-programming pass.

patterns.title: Materialized View
patterns.short_description: Store a query’s derived result for reuse, with explicit maintenance and freshness rules that keep consumers aware of when the stored answer is valid.
use_when: Many reads reuse expensive joins, aggregates or transformed source data.
Consumers need a maintained read shape different from authoritative write storage.
The freshness contract and refresh cost justify precomputation with explicit correction and failure handling.
not_ideal_when: Direct queries or ordinary views with indexes already meet the budget.
Query shapes rarely repeat or maintenance costs exceed saved read work.
Immediate authoritative state is needed without an established synchronous or stronger freshness protocol.
prerequisites: Understand grain and currency units, full versus incremental maintenance, covered source boundaries, correction/deletion/duplicate handling, atomic publication, consumer privileges and refresh versus ingestion lag.
example_user_queries: Every dashboard request joins and groups the same sales records again.
I want a small summary table while preserving authoritative transaction records.

I need counts and totals to change together with their publication version.

The database returns correct answers but suddenly stops using its precomputed acceleration.
I need to backfill historical data without a gap or overlap with ongoing changes.
A refresh completes successfully while older source events still have not arrived.

patterns.title: Sharding
patterns.short_description: Distribute rows across independently operated shards and route requests to their owners, increasing capacity while making cross-shard work and resharding explicit responsibilities.
use_when: One storage group is a measured capacity or throughput bottleneck after ordinary tuning.
A stable distribution key keeps important requests and transactions local.
The team can own placement metadata, migration, hot-key handling and cross-shard failure semantics.
not_ideal_when: Indexes, query changes, archiving or a larger database already meet the budget.
Read replicas address the actual read-only pressure.
Most requests require expensive joins or strict transactions across every shard.
prerequisites: Understand logical versus physical partitions, key locality/skew, targeted versus scatter/gather work, shard-local transactions, authoritative ownership validation and safe migration lifecycle.
example_user_queries: Our order database has reached one machine’s write and storage limits.
Adding read replicas does not reduce the amount of data each database must hold.
How can we keep each customer’s orders and order lines together as we add machines?

We have evenly sized partitions but one tenant generates most of the traffic.
Queries without a customer key now contact every database and time out.
Adding a server changes where nearly every record should live.
An old application instance keeps writing to the previous owner after data moves.
I need to move a subset of records without changing how keys are classified.
Our cross-database joins and transactions erase the gains from horizontal scaling.

patterns.title: Competing Consumers
patterns.short_description: Let interchangeable workers share one logical work channel so each delivery goes to one worker, increasing concurrent processing while keeping redelivery and completion explicit.
use_when: Independent jobs accumulate behind one worker and more interchangeable consumers can share them.
Producers should target one logical work stream rather than choose a free instance.
Delivery recovery, completion tracking and safe business retries have explicit contracts.
not_ideal_when: One worker meets demand or global ordering dominates.
Independent interests each require the same publication.
Extra workers would overload an already saturated downstream dependency.
prerequisites: Understand logical message versus delivery identity, acknowledgment versus business completion, bounded outstanding ownership, redelivery, ordering, graceful shutdown and queue versus consumer-group semantics.
example_user_queries: One background worker cannot drain our upload jobs fast enough.
Each new worker receives every job instead of sharing the pending work.
A large image blocks smaller jobs that could finish on another machine.
We acknowledge work early and lose jobs when a worker crashes.
A worker saved its output but disconnected before confirming completion.
One consumer has reserved all the pending work while other workers are idle.
Our FIFO queue produces business updates in a different completion order.
Adding more stream readers than partitions does not increase throughput.
I need to stop a worker without abandoning its accepted deliveries.
The queue looks empty even though several jobs are still running.

graphics.alt_text: One thumbnail work queue contains jobs J1, J2, and J3. Consumer A receives J1 while consumer B receives J2. J3 remains ready until a consumer requests more work. These workers divide one logical stream; they do not each receive every job.
graphics.caption: Each arrow represents one delivery to one recipient. A and B can hold different jobs at the same time. The illustrated assignment is an example, not a round-robin or fairness guarantee.

graphics.alt_text: J1 is first delivered to A with token 1. Explicit disconnection retires that delivery and returns J1 to the ready queue. B receives J1 with token 4; a token-1 acknowledgment is rejected and token 4 can be acknowledged. The previous attempt’s business effect remains unknown.

patterns.title: Batching
patterns.short_description: Group compatible operations into bounded execution units to share fixed overhead, with explicit limits on size, waiting, and completion semantics.
use_when: Repeated fixed call, scheduling, serialization or commit overhead dominates useful per-item work.
The destination supports compatible grouped execution and callers tolerate bounded formation delay.
Pending, outstanding and retry ownership plus individual outcome semantics are explicit.
not_ideal_when: Sparse demand or strict latency budgets favor immediate operations.
The destination merely loops over equally expensive separate calls without saving meaningful overhead.
Grouping crosses authorization, ordering or transactional boundaries without a supported contract.
prerequisites: Understand item-count versus serialized-byte limits, oldest-item age and timer progress, residual shutdown drain, pending versus emitted ownership, per-member outcomes and unknown transport results.
example_user_queries: Each tiny telemetry message pays for a separate remote call.
Our count-based buffer never sends its last few records when traffic slows.
I need to combine writes without delaying the oldest item indefinitely.
A payload fits the record-count limit but exceeds the service’s byte limit.

The bulk request returns HTTP 200 even though some operations failed.
After a network timeout I do not know which grouped writes already happened.
Resetting a timer on every arrival keeps old records waiting too long.
Fewer calls improve total work but individual requests now wait longer.
Each collector is small but emitted requests and retries keep accumulating.

graphics.alt_text: Seven individual calls would each pay five milliseconds of fixed overhead plus one millisecond per item, totaling 42 milliseconds of modeled service work. The example emits four batches containing three, one, one, and two items, totaling 27 milliseconds under the same assumptions. Collection waiting is excluded.
graphics.caption: This is an illustrative additive cost model, not a latency benchmark. Seven items remain seven operations; four batches pay the fixed cost four times. Waiting, contention, and destination behavior determine actual response time.

graphics.alt_text: The program emits a, bb, and c at 8 milliseconds because three items have accumulated. At 13 milliseconds it emits dddd before adding eee because seven bytes would exceed the six-byte limit. At 23 milliseconds eee reaches ten milliseconds of age. Closing at 26 milliseconds emits the remaining f and g.
graphics.caption: Count and byte limits can emit early; age releases a partial group when traffic stops; close drains the residual group. Ten milliseconds is a formation policy checked by advance, not a guaranteed delivery deadline.

patterns.short_description: Let overlapping callers for an equivalent operation share one in-flight execution, then retire that shared work without implying a completed-result cache.

A service can own shared-work lifetime separately from individual waits.
not_ideal_when: Overlap is rare or source work is cheap.
Each command must execute independently or readers require independent snapshots.
Keys omit authorization, representation or version context needed for safe sharing.
prerequisites: Understand complete immutable operation identity, local coordinator scope, registration before suspension, waiter versus loader cancellation, strong task ownership, failure retirement, active-work limits and freshness/invalidation independence.
example_user_queries: Every request on a popular expired cache entry starts the same database read.
Overlapping readers need the same metadata but each triggers a fresh remote call.

Users from different tenants accidentally share a response under the same resource ID.
A failed shared lookup stays registered and prevents every later recovery attempt.
I need to stop accepting requests and drain the backend work my service owns.
A slow shared read attracts so many waiters that memory usage keeps growing.
I want later requests to refresh the answer after the current shared read finishes.

When the policy service fails our fallback accidentally permits access.

Permission tests pass but callers can still modify or skip the enforcement component.
I need a small, reviewable enforcement boundary instead of many scattered security checks.

patterns.title: Gatekeeper
patterns.short_description: Screen public requests in a limited-privilege tier that forwards a narrow contract to private services holding the data access and business authority.
use_when: Public protocol handling should have less privilege than private business operations.
Storage credentials or broad service authority currently live alongside exposed parsing code.
A narrow public contract can be validated separately from current object-level authorization.
not_ideal_when: Existing platform controls already provide the required admission and enforceable privilege separation.
A second class or wrapper is being mistaken for an isolated deployment boundary.
Added network hops and operational dependencies outweigh the required separation.
prerequisites: Define runtime identities, private endpoint reachability, allowed internal operations, end-user authentication context, authoritative business authorization, body/concurrency limits, deadlines and safe failure behavior.
example_user_queries: Our public API parser runs with the same database credentials as the core application.
I want internet-facing request handling separated from privileged business processing.
We added validation middleware but a compromised endpoint could still read all our storage.
How can we expose a narrow operation without exposing the private service interface?
The front end forwards every caller header and URL to an internal service.
Our internal API trusts an owner field just because it came through the gateway.
Valid JSON requests can still ask for operations the customer is not allowed to perform.
We need to keep storage keys out of the service that accepts untrusted traffic.
Our outage fallback exposes the back end directly when request screening is unavailable.
I need a clear split between public admission checks and current business authorization.

graphics.alt_text: Public clients reach a limited-privilege gatekeeper, which screens requests and forwards only the fixed label-preview operation over an authenticated internal channel. A separate private service owns authorization and order access. Only that service reaches the order store; the gatekeeper has no storage credentials or direct storage route.
graphics.caption: The deployed boundary separates exposure from privilege. A private address alone is insufficient: restrict reachable operations, authenticate the service hop, and keep storage authority out of the public tier.

graphics.alt_text: Five requests divide into three outcomes: a two-copy preview for Alice’s O100 order is admitted and allowed; an extra owner field and boolean copy count are rejected before forwarding; four copies and another owner’s order pass admission but are denied by the private service.
graphics.caption: Admission and business authorization answer different questions. A valid request may still be denied; a blocked request must not reach the service. These are simulator outcomes, not proof of deployment isolation.

Function calls and underscore fields supply no runtime/identity/network isolation, authentication, credential protection, durable effects or security proof. Real deployment must bind user context to authenticated protocols, authenticate service hops, restrict credentials/reachability, authorize current operations, bound ingress reading and calls, and fail without exposing a bypass. The read-only preview makes no retry/exactly-once claim.

patterns.title: Federated Identity
patterns.short_description: Accept authentication assertions from explicitly trusted identity providers, then resolve the federated identity to a local account whose access the application controls.
use_when: Partner, employee or customer authentication is already operated by an explicitly trusted external identity provider.
Several applications should consume organizational authentication without handling the organization’s passwords.
An application must distinguish multiple issuers, associate verified identities with local accounts and retain local authorization.
not_ideal_when: No external trust relationship is needed and a managed application-local identity service suffices.
A decoded token or arbitrary identity header is being treated as authenticated evidence.
Account linking, provisioning, local session lifetime and deprovisioning responsibilities are unspecified.
prerequisites: Understand trusted issuers, RP registration, protocol-library validation, transaction binding and PKCE, issuer-qualified subject identity, authorized account linking, local permissions, separate assertion/IdP/RP session lifetimes, privacy and provider failure/key rotation.
example_user_queries: Our partners already sign in at their own companies, but our portal asks them to create another password.
We want several applications to use organizational sign-in without collecting directory passwords.
Two identity providers send us the same email address and we accidentally merge their users.
The same subject identifier appears at different providers and our account lookup gets confused.
A user changed their email address and lost access to their existing application account.
An authenticated partner is being granted reports that their local account should not be allowed to read.
We disabled an employee at the identity provider but their application session is still active.
I need to distinguish a verified login identity from an API access token or an unverified token payload.
We are migrating a partner to a new sign-in provider and need safe account association.
Our external sign-in service can fail, and we need to define what happens to new logins and existing sessions.

graphics.alt_text: Four summarized phases of an OpenID Connect code-flow sign-in: the portal starts a transaction bound to its browser session; the identity provider authenticates the user; a code callback and server token exchange let the portal verify the resulting identity; the portal creates its own session and applies local report permissions. The user’s credentials remain with the provider.
graphics.caption: These arrows order summarized protocol phases. The code returns through the browser; the portal exchanges it over a protected back channel. Federation establishes an authenticated identity, while local account and resource rules still govern access.

graphics.alt_text: Five post-validation cases retain issuer-qualified identities: North subject 17 resolves to a1 and may read the summary; South subject 17 resolves to b9 and is denied; North subject 18 is unlinked and denied. North subject 17 still resolves to a1 after its email changes. After a1 loses its local report grant, it remains recognized but the next summary request is denied.
graphics.caption: Account recognition and resource permission remain separate. These fixtures assume protocol validation already succeeded. Neither a matching email nor a matching subject from a different issuer authorizes account linking.

patterns.title: Externalized Authorization
patterns.short_description: Move access-decision policy behind a dedicated decision interface while keeping enforcement beside every protected operation.
use_when: Several services repeatedly implement the same resource access rules and diverge during changes.
Policy ownership, review or rollout should be separated from business application ownership.
Applications need a consistent decision interface while keeping enforcement at each protected operation.
not_ideal_when: A small application with stable rules already has an adequate well-tested local authorization module.
A remote service is being added without a need for independent policy governance or operation.
Trusted attributes, alternate access paths, decision failure semantics and acceptable revocation staleness are undefined.
prerequisites: Distinguish PDP decisions from PEP enforcement; define trusted subject/resource/context provenance, policy administration and attribute-source ownership, explicit reply and obligation contracts, check/use binding, version/freshness semantics, deployment and distribution, deadlines, capacity, failure handling and decision-cache lifetime.
example_user_queries: Our API, export worker and web application apply different versions of the same permission rule.
We keep copying tenant-access checks into every service repository.
The security team needs to review access policy without changing business-processing code.
I need one decision interface while each service still controls its own protected operations.
Our application logs a policy denial but still reads the requested data.
A cached permit remains valid after the user loses the underlying grant.
We need to choose between an in-process policy engine, a sidecar and a remote authorization service.
When the permission service times out our fallback accidentally allows the operation.
The policy engine requires masking but the handler returns the full report anyway.
Clients can supply the tenant and role values that our access decision trusts.

graphics.alt_text: A resource handler builds a decision request from a trusted subject and report metadata, sends it to a separate policy engine, and receives a decision with query binding, policy version, and obligations. The same handler validates and enforces that response before reading a protected body. Missing, denied, unusable, or failed decisions never reach the body read.
graphics.caption: The arrows distinguish a decision request, a decision response, and the guarded resource operation. The repeated handler steps are the same enforcement point. The policy engine returns a decision; the handler must enforce its limits.

graphics.alt_text: Four evaluations show enforcement outcomes. Under policy version 1, Alice’s R1 request is allowed and reads North’s body; R2 is denied without a body read. After revocation, version 2 denies R1. An unavailable decision service produces no response and no body read. Unsupported obligations also block an otherwise permitted read.
graphics.caption: Policy denial and decision-service failure have different operational meanings, but neither releases a body here. Policy revisions label evaluations; they do not prove fleet-wide freshness or make old cached permits safe.

patterns.title: Valet Key
patterns.short_description: Authorize a client to obtain a short-lived, narrowly scoped grant that the resource service validates during direct data access.
use_when: Large or frequent transfers consume application workers while the application adds little value to the byte stream.
Storage can enforce narrow direct-access grants without giving clients the application’s broad storage credentials.
The application should authorize issuance while resource, operation and time restrictions are enforced by the resource service.
not_ideal_when: Every byte must be inspected, transformed or metered through the application before delivery.
Direct client identity at storage already provides the required controlled access.
Required single-use, immediate revocation, version binding, upload constraints or audit semantics are unsupported by the chosen grant mechanism.
prerequisites: Understand issuance authorization, privileged signing/delegation, exact resource/verb/time scope, bearer possession and secure delivery, storage enforcement, provider credential lifetime/revocation semantics, reuse versus single-use, request-time expiry, upload quarantine/validation, direct-transfer audit/capacity controls and immutable object versions.
example_user_queries: Our application workers spend most of their time relaying large downloads from object storage.
I want clients to upload or download one object without handing them an account-wide storage key.
We need the application to approve access while storage handles the actual bytes.
An object URL should allow only a particular operation for a short period.
We assumed a signed download link could be used only once, but users can reuse it.
A user lost application access but an already issued download link still works.
Our download expires while a large transfer is running and we need to define retry behavior.
Clients can choose arbitrary object paths when asking us to sign a storage request.
A leaked URL appeared in logs and could still be used to retrieve a private export.
We need to separate permission to upload bytes from approval to publish the uploaded content.

graphics.alt_text: The client first requests an export download from the application. The application authenticates and authorizes the request, then returns a grant restricted to GET on export E7 for a short window. The client presents that grant directly to storage. Storage validates it and returns archive bytes directly to the client; those bytes do not pass through the issuing application.
graphics.caption: Grant issuance and data transfer are separate paths. The application retains broad signing or delegation authority; storage enforces the limited grant. Direct access is deliberate, and its restrictions must survive every request the resource service accepts.

graphics.alt_text: A ticket issued at virtual second 100 permits GET on exports/E7.zip until but not including second 160. GET for E8 and PUT for E7 are denied. Reuse and a new GET at second 159 succeed. A new GET at second 160 is denied. This is a request-admission window, not a promise to cancel an existing transfer.
graphics.caption: Resource, verb, and time are independent restrictions. The example permits repeated reads, and storage receives no user identity with the ticket. Possession must therefore be protected; expiry does not erase previously downloaded bytes.

patterns.title: Test Double
patterns.short_description: Replace a production collaborator with a test-controlled substitute to supply specific responses or observe interactions while exercising the real subject.
use_when: An external collaborator makes focused tests slow, unsafe, unavailable or unpredictable
A rare reply or failure needs a deterministic trigger
A requirement is observable through a significant outgoing interaction
not_ideal_when: The real collaborator is fast, deterministic and easy to construct
Replacing the subject would remove the behavior being tested
A substitute is expected to prove real network, storage or concurrency guarantees
prerequisites: Function calls and dependency boundaries
Basic assertions, exceptions and test fixtures
example_user_queries: Our unit tests fail whenever the payment sandbox is unavailable.
How can I test a declined transaction without sending a real charge?
I need to check that invalid input never calls an external service.
We need deterministic tests for rare network failures.
Our tests send real emails and need a safer replacement.
What should I use when I only need to supply a fixed response?
I need to inspect the outgoing request after the application runs.
Our in-memory database tests pass while the actual database behaves differently.
Tests break whenever we rearrange internal helper calls.
How can each test get fresh recorded calls without sharing mutable fixtures?

graphics.alt_text: Production checkout calls a payment adapter. In a focused test, the same real checkout calls a test double through the charge contract; the test arranges its response and verifies the returned status and recorded call. The real payment adapter and provider are outside this test.
graphics.caption: Only the collaborator changes. The test exercises checkout itself; its success does not establish that the production adapter can reach or correctly translate the provider.

graphics.alt_text: Four checkout scenarios use a fresh gateway double. Approval returns accepted:r-17 and refusal returns declined, each after one charge call. Zero cents raises ValueError with no charge call. TimeoutError propagates after one attempted call and does not mean declined.
graphics.caption: Assertions cover both the visible result and the relevant boundary interaction. The timeout test establishes checkout's handling of uncertainty, not the provider's eventual charge outcome.

patterns.title: Test Data Builder
patterns.short_description: Create real test inputs from reusable defaults while letting each test override the values that explain its scenario.
use_when: Many tests repeat substantial object construction while differing in a few important values
Constructor changes force edits to otherwise unchanged scenarios
Related test inputs need reusable recipes without shared mutable state
not_ideal_when: A direct constructor with named arguments already communicates the scenario
Only a few fixed examples are needed and rarely vary
A builder would duplicate the production rules whose results the test asserts
prerequisites: Basic object construction and assertions
Mutable versus immutable data and shallow copying
example_user_queries: Our tests repeat long constructors just to change one relevant value.
Adding a required field breaks fixture setup across dozens of unrelated tests.
I cannot tell which values in a large test fixture actually explain the assertion.
One test appends to a nested list and changes the data another test uses.
We need several similar orders without sharing mutable child objects.
Our fixture factory has a new method for every combination of options.
I want boundary values to be visible instead of buried among setup details.
A helper automatically fixes invalid input and prevents testing rejection.
Shared default data changed and silently altered what our tests exercise.
The IDs in reusable test recipes collide when we persist fixtures in parallel.

graphics.alt_text: A default order recipe supplies a customer, US destination, standard delivery, and empty notes. One test overrides the subtotal to 4999 cents; another overrides it to 5000 cents. Each build creates a separate real order, which the same delivery rule evaluates.
graphics.caption: The defaults provide construction context. The two subtotals stay visible because they explain the free-delivery boundary; the builder does not calculate the expected fee.

graphics.alt_text: One immutable order builder produces Order A and Order B, each with its own empty notes list. Adding fragile to Order A changes only A’s list. Configuring an express variant creates a separate builder recipe and leaves the base recipe standard.
graphics.caption: Recipe reuse and result isolation are separate decisions. Immutable builder state protects configuration; fresh mutable children protect built objects. The fixed order identifier is a fixture value, not a uniqueness guarantee.

patterns.title: Consumer-Driven Contract Tests
patterns.short_description: Let consumers define executable expectations for the interfaces they actually use, then verify those expectations against provider changes before rollout.
use_when: Identifiable consumer and provider teams deploy independently across API, event, file or dataset boundaries
Provider tests pass while changes repeatedly break actual readers
Shared end-to-end environments make interface feedback slow or unreliable
not_ideal_when: Components are released together and direct integration checks are sufficient
A public provider cannot participate and the goal requires its verified compatibility evidence
The proposed contracts copy the whole provider functional suite or claim to verify broker operations
prerequisites: Client/provider boundaries and controlled test interactions
Field matching, provider-state isolation and semantic units
Versioned artifacts and release evidence for deployed combinations
example_user_queries: Our API tests pass but a field rename breaks a downstream client.
How can consumers share only the response details they really depend on?
We want early compatibility feedback without running every service together.
A mock response still passes client tests after the provider stopped returning that shape.
We need to test a real message handler against examples the producer can verify.
Adding an unused JSON field should not break every consumer test.
A response matches the schema but changed units or dataset grain break the consumer.
We verified the newest client but older client versions are still running.
There is no verification result for the pair of versions we plan to release.
Provider tests replace the serializer and fail to catch the actual integration defect.

graphics.alt_text: The real stock reader runs against a controlled interaction and produces a versioned consumer contract. Separately, a verifier arranges provider state and calls the candidate inventory API with the same request. Its actual response is checked against that contract. Consumer success alone and provider success alone leave different evidence gaps.
graphics.caption: Two checks share one agreement. Consumer execution grounds the expectations; provider verification checks the implementation intended for release. Neither check requires the other application to run alongside it.

graphics.alt_text: For reader-3, an original provider response with available equal to seven and unit EA passes. Adding an unused zone field also passes. Renaming available to quantity fails. A separate version matrix shows reader-3 with provider-8 passing, reader-3 with provider-9 failing, and an unverified reader-4/provider-8 pair remaining unknown.
graphics.caption: Matching permits harmless extensions but protects required fields and units. The version matrix is an illustrative release-evidence example, separate from the runnable simulation; unknown is not a passing result.

patterns.title: Strangler Fig
patterns.short_description: Replace a legacy system in useful slices through controlled seams, shifting responsibility to the new implementation while old and new coexist.
use_when: A substantial legacy replacement needs useful progress before the entire system is rebuilt
Coherent capabilities, workflows, datasets or tenant cohorts can move through controlled seams
The legacy system can remain operational while dependencies, data and ownership transition
not_ideal_when: A small system has a simple rehearsable cutover
No feasible boundary or integration point can intercept relevant work
Legacy must be decommissioned immediately without time for coexistence
Shared state prevents meaningful independent slices without first changing the boundary
prerequisites: An inventory of callers, data dependencies and business invariants
Observable routing or ownership records controlled by trusted migration operators
Comparison criteria, data catch-up and a realistic recovery/retirement plan
example_user_queries: Our replacement project keeps chasing changes in the old system and never reaches launch.
We need to move one business capability while the rest of the legacy system keeps running.
How can clients keep one entry point while implementations move gradually?
A routing switch moved reads but left writes and corrections in the old store.
Randomly splitting events between implementations breaks complete customer state.
We need to know which implementation may publish for each migrated tenant.
A replacement timeout triggers fallback even though the new system may have completed a write.
We want rollback but the old database is no longer current.
Most easy workflows migrated while hidden dependencies keep the old platform alive.
How do we decide when migration adapters and old paths can finally be removed?

graphics.alt_text: During migration, clients keep using one entry point. Its routing seam sends the catalog capability to the replacement and the invoice capability to the legacy implementation. The request selects one owner; no error path automatically sends it to both.
graphics.caption: The seam separates client access from implementation ownership. Catalog has moved; invoices have not. Routing is transitional architecture, and completion requires retiring displaced responsibilities and remaining dependencies.

graphics.alt_text: Tenant cohorts A, B, and C start with the old publisher. Successive handovers move A, then B, then C to the new publisher. Each cohort has one authoritative publisher per stage. Preparation and stale-writer fencing precede authority transfer; rollback requires current and representable data.
graphics.caption: This stateful cohort example is separate from the read-only routing program. A route change alone cannot synchronize stores or revoke an in-flight writer. One published result per cohort requires an enforced ownership boundary.

patterns.title: Expand–Migrate–Contract
patterns.short_description: Introduce a replacement alongside the old interface, migrate data and consumers, then remove the old representation after verifying that dependencies have moved.
use_when: Old and new consumers or binaries must coexist during an incompatible interface change
Large stored datasets and live writers cannot migrate in one coordinated instant
API, schema or reporting model dependencies have different release schedules
not_ideal_when: A small internal interface and all callers can change atomically
A rehearsed maintenance window costs less than prolonged coexistence
There is no owner or credible path to eventual contraction
prerequisites: Known reader/writer/recovery dependencies and accountable owners
One authoritative meaning/state and a bridge for coexistence
Backfill, concurrency, reconciliation and recovery rules where physical copies exist
example_user_queries: A field rename breaks older application instances during rolling deployment.
We cannot update every consumer of a shared interface at once.
Our new column is populated but older writers keep making it stale.
A delayed historical backfill overwrote a newer live update.
How can an old and new method name use one authoritative value?
The migration job was scheduled but nobody knows whether it actually finished.
A monthly export still depends on the column we plan to remove.
We need to know when it is safe to delete a compatibility bridge.
Rolling back code does not restore data from a dropped column.
A reporting model changes grain and existing reports need time to migrate.

graphics.alt_text: Expand supports both old and new interfaces. Migrate moves consumers while both remain available. A readiness gate checks data, consumers, and recovery obligations before Contract removes the old interface. Removing it is not an automatic consequence of adding the new one.
graphics.caption: The temporary state must be a supported operating state. Contraction follows evidence that required dependencies have moved, not merely successful deployment of the replacement.

graphics.alt_text: A backfill holds account A at revision 10 with standard tier. A live update has already advanced the target to revision 11 with premium tier. A guard rejects the stale revision-10 write, leaving premium at revision 11. This versioned-copy example is separate from the single-value Python API bridge.
graphics.caption: Coexistence alone cannot keep copies consistent. The illustrated guard assumes comparable revisions from one authoritative source per account; ordered deletion handling and durable recovery remain separate requirements.

patterns.title: Branch by Abstraction
patterns.short_description: Replace an implementation incrementally behind a shared abstraction, keeping the system releasable while old and new implementations coexist.
use_when: A supplier replacement or internal restructuring spans several releases
Existing callers can migrate behind an application-owned behavioral boundary
The team must integrate everyday feature work while old and new implementations coexist
not_ideal_when: A small local replacement can be reviewed and delivered together
Implementations cannot coexist safely and coordinated transition is simpler
No owner or credible retirement conditions exist
prerequisites: A useful caller-facing behavioral contract and tests
A coherent implementation-selection boundary and state compatibility plan
Known old usages, resource owners, and evidence-gated retirement
example_user_queries: Replacing our persistence library will take months, but we need to keep shipping features.
A long-lived rewrite branch keeps drifting from the application everyone else is changing.
Every checkout and preview calls the shipping vendor API directly.
How can we move callers behind a stable seam before the replacement is ready?
We need to exercise a new implementation while production still uses the old one.
The new supplier has the same methods but different rounding and failure behavior.
Can we replace one repository at a time without migrating every service together?
Our feature switch changes implementation halfway through a transaction.
We switched the library but scheduled jobs still depend on the old API.
When is it safe to delete the migration adapter and old dependency?

graphics.alt_text: Checkout and basket preview call an application-owned Rates boundary. One configured implementation serves each application instance: the legacy adapter or the new rate engine. Both are checked against the same behavioral contract.
graphics.caption: During migration, callers use one contract and one selected implementation. Coexistence does not require executing both paths for each request.

graphics.alt_text: Four releasable stages: introduce the seam with the old supplier active, build and verify the new supplier alongside it, switch after compatibility evidence, and retire the old supplier after remaining uses and recovery obligations are closed.
graphics.caption: Progress is measured by migrated behavior and retired dependencies. A working replacement is not evidence that every old use is gone.
