patterns.title: Blue-Green Deployment
patterns.short_description: Prepare a release in a separate production-capable environment, then switch incoming traffic to it while retaining the previous environment for a controlled return.
use_when: A routable application can be validated in parallel before serving production traffic
A quick traffic return matters more than the cost of temporary duplicate capacity
Replacing an environment is more reliable than repairing an in-place installation
not_ideal_when: A normal rolling update already provides adequate recovery and availability
Incompatible state changes cannot be separated from the environment switch
A rehearsed maintenance window is simpler and acceptable
prerequisites: Production-capable candidate and retained recovery capacity
Readiness, routing convergence, drain and background-job ownership rules
Data compatibility and an explicit recovery window with accountable promotion owners
example_user_queries: Updating the live application in place leaves us rebuilding it during an outage.
We want to verify the candidate environment before routing customers to it.
How can we direct new requests to a release without killing requests already running?
We need a quick return to the previous application version if promotion fails.
Our old deployment still exists but cannot read the data written by the new version.
Switching the web load balancer did not stop the old background jobs from sending messages.
Long-lived connections remain on the old environment after we move new traffic.
We need to know when it is safe to release the retained environment’s capacity.
The candidate passed startup checks but its cold cache cannot handle production load.
We cloned the database before release and now rolling back would lose later orders.

graphics.alt_text: Before cutover, the router sends new requests to blue version 1 while green version 2 is validated. After cutover, new requests go to green; an already admitted request can still complete on blue. The shared compatible data store remains outside the application-environment boundary.
graphics.caption: Changing the destination of new traffic does not move requests already executing. This example switches application environments while retaining one compatible shared data store.

graphics.alt_text: A recovery gate asks whether the retained old environment is ready, adequately provisioned, and compatible with current data. If it is eligible, route future traffic back and drain candidate work. If it is not, hold the return and use the separately planned recovery procedure; neither branch undoes committed effects.
graphics.caption: Retaining old capacity makes a return possible. Eligibility and current data determine whether that return is safe; already committed effects need their own recovery policy.

patterns.title: Canary Release
patterns.short_description: Give a candidate release a limited share of real traffic, evaluate release-specific evidence, and expand, hold, or restore the incumbent under explicit rules.
use_when: Prior checks pass but actual production serving or outcome behavior remains uncertain
Work can be partitioned meaningfully and limited candidate exposure is acceptable
An incumbent can take traffic back under compatible current-state conditions
not_ideal_when: Even limited candidate mistakes are unacceptable
Traffic or outcome delays cannot support the intended release conclusion
No trustworthy version-attributed monitoring or viable restoration path exists
prerequisites: Identified release artifacts and stable assignment where journeys need consistency
Explicit advance/hold/restore policy, observation bounds and accountable ownership
Healthy retained capacity plus protocol and data compatibility for restoration
example_user_queries: A service passes staging but we cannot tell how it behaves with real customer traffic.
We want to expose a new release gradually instead of replacing every instance at once.
Our endpoint average looks healthy while requests to the new version are failing.
We need explicit rules for expanding, pausing, or restoring release traffic.
The candidate has too few requests and someone wants to call the canary successful.
Quality labels arrive late even though the new model returns successful responses.
Customers keep moving between versions halfway through a journey.
We paused a rollout but users are still being exposed to the faulty candidate.
More customers reached the bad version while the rollback was taking effect.
We need to keep the incumbent ready and data-compatible until the recovery window closes.

graphics.alt_text: A router assigns a limited share of real requests to the candidate and the remainder to the incumbent. Separate release metrics reach an evidence gate that chooses expansion, a bounded hold, or restoration of future traffic.
graphics.caption: Both versions serve real users. Release-specific evidence controls the next allocation; elapsed time alone does not approve expansion.

The combined endpoint rate is five percent, but the candidate rate is twelve percent. Thirty-five candidate requests remain part of the exposure after future candidate traffic becomes zero.

patterns.short_description: Move a versioned release artifact through ordered validation and deployment stages, accumulating evidence before allowing promotion to the next environment.

Teams cannot establish which package passed which checks
Comprehensive validation must coexist with fast initial feedback
not_ideal_when: A simple complete build/test/deploy path already suffices
Extra environments and manual gates have no concrete purpose

An older deployment run finished late and overwrote a newer release.
Retrying deployment leaves partially applied changes behind.

patterns.title: Golden Master / Approval Testing
patterns.short_description: Compare a reproducible observed result with an explicitly reviewed baseline, and require deliberate review when the result changes.
use_when: A refactoring changes a huge legacy report and our tests check only its heading.

not_ideal_when: A simpler direct check already supplies the needed evidence
prerequisites: Explicit behavior and observation boundaries

example_user_queries: A refactoring changes a huge legacy report and our tests check only its heading.
We need to preserve observed behavior before fixing it separately.
A generated document is easier to review as a complete result than hundreds of assertions.
Snapshot updates are automatically accepting regressions.
Timestamps make every report comparison fail even when meaningful fields agree.
Our normalizer removed an amount that should have exposed a bug.
We need received output saved separately from the approved baseline.
A one-cent change should remain visible inside a large formatting diff.
Parallel snapshot tests overwrite each other’s received files.
Stored test reports must not contain production secrets.

graphics.alt_text: A fixed scenario produces an actual report that is compared with a reviewed approved file. A mismatch writes a separate received file and a diff. Only a deliberate review can replace the approved baseline; the normal test never updates it.
graphics.caption: Keep observation and approval separate. A failed comparison is evidence to inspect, not permission to bless the new output automatically.
